questions.question: Homeostasis is called as dynamic equilibrium because______
options: All variables are given equal importance
Can achieve a constancy in extreme environmental challenge
The set-point for all homeostatic variables is always fixed
Body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits
questions.answer: D. Body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits
questions.explanation:
Homeostasis is called dynamic equilibrium because the body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits. It describes the maintenance of nearly constant conditions in the internal environment despite changes in the outside world.

A number of variables such as body temperature, blood sugar levels, blood pH, etc. are regulated within a range of values (homeostatic ranges) and not at fixed values.

These variables are not given equal importance. There is a hierarchy of importance so that the constancy of certain variables may be altered markedly to maintain others within their normal range. For example, respiratory or metabolic compensation to maintain blood pH.

The disruption of homeostasis either due to extreme environmental challenge or a breakdown of internal homeostatic mechanisms is termed as a disease.

questions.question: Which is a component of homeostatic control system?
questions.explanation:
Stimulus, receptor and effector are all components of a homeostatic control system.

Components of homeostasis include:

• Stimulus - It is a detectable change in the internal or external environment, such as change in temperature.

• Receptor - It detects environmental changes.

• Integrating centre

• Effector - It is an organ or cell that acts in response to a stimulus.

questions.question: Feedback regulation is seen in ______
options: The increased heart rate that occurs in an athlete just before a sprint begins
Smell of food triggers secretion of salivary and gastric juices
An increase in insulin before glucose absorption has raised blood glucose levels
The increased heart rate in response to a decrease in blood pressure
questions.answer: D. The increased heart rate in response to a decrease in blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Feedback regulation is seen in the increased heart rate in response to a decrease in blood pressure. This is because, in feedback regulation, the homeostatic response (increased heart rate) occurs after the change (decrease in blood pressure) has occurred.

On the other hand, in feedforward regulation, the homeostatic responses take place before the change has occurred. This is done in anticipation of the change to minimize fluctuations. Examples of feedforward regulation include:

• The increased heart rate that occurs in an athlete just before a sprint begins.

• The smell of food triggers the secretion of salivary and gastric juices.

• An increase in insulin before glucose absorption has raised blood glucose levels.

questions.question: Positive feedback is seen in all except_____
questions.explanation:
Positive feedback is seen in all except gastric secretion. It is under negative feedback control.

Negative feedback consists of certain changes that affect a deficient or excessive variable to pull it back to a certain mean value to maintain homeostasis. Most processes in the body are under negative feedback. For example, an increase in gastric acids leading to a decrease in gastric secretion.

Positive feedback consists of changes that affect a variable to push it further away from a certain mean value. For example, an increase in LH leading to a further increase in LH. Instances, where positive feedback plays an important role are:

• Clotting of blood

• Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

• LH Surge

• Action potential

• Shock

• Parturition

questions.question: On infusion of a large volume of blood, the MAP rises from 100 mmHg to 175 mmHg. Due to the baroreceptor feedback mechanism, the MAP falls down to 125 mmHg. Calculate the gain of the feedback system.
questions.explanation:
The gain of the feedback system in the above case is -2.

The gain of the system is then calculated by using the following formula:

Gain = C/E

Here, C is correction achieved from the deviated value and E is the remaining error post-correction.

Calculation

• The original value in the given case is 100 mmHg.

• The deviated value in the given case is 175 mmHg.

• The corrected value in the given case is 125 mmHg.

• C is given by correction achieved from deviated value, Corrected value - Deviated value = 125 - 175 = -50 mmHg.

• E is given by the remaining error post-correction, Corrected value - Original value = 125 - 100 = 25 mmHg.

• Gain = -50/25 = -2.

The negative symbol indicates that the homeostatic mechanism acts in a direction opposite to the initial deviation.

questions.question: Plasma membrane in eukaryotes is made up of all except _______
questions.explanation:
Plasma membrane in eukaryotes does not contain triglycerides.

The plasma membrane is composed almost entirely of proteins and lipids. The major lipids include:

• Phospholipids: Lecithin, cephalin, phosphatidylserine

• Sphingolipids: Sphingomyelin

• Cholesterol

questions.question: Membrane fluidity is increased by ____.
questions.explanation:
Membrane fluidity is increased by linoleic acid, an unsaturated fatty acid. All other options are saturated fatty acids.

Longer and saturated fatty acids decrease the fluidity because their side chains are straight and interact more strongly with each other. Conversely, unsaturated fatty acids increase the fluidity because their side chains are kinked and less compact.

Cholesterol, also known as fluidity buffer helps to maintain the fluidity of the cell membrane.

questions.question: The sequence of vesicular transport in a cell is
questions.answer: D. ER - Cis - Trans - Cell membrane
questions.explanation:
The sequence of vesicular transport in a cell is ER - Cis - Trans - Cell membrane.

Rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) - It is the site of protein synthesis. Proteins are taken to the Golgi apparatus through transport vesicles.

Cis end of Golgi apparatus - Also called as receiving end, it is closest to RER

Trans end of Golgi apparatus - Also called as releasing end, it is furthest away from RER.

Cell membrane - Synthesised proteins within secretory vesicles are released into the extracellular space through the process of exocytosis.

questions.question: All of the following are enzyme markers of mitochondria except____
questions.explanation: 5’ Nucleotidase is an enzyme marker for plasma membrane. All the other options are mitochondrial enzyme markers.

questions.question: Which of the following will test negative for all mitochondrial markers?
questions.explanation:
Mature red blood cells will test negative for all mitochondrial markers are as they do not have mitochondria.

Lack of mitochondria is the reason why red blood cells exclusively use anaerobic glycolysis to generate ATP.

questions.question: Which is the characteristic enzyme present in peroxisome?
questions.explanation: Catalase is the characteristic enzyme of peroxisomes. All other are lysosomal enzymes.

questions.question: Gap junctions are found in all except ______
questions.explanation:
Gap junctions are absent in adult skeletal muscles.

Gap junctions are intercellular connections with a channel in between. They are present in excitable tissues such as cardiac muscle, smooth muscle and neurons but not in skeletal muscles.

questions.question: Tight junctions are not seen in ____.
questions.explanation:
Tight junctions are not seen in cardiac muscle.

Tight junctions form a water-tight seal between cells. They are characteristically seen in the following:

• Intestinal mucosa

• Renal tubules

• Choroid plexus

• Sertoli cells

Functions of tight junctions are:

• Prevents the diffusion of macromolecules between cells.

• Maintains cell polarity.

• Seals the paracellular pathway.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a cell adhesion molecule (CAM)?
questions.explanation:
Spectrin is a cytoskeletal protein but not a cell adhesion molecule.

Cells are attached to each other or to the basal lamina by cell adhesion molecules (CAMs). Some important classes of CAMs are:

• Integrins: heterodimers that bind to various receptors

• IgG superfamily of immunoglobulins

• Cadherins: Ca2+-dependent molecules that mediate cell-to-cell adhesion by homophilic reactions

• Selectins which have lectin-like domains that bind carbohydrates

Clinical significance

• Cancer cells have abnormal CAMs and hence cause decreased cell adhesion and allow individual cancer cells to detach from the parent cancer.

• The decrease in the amount of E-cadherin maybe the reason for early metastasis of numerous tumors.

questions.question: Identify the incorrectly matched pair of intercellular connections and their structural units
questions.explanation:
Gap junctions are made of connexons. Connexons are in turn made of units called connexins.

The different intercellular connections and their structural units are given below:

Intercellular connections

questions.question: The force-generating proteins are _____.
questions.explanation:
The force-generating proteins are dynein and kinesin.

There are three superfamilies of proteins namely kinesin, dynein, myosin referred to as molecular motors.

The molecular motors are the force generating proteins as they move proteins, organelles, and other cell parts (collectively referred to as “cargo”) to all parts of the cell.

questions.question: An absent dynein arm in cilia can lead to all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
An absent dynein arm in cilia leads to primary ciliary dyskinesia. Kartagener syndrome is a primary ciliary dyskinesia characterized by the classical triad of situs inversus, chronic sinusitis, and bronchiectasis.

Ciliocytophthoria is the degradation of ciliated cells due to viral infections. It is not seen in primary ciliary dyskinesia.

questions.explanation:

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a polypeptide hormone?
questions.explanation:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is an example of a polypeptide hormone.

Cortisol is a steroid hormone. Adrenaline and thyroxine are derivatives of the amino acid tyrosine.

questions.question: Which of the following hormone is not stored before release?
questions.explanation:
Cortisol is not stored before release.

Usually, the polypeptide and protein hormones such as insulin, thyroxine or renin are stored in secretory vesicles before release. They are synthesized as much larger polypeptide chains (preprohormones) that are biologically inactive and then processed intracellularly by specific proteases to yield the final hormone molecule which is stored in the secretory vesicle until needed.

On the other hand, steroid hormones such as cortisol are synthesised as needed and are not stored. They are lipid soluble and easily diffuse across cell membrane to enter the interstitial fluid and then blood.

questions.question: Downregulation of receptors occurs due to all except_____
questions.answer: D. Decreased level of stimulating hormone
questions.explanation:
Downregulation of receptors occurs due to internalisation, inactivation of receptors or desensitisation.

A decrease in the level of stimulating hormones generally leads to an increase in the level of active receptors. This is called upregulation of receptors.

On the other hand, an increase in the level of stimulating hormones generally leads to a decrease in the level of active receptors. This is called downregulation of receptors.

Downregulation of receptors can occur by one of the following mechanisms:

• Desensitisation - Receptors undergo chemical modifications that make them less responsive.

• Internalisation - It is the temporary sequestration of the cell membrane receptors to the inside of the cell, away from the action of hormones. Following internalisation, the receptors are either destroyed or recycled.

• Inactivation of receptors.

• Decreased production of receptors.

questions.question: Receptors on cell membrane that activate ion channel after binding with agonists are_____
questions.explanation:
Nicotinic cholinergic receptors activate an ion channel after binding with its agonist. These receptors are called ligand-gated channels or ionotropic receptors.

Receptors for neurotransmitters are classified into two broad families based on structure and function. They are:

• Ligand-gated channels (Ionotropic receptors)

• When bound to these receptors, a membrane channel is opened leading to a brief increase in ionic conductance.

• Important for fast synaptic transmission.

• Examples - GABAA, GABAC, Nicotinic cholinergic, Glycine and Serotonin (5HT3 subtype).

• G-protein coupled receptors (Metabotropic receptors)

• When bound to these receptors, secondary messengers are released that modulate voltage-gated channels on neuronal membranes.

• Examples - GABAB, Muscarinic cholinergic, Catecholamines, Serotonin (all subtypes except 5HT3) and opioid receptors.

questions.question: Adrenaline, noradrenaline and dopamine act through_____
questions.explanation:
Adrenaline, noradrenaline and dopamine act through a 7 pass receptor called G-protein coupled receptor (GPCR).

The catecholamines act through GPCRs which are cell membrane receptors that span across the membrane 7 times hence called seven helix or serpentine receptors.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true about the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)?
options: G proteins bind to hormones on the surface of the nucleus.
All the three subunits α, β, and ɣ should bind to each other for G proteins to act.
G proteins act as inhibitory or excitatory because of differences in α subunit.
G protein is bound to GTP in resting state.
questions.answer: C. G proteins act as inhibitory or excitatory because of differences in α subunit.
questions.explanation:
G proteins act as inhibitory or excitatory because of differences in α subunit.

G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell membrane receptors that span across the membrane 7 times hence called seven helix or serpentine receptors.

G proteins have 3 subunits (α,β and ɣ). In its resting state, α subunit is bound to GDP.

Upon ligand binding to GPCR, it undergoes a conformational change that activates G protein within the cell. The α subunit dissociates and in turn alters the activity of second messengers such as cAMP, cGMP or Ca2+.

Once the ligand is unbound, the intrinsic GTPase activity of the α subunit converts GTP to GDP. This leads to reassociation of α with the β-ɣ subunit and termination of effector activation.

questions.question: Action of α subunit of G protein is_____
questions.answer: A. Breakdown of GTP to GDP
questions.explanation:
The action of α subunit of G protein is the breakdown of GTP to GDP as it has an intrinsic GTPase activity.

Guanine exchange factors (GEFs) convert GDP to GTP by nucleotide exchange.

G proteins can be either stimulatory (GS) or inhibitory (Gi) with respect to the production of the 2nd messenger cAMP by the enzyme adenylyl cyclase. Stimulatory or inhibitory activity resides in the α subunit.

• Cholera toxin acts on α subunit of GS

• Pertussis toxin acts on α subunit of Gi

questions.question: PDGF acts through which of the following signaling pathways?
questions.explanation:
PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) acts through the activation of tyrosine kinases.

All growth factors that foster the multiplication or development of various types of cells act through the activation of tyrosine kinases.

questions.question: Which hormone acts on JAK-STAT kinase receptor?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone acts on JAK-STAT receptors.

Janus tyrosine kinase receptors (JAK-STAT) serves as receptors for:

• Growth hormone

• Prolactin

• Erythropoietin

• Leptin

Thyroxine acts on nuclear receptors. TSH and FSH act on G protein-coupled receptors.

questions.question: All of the following act through cell surface receptors except____
questions.explanation: Cortisol is a steroid hormone and acts on intracellular (cytoplasmic) receptor.

questions.question: Steroid hormone receptors have an attachment site for all except_____
questions.explanation:
Steroid hormone receptors have an attachment site for steroid hormone, hormone-responsive element, and transcription activators, but not transcription repressors.

Transcription repressors are proteins that bind to specific sites on DNA and prevent transcription of nearby genes.

questions.question: True statement about second messengers is _____
options: Are substances that interact with first messengers outside cells.
Mediate the intracellular responses to many different hormones and neurotransmitters
Are hormones secreted by cells in response to stimulation by another hormone
Are substances that bind to first messengers in the cell membrane.
questions.answer: B. Mediate the intracellular responses to many different hormones and neurotransmitters
questions.explanation:
Second messengers mediate the intracellular responses to many different hormones and neurotransmitters.

Cell surface receptors are substances that interact with the first messengers which are hormones and neurotransmitters.

The second messengers are the intracellular signalling molecules. They bring about many short-term changes in cell function by altering enzyme function, triggering exocytosis, and other physiological effects. They can also lead to the alteration of transcription of various genes (long term effect).

Examples of second messengers are cAMP, cGMP, Ca2+ and IP3-DAG (Inositol triphosphate and diacylglycerol).

questions.question: Which one of the following acts as a second messenger?
questions.explanation:
Among the following calcium (Ca2+) acts as a second messenger.

Increased cytoplasmic Ca2+ binds to and activates calcium-binding proteins (calmodulin, troponin) or activate protein kinases (or phospholipase C) to bring about physiological effects.

Cytoplasmic Ca2+ is increased by:

• Direct entry of Ca2+ from the ECF through Ca2+ channels that could be ligand-gated, voltage-gated or stretch-activated (mechanically gated).

• Mobilisation of Ca2+ that are stored in high concentrations in the endoplasmic reticulum by other second messengers such as IP3-DAG (Inositol triphosphate and diacylglycerol).

questions.question: A primigravida with 38 completed weeks of gestation has gone into labor. Oxytocin was started to augment labor. The second messenger system through which oxytocin acts is _____
questions.explanation:
The second messenger system through which oxytocin acts is the phospholipase C system.

It activates the enzyme phospholipase C which breaks down some phospholipids in the cell membrane into IP3 (phosphoinositol triphosphate) and DAG (diacylglycerol). DAG then activates protein kinase C and IP3 mobilises Ca2+ from mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum to bring about smooth muscle contraction and other cellular responses.

questions.question: cAMP is the exclusive second messenger for all the following except _________
questions.explanation:
Vasopressin does not use cAMP exclusively.

Vasopressin (ADH) acts on at least 3 kinds of receptors: V1A, V1B and V2

• All the 3 are G-protein coupled receptors

• V1A and V1B receptors (Gq) act through IP3 as a second messenger, to increase the intracellular calcium concentration

• V2 receptors (Gs) use cAMP as a second messenger

cAMP is the exclusive second messenger for dopamine, corticotropin and glucagon.

Dopamine has 5 receptors (D1, D2, D3, D4, D5)

• all use cAMP as second messengers

• D1, D5 act by increasing cAMP

• D2, D3, D4 act by decreasing cAMP

questions.question: Which of the following is not a second messenger?
questions.explanation:
Guanylyl cyclase is the enzyme that catalyzes the formation of cGMP. It is cGMP that acts as the second messenger.

cAMP, IP3 and DAG are all second messengers.

questions.question: Activation of protein kinase C causes_____
questions.explanation:
Activation of protein kinase C causes phosphorylation of proteins

Cellular Phosphorylation is under the control of two groups of proteins:

• Kinases

• enzymes that catalyse the phosphorylation of tyrosine or serine residues in protein

• Example- Protein Kinase A, Protein Kinase C, Ca2+/Calmodulin Kinase

• Phosphatases

• that catalyses the dephosphorylation of tyrosine or serine residues in the protein

Kinases play important roles in regulating cellular physiology, including cell growth and cell death. Philadelphia chromosome, t(9:22) or the bcr-abl fusion gene codes for an abnormal kinase that leads to chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). The drug imatinib was developed to block the tyrosine kinase activity of bcr-abl protein and is an effective treatment option for CML.

On genetic studies, it was found that there is a gain of function mutation of G Protein. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:

questions.question: Transport of lipid-soluble substances across the cell membrane occurs via which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Lipid-soluble substances are transported across the cell membrane via diffusion.

• The rate of diffusion depends directly on lipid solubility.

• Characteristics of simple diffusion

• The only form of transport that is not carrier-mediated

• Occurs down an electrochemical gradient (“downhill”)

• Does not require metabolic energy and therefore is passive

• Permeability

• Describes the ease with which a solute diffuses through a membrane

• Depends on the characteristics of the solute and the membrane

• Small hydrophobic solutes (e.g., O2) have the highest permeabilities in lipid membranes.

• Hydrophilic solutes (e.g., Na+) must cross cell membranes through water-filled channels, or pores. If the solute is an ion, then its flux will depend on both the concentration difference and the potential difference across the membrane.

questions.question: Which of the following will diffuse more rapidly through phospholipid membranes?
questions.explanation:
Among the following substances, oxygen diffuses more rapidly through phospholipid membranes as it is a lipid-soluble substance.

Phospholipid membranes are:

• Permeable to lipid-soluble substances (e.g., O2, CO2, NH3, steroid hormones)

• Impermeable to water-soluble substances (e.g., Na+, Cl-, glucose)

• Semipermeable to water

questions.question: Which of the following is explained by the fick’s law of diffusion?
questions.answer: B. Passive diffusion along concentration gradient
questions.explanation:
Fick’s law of diffusion explains passive diffusion along the concentration gradient.

Fick’s law of diffusion: The magnitude of the diffusing tendency is directly proportional to the cross-sectional area across which diffusion is taking place and the concentration gradient, or chemical gradient, which is the difference in concentration of the diffusing substance divided by the thickness of the membrane.

questions.question: For a membrane permeable substance, the intracellular concentration (IC) is 10 units and extracellular concentration (EC) is 5 units. If the intracellular concentration, surface area of the membrane and thickness of the membrane are doubled, and the EC remains the same, What will be the net effect on the diffusion?
questions.explanation:
The net effect on the diffusion is, it becomes 3x.

The magnitude of the diffusion:

where,

• J = net rate of diffusion

• D = diffusion coefficient

• A = area of the membrane

• Δx = thickness of the membrane or the distance the molecule must travel across for diffusion

• Δc = concentration gradient

In the condition mentioned above, the surface area, the thickness of the membrane and intracellular concentration becomes doubled. This means,

• A is doubled = 2A

• Δx is doubled = 2Δx

• IC is doubled. 10x2= 20 units; EC is 5 units.

So, Δc = 20 - 5 = 15. Δc was 5 with the original concentrations. Hence Δc has been tripled.

Now,

J=-D x 2A x 3Δc/2Δx = 3 x [DA Δc/Δx]

Therefore the diffusion of the substance increases by three-fold.

2nd method :

J = - DA (Δc / Δx )
After applying changes,Δc = intracellular conc. - extracellular conc. = 10 - 5 = 5

Therefore, J1 = - DA (5 / Δx )

After appropriate doublings, New intracellular conc. = 10 * 2 = 20 New extracellular conc. = 5 (since no change) Δc = 20 - 5 = 15

Therefore, J2 = - D 2*A (15 / 2*Δx )

 = - D A (15 / Δx )

Now, J2 / J1 = [- DA (15 / Δx ) ] / [ = - DA (5 / Δx ) ]

 J2 / J1 = 15 / 5

 = 3

Therefore the diffusion of the substance increases by three-fold.

questions.question: Which of the following does not follow transport saturation kinetics?
questions.explanation:
Simple diffusion is not carrier-mediated transport hence do not follow saturation kinetics.

• Facilitated diffusion, primary active transport, and secondary active transport all involve integral membrane proteins and are called carrier-mediated transport.

• All carrier-mediated transport system follows saturation kinetics.

• The figure shows that as the concentration of the diffusing substance increases, the rate of simple diffusion continues to increase proportionately, but in the case of facilitated diffusion, the rate of diffusion cannot rise greater than the transport maximum (Tm). Tm is analogous to the maximum velocity (Vmax) level in enzyme kinetics.

questions.question: Which statement about the facilitated diffusion is true?
questions.explanation:
When carrier proteins help in the movement of substances in the direction of their chemical or electrical gradients (downhill movement), no energy input is required and the process is called facilitated diffusion.

Examples

• GLUT

• Urea Transporters :

• UTA 1, 2, 3, 4 in Kidney

• UTB in RBC

• Amino Acid Transporters

Other options are wrong because:

• Facilitated diffusion is a type of passive transport.

• It follows saturation kinetics.

• No energy input is required in facilitated diffusion.

questions.question: The movement of which of the following substance across the membrane is most affected by osmotic pressure?
questions.explanation:
The movement of water across the membrane is most affected by osmotic pressure.

Osmotic pressure is the pressure that would have to be applied to prevent the movement of water molecules to the more concentrated solution i.e. to a region in which there is higher concentration of a solute to which the membrane is impermeable.

• Osmotic pressure is calculated by Vant Hoff’s law.

questions.question: Osmolarity is defined as _______
questions.answer: A. Number of osmole per litre
questions.explanation:
Difference between osmolarity & osmolality:

• Osmolarity is the number of osmoles per litre of solution,

• Osmolality is the number of osmoles per kilogram of solvent.

• Therefore, osmolarity is affected by the volume of the various solutes in the solution and the temperature, while the osmolality is not.

questions.question: Passive transfer of only solvent occurs in ______
questions.explanation:
Passive transfer of the only solvent occurs in Osmosis.

The diffusion of solvent molecules into a region in which there is a higher concentration of a solute to which the membrane is impermeable is called osmosis.

Note: Membrane is impermeable to the solute.

questions.question: A 47-year-old diabetic man takes a low-dose aspirin daily due to cardiovascular risk. The absorption of aspirin in the stomach is an example of which type of transport?
questions.explanation:
The absorption of salicylates like aspirin in the stomach is an example of nonionic diffusion.

• Some weak acids and bases are quite soluble in cell membranes in the undissociated form, but they cannot cross membranes in the charged (i.e. dissociated) form. Consequently, molecules of the undissociated substance diffuse from one side of the membrane to the other and then dissociate. This phenomenon is called nonionic diffusion.

Examples

• Ammonia excretion in collecting ducts

• Excretion of weak acids and bases in the kidney

• Absorption of salicylates in the stomach

• Absorption of bile acids in the distal ileum

questions.question: Energy is required in which of the following mode of transport.
questions.explanation: When a carrier protein transports substances against their electrical and chemical gradients (uphill movement) it requires energy and this type of transport is called active transport.

questions.question: Movement of calcium from the cytosol to the extracellular space takes place by
questions.explanation:
The movement of calcium from the cytosol to the extracellular space takes place by primary active transport.

Two primary active transport calcium pumps maintain low intracellular calcium levels. One pumps calcium ions to the extracellular space and another to the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Calcium transport also takes place via secondary active transport. A sodium-calcium exchanger/antiporter moves sodium ions to the interior and calcium ions to the exterior.

questions.question: Na+-K+ ATP pump uses ________
questions.explanation:
Na+- K+ ATPase or Na+-K+ ATP pump catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and uses the energy to extrude three Na+ from the cell and take two K+ into the cell for each molecule of ATP hydrolyzed.

Sodium-Potassium Pump/ Na+– K+ Pump:

• Carrier protein located on the plasma membrane of all cells

• Pumps 3 Na+ out of the cell & 2 K+ into the cell (coupling ratio 3:2)

• 2 separate globular proteins:

• Larger- α subunit & smaller- β subunit, α subunit concerned with Na+- K+ transport

• Binding sites on α subunit:

• 3 intracellular sites- for Na+, ATP, and one phosphorylation site

• 2 extracellular sites- for K+ and oubain

Mechanism Of Action

Functions:

• Controlling Cell Volume.

• Electrogenic Nature- maintains Resting membrane potential

• The energy from the Na+–K+ pump also indirectly serves as the energy source for secondary active transport.

Regulation:

• Pump activity is altered by second messenger molecules eg. cAMP, DAG

• Stimulated by thyroid hormones, insulin and aldosterone

• Inhibition by dopamine ,digitalis glycosides, ouabain

questions.question: Primary active transport is mediated by which one of the following enzymes?
questions.explanation:
In active transport the energy is provided almost exclusively by the hydrolysis of ATP. Hence many carrier molecules are ATPases (eg. Na+-K+-ATPase), enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of ATP.

PRIMARY ACTIVE TRANSPORT
SECONDARY ACTIVE TRANSPORT

Requires direct input of metabolic energy in the form of adenosine triphosphate (ATP)
The transport of two or more solutes is coupled and metabolic energy is provided indirectly from the Na+ gradient that is maintained across cell membranes by Na+-K+-ATPase pump

a) Na+-K+-ATPase or sodium potassium pump

b) Ca2+ -ATPase

c) H+-ATPase or proton pump d) H+-K+-ATPase

a) Na+- glucose cotransport

b) Na+-Ca2+ counter transport

questions.question: For Na+-K+ ATPase coupling ratio is _____
questions.explanation:
Na+-K+ ATPase or Na+-K+ ATP pump is an electrogenic pump in that it moves three positive charges out of the cell for each two that it moves in, and it is therefore said to have a coupling ratio of 3:2.

Note:

• Na+-K+ ATP pump is found in almost all parts of the body, and it catalyzes the hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and uses the energy for its activity

• It is one of the major energy using process in the body. On an average, it accounts for 24% of the energy utilized by the cells, and in neurons it accounts for 70%. Thus, it accounts for large share in basal metabolism

questions.question: A 40-year-old diabetic man has been prescribed empagliflozin. Which of the following processes will most likely be affected by this drug?
questions.explanation:
Empagliflozin is an SGLT-2 inhibitor. SGLT-2 or sodium-glucose transport protein 2 is an example of a cotransporter that plays a key role in glucose absorption from renal tubule by secondary active transport. This process is blocked by SGLT-2 inhibitors, leading to renal loss of glucose and improved glycemic control.

• A special property of the transport protein involved in secondary active transport is that a conformational change to allow Na+ movement to the interior will not occur until a glucose molecule also attaches to the transport protein. When they both become attached, the conformational change takes place automatically, and the Na+ and glucose are transported to the inside of the cell at the same time.

• The figure shows glucose is transported uphill and Na+ is transported downhill. Energy derived from the downhill movement of Na+ is maintained by the Na+-K+ ATPase pump on the basolateral side.

questions.question: A 40-year-old lady is diagnosed with Lambart- Eaton syndrome. Radioimmunoassay reveals the presence of serum antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following process will be affected as a result of this pathology?
questions.explanation:
Exocytosis of neurotransmitters at the nerve terminals will be affected as a result of antibodies against voltage-gated calcium channels.

After an action potential reaches the terminal endings of a nerve, the influx of Ca2+ via voltage-gated calcium channels leads to the fusion of intracellular vesicles with cell membranes. This results in the release of neurotransmitters into the synaptic space. This process will be impaired in the case of Lambert-eaton syndrome.

Exocytosis is the extrusion of membrane-bound vesicles. In exocytosis, intracellular vesicles move to the cell membrane, fuse with it and then release their contents to the extracellular fluid. Solute and water can be released from the cell via vesicles by the process of exocytosis.

Exocytosis can be:

Constitutive exocytosis:

• Involves prompt transport of proteins to the cell membrane in vesicles, with little or no processing or storage

• Examples

• Goblet cells in the intestine continuously to release mucus

• Fibroblasts in connective tissue release collagen

Regulated/ Non constitutive exocytosis:

• Here the proteins from golgi apparatus initially enter the secretory granules, where the processing of prohormones to mature hormones occurs before exocytosis

• Examples

• Endocrine cells, hormones are stored in secretory vesicles and released in response to a signal from outside the cell.

• To insert proteins into the cell membrane like aquaporin insertion

Note:

• The term ‘regulated exocytosis’ is misleading because even constitutive exocytosis is regulated.

• Exocytosis involves two families of proteins: Rabs, which help vesicles dock onto the membrane, and SNAREs, which facilitate membrane fusion.

• This is Ca2+ -dependent process

• Exocytosis, like endocytosis, requires energy in the form of ATP.

questions.question: Which pathway is called regulated pathway?
questions.explanation:
The non constitutive pathway of exocytosis is called the regulated pathway.

Exocytosis can be either constitutive or non constitutive(regulated):

• Regulated or nonconstitutive pathway: Proteins from the Golgi apparatus initially enter secretory granules, where processing of prohormones to the mature hormones occurs before exocytosis.

• Constitutive pathway: Involves the prompt transport of proteins to the cell membrane in vesicles, with little or no processing or storage.

questions.question: A 30-year-old gentleman is diagnosed with elevated blood cholesterol levels. A defect in a process that involves the protein 'clathrin' is being suspected. Which of the following process will be most likely affected by this defect?
questions.explanation:
Receptor-mediated endocytosis takes place in coated pits or indentations where the cytoplasmic side of the membrane has high concentrations of protein. The most common protein found in coated pits is clathrin.

A GTP binding protein dynamin is involved in pinching off the vesicle formed in clathrin-mediated endocytosis

Importance:

• Internalisation of many receptors and ligands bound to them eg. LDL, Nerve Growth Factor.

• Receptor-mediated endocytosis transports a variety of substances including protein hormones, growth factors, antibodies, and plasma proteins that serve as carriers for iron and cholesterol.

• Synaptic function

• Abnormalities in receptor-mediated removal of cholesterol from the blood are associated with elevated plasma cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about secretory vesicle transport?
questions.answer: B. No relation with concentration gradient
questions.explanation:
Vesicular transport has no relation to the concentration gradient.

Vesicular transport requires energy expenditure by the cell, so this is an active method of membrane transport. Energy is needed to accomplish vesicle formation and vesicle movement within the cell.

questions.question: Transcytosis occurs in which of the following cell types?
questions.explanation:
Transcytosis is seen in epithelial cells of intestine. Transcytosis is endocytosis across one membrane of the cell followed by exocytosis across the opposite membrane.

Transcytosis across epithelia or endothelia: Some molecules, such as proteins, are too large to diffuse through the membrane or cross the membrane transporters of epithelia. Instead they are moved across epithelia by transcytosis.

Steps:

• The molecule is brought into the epithelial cell via receptor-mediated endocytosis.

• The resulting vesicle attaches to microtubules in the cells cytoskeleton and is transported across the cell by vesicular transport.

• At the opposite side of the epithelium, the contents of the vesicle are expelled into the interstitial fluid by exocytosis.

Significance:

• Transcytosis makes it possible for large proteins to move across an epithelium and remain intact.

• It is the means by which infants absorb maternal antibodies in breast milk. The antibodies are absorbed on the apical surface of the infant’s intestinal epithelium and then released into the extracellular fluid.

questions.question: Which of the following ion is used in exocytosis?
questions.explanation: As exocytosis, begins → ↑in intracellular Ca2+ → Ca2+interacts with a calcium sensing protein → secretory vesicle docking and fusion → fused area of membrane opens, the vesicle contents diffuse into the extracellular fluid while the vesicle membrane stays behind and becomes part of the cell membrane.

questions.question: A 35-year-old diabetic man is started on an insulin secretagogue. Which of the following ions is required for emeiocytosis or reverse pinocytosis during the insulin secretion process?
questions.explanation:
Emeiocytosis requires Ca2+ directly.

Emeiocytosis is the movement of secretory granules to the plasma membrane of the cell, fusion of the granule surface membrane with the cell membrane, rupture of membranes, and liberation of granular contents into the pericapillary space.

Insulin secretion (as shown in the image below):

• Glucose enters B cells by GLUT-2 transporters.

• It is phosphorylated and metabolized to pyruvate (Pyr) in the cytoplasm.

• The Pyr enters the mitochondria and is metabolized via the citric acid cycle. The ATP formed by oxidative phosphorylation inhibits ATP-sensitive K+ channels, reducing K+ efflux.

• This depolarizes the B cell, and Ca2+ influx is increased. The Ca2+ stimulates the release of insulin by exocytosis. Glutamate (Glu) is also formed, and this primes secretory granules, preparing them for exocytosis.

It is promoted by Ca2+, ↑ K+

It is inhibited by Mg2+, K+ depletion.

The process of emeiocytosis for insulin secretion is depicted in the image below.

questions.question: Which of the following equations is used to calculate the equilibrium potential for an ion?
questions.explanation:
Equilibrium potential for an ion is calculated using the Nernst equation.

When there is a concentration gradient for an ion across the membrane, the ion tends to diffuse down the concentration gradient. The electric potential that exactly opposes this net diffusion is called the equilibrium potential for that ion. This is calculated using the Nernst equation.

It is expressed as the potential inside the cell (intracellular potential relative to the extracellular potential).

To calculate the value of the equilibrium potential:

Note: In this formula, the choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign ( +/- ). Mathematically, log (100/10) = 1 and log (10/100) = - 1. Hence, changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same.

This equation is used only to derive the numerical value of the potential. It is NOT used to derive the sign/charge (+/-).

The sign/charge is derived from logic:

• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater outside, then the + ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more + relatively. Hence, the potential will be positive.

• In a positive (+) ion, if the concentration of the + ion is greater inside, then the + ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more - relatively (as + ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be negative.

• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater outside, then the - ion moves from outside to inside. The intracellular potential becomes more - relatively. Hence the potential will be negative.

• In a negative (-) ion, if the concentration of the - ion is greater inside, then the - ion moves from inside to outside. The intracellular potential becomes more + relatively (as - ion moves outside). Hence the potential will be positive.

questions.question: Which of the following is used to calculate the equilibrium potential for diffusion of multiple ions?
questions.explanation:
The Goldman equation is used to calculate the diffusion potential when the membrane is permeable to several different ions.

Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation

Here,

• P= permeability of the membrane to each ion, and

• C= concentrations of the respective ions on the inside (i) and outside (o) of the membrane.

The Na+, K+ and Cl- are the most important ions involved in the development of membrane potentials in nerve fibres and muscle fibres.

questions.question: Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium explains the ______
options: Effect of one non-diffusible ion on the distribution of other non-diffusible ions
Effect of one permeant ion on the distribution of other permeant ions
Effect of a permeant ion on the distribution of nondiffusible ions
Effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions
questions.answer: D. Effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions
questions.explanation:
Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium explains the effect of a non-diffusible ion on the distribution of permeant ions.

Consider the situation depicted below,

The membrane is permeable to K+ and Cl-. However, it is impermeable to the proteins. The impermeable protein molecules hinder the movement of K+ (negative charge of the proteins holding back positive charge of the K+) and favor the movement of Cl- (like charges repel). According to the Gibbs-Donnan equation, at equilibrium, the concentration ratios of diffusible ions are equal across the membrane.

questions.question: Extracellular concentration of a positive ion (with valency = 1) is 100mmol/L and its intracellular concentration is 10mmol/L, the potential across the membrane using Nernst equation is (mV)_______
questions.explanation:
The potential of a positive ion across the membrane using Nernst equation is +60mV.

Where, z is valency in the formula.

Deriving the numerical value:

EMF = 61/1 *log 10/100

 = 61

The choice of concentration of the ion placed in the numerator and denominator does not matter because the formula is only used to derive the numerical value and not the sign ( +/- ). Mathematically, log (100/10) = 1 and log (10/100) = - 1. Hence, changing the numerator and denominator only changes the sign and the numerical value remains the same.

Deciding the sign/charge: A positive ion with greater concentration extracellularly will try to diffuse inside the cell. A positive intracellular potential is required to prevent this. Hence the sign/charge (potential) is positive (+).

Hence, the potential across the membrane using the Nernst equation is +60mV (the closest answer chosen).

questions.question: Extracellular concentration of a negative ion (with valency = 1) is 10mmol/L and its intracellular concentration is 100mmol/L. The equilibrium potential for this ion using Nernst equation is (mV) _____
questions.explanation:
The equilibrium potential for this negative ion using the Nernst equation is +60mV.

Where, z is valency in the formula.

Deriving the numerical value:

EMF = 61/1 *log 100/10

 = 61

Deciding the sign/charge: A negative ion with greater concentration intracellularly will try to diffuse outside the cell. A positive intracellular potential is required to prevent this. Hence, the potential is positive.

Hence, the Nernst potential is +60mV (the closest answer chosen).

questions.question: What is the Nernst potential for K+ in milivolt (mV)?
questions.explanation:
The Nernst potential for K+ is −90mV.

Note:

• For K+ ions, the concentration gradient is directed outward and the electrical gradient is directed inward.

• In general, all excitable cell membranes at rest are maximally permeable to K+ and thus their RMP is close to equilibrium potential of K+ ion.

questions.question: Which of the following ions have the highest positive equilibrium potential?
questions.explanation: The ion with the highest positive equilibrium potential is Na+ that is +60mV.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a nerve fibre depends on ______
questions.explanation:
The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a nerve fibre depends on the diffusion of both K+ and Na+ and the Na+-K+ ATPase pump.

The most predominant factor, however, is the diffusion of K+ ions. This is because, at rest, the permeability of the membrane of the nerve fibre to K+ ions is almost 100 times greater than that to Na+.

questions.question: Resting membrane potential of the nerve fibre is equal to equilibrium potential of ______
questions.explanation: Resting membrane potential of a nerve fiber is equal to the equilibrium potential of Cl- and is -70mV.

questions.question: Driving force of a charged ion is____
options: Measured membrane potential - calculated equilibrium potential
Measured membrane potential + calculated equilibrium potential
Calculated equilibrium potential - Measured membrane potential
questions.answer: A. Measured membrane potential - calculated equilibrium potential
questions.explanation:
The driving force on a charged ion is measured membrane potential (Em) - calculated equilibrium potential (Ex).

Net driving force (mV) = Em - Ex

where,

Em = Actual membrane potential (mV)

Ex = Equilibrium potential for X (mV)

When the driving force is negative (i.e., Em is more negative than the ion’s equilibrium potential), then

• A cation will enter the cell

• An anion will leave the cell

questions.question: If the membrane potential of this cell is -80mV the driving force is greatest for which ion?
questions.explanation:
The driving force is greatest for Ca2+.

Net driving force is the difference between the membrane potential and the equilibrium potential for that particular ion. Hence Em - EX. Where:

Em = Actual membrane potential (mV) = -80mV

EX = Equilibrium potential for X (mV)

For the respective ions:

E Ca2+ = +120 ; Driving force = -80 – (120) = -200mV

E Na+ = +60 ; Driving force= -80 – (60) =-140mV

E K+ = -90, Driving force = -80 – (-90) =10mV

E Cl-= -70, Driving force = -80 – (-70) =-10mV

Thus, Ca2+ will have the largest driving force and it will move inwards or into the cell.

questions.question: Which of the following techniques is used to study the current flow across single ion channel?
questions.explanation:
The patch-clamp technique is used to record ion current flow through a single protein channel.

In the patch-clamp experiment, a small pipette is carefully maneuvered to seal off a portion of a cell membrane. The pipette has an electrode bathed in an appropriate solution that allows for the recording of electrical changes through any pore in the membrane.

questions.question: What is the effect on the cellular membrane when the extracellular concentration of K+ is decreased?
questions.explanation:
When the extracellular concentration of K+ is decreased (hypokalemia), there is increased negativity of RMP.

RMP predominantly depends on the diffusion of K+ from inside to outside the cell. This diffusion depends on the concentration gradient with the inside of the cell having a larger concentration of K+ ions. When the extracellular concentration of K+ decreases, the concentration gradient for K+ rises. Therefore, more K+ ions diffuse out of the cell. This leaves the inside of the cell more negative relative to the extracellular space. This increases the negativity of the RMP, leaving the membrane hyperpolarised.

When expressed as the percentage of body weight, 40% of body weight is in ICF (2/3rd of 60%), and 20% of body weight is in ECF (1/3rd of 60%).

The 60-40-20 rule is: 60% of body weight is water, 40% is ICF, and 20% is ECF.

questions.question: A 60 kg adult male has a haematocrit reading of 40% and a plasma volume of 3L. What is his total blood volume in L?
questions.explanation:
His total blood volume is 5 litres.

Calculation:

Hematocrit is a percentage, as it is 40% which equals 40/100= 0.4.

(Normally, Total blood volume is 8% of body weight).

questions.question: What is the volume of blood in ml, in a child per kg body weight?
questions.explanation:
The total blood volume of a child is around 75–80 ml/kg.

In the neonatal period, it is 85 ml/kg. It rises to a peak of 105 ml/kg by the end of the first month and then drops progressively over ensuing months.

questions.question: What is the water content of lean body mass is (in mL/100g of tissue)?
questions.explanation:
The water content of lean body tissue is constant at 71–72 mL/100 g of tissue.

Lean body mass = Body mass - ( Adipose tissue fat mass + Bone Mass + Non-Adipose Tissue Fat Mass)

questions.question: How do we measure the volume of distribution of body fluid compartments?
questions.explanation:
The volume of a fluid compartment in the body can be measured by "indicator (dye)-dilution" method. This method is based on the conservation of mass principle, which means that the total mass of a substance after dispersion in the fluid compartment will be the same as the total mass injected into the compartment.

questions.question: 500 mg of mannitol was injected out of which 10% is excreted. After equilibrium, plasma concentration is 3.2 mg/100 ml. Calculate ECF Volume (L).
questions.explanation:
The volume of distribution can be calculated using the formula:

• V = volume of compartment

• Amount injected = 500 mg

• Amount of indicator excreted = 10% of 500 mg = 50mg

• Plasma concentration of the indicator = 3.2 mg/100mL

Calculation:

2nd method :

Mannitol is a substance which leaves blood vessel but can't enter the cell. Therefore, after attaining equilibrium, conc. of mannitol is same in plasma and interstitial fluid

Therefore, by applying dye-dilution technique, mannitol can be used to measure the volume of ECF (x)

Since, 10% is excreted and 10% of 500mg is 50 mg, the amount of mannitol diluted in ECF is 450 mg (500 - 50) i.e, 450 mg is present in x

From the given values, 3.2 mg is present in 100 ml, which can be re-written as

 3.2/100 = 450/x

Therefore x = 450 * 100 / 3.2 mL

 = 14,062.5 mL

 = 14 L

Clinical :

IV Mannitol is used to treat cerebral oedema (since, it doesn't cross cell membrane, it extracts fluid from brain cells), whereas it is contra-indicated in pulmonary edema (here the fluid collection is in the interstitial space)

questions.question: 10 g of inulin is injected IV and after equilibrium the concentration of inulin in plasma is 50mg/100ml. If 10% of the inulin is excreted, what is the ECF volume?
questions.explanation:
Inulin is the indicator used to measure the ECF volume. (Since, inulin can cross blood vessel but not cell wall)

Calculation:

• Since 10% is excreted, volume of inulin excreted is 1 gm. The amount of inulin diluted in ECF is 9 g ( 10 - 1) i.e, 9000mg is present in x

From the given values, 50 mg is present in 100ml, which can be re-written as

 50/100 = 9000/x

 x = 9000 * 100 / 50

 = 9000 * 2

 = 18,000mL

 = 18L

Second method :

• Since 10% is excreted, volume of inulin excreted is 1 gm.

• Amount injected = 10g

• Amount excreted = 1g

Now, the concentration of inulin after equilibrium is 50 mg/100ml which is equal to 0.05 g/100ml. (Convert the values into same units).

Therefore, ECF volume = (10-1)*100/0.05 =18000ml = 18 L

questions.question: Of the following compartment and indicator combinations which is true?
options: Total body water-Cannot be measured directly.

questions.question: A dye X which measures the plasma volume is replaced by dye Y which can diffuse out of the capillaries. Which of the following is true regarding the newly measured plasma volume?
questions.explanation:
As the dye diffuses out of the capillaries, the measured concentration of the dye after equilibrium will be less. So, as per the formula, the volume measured will be falsely high.

V = (Amount Injected - Amount Excreted) / Plasma concentration of dye

Detailed explanation:

• Dye x measures plasma volume:- dye x doesn't have the property of crossing blood vessel. If the dye x have been used properly, for a normal person then the value would come around 3 L

• Dye y crosses capillaries, which means it can cross any blood vessel. This property is used to measure the value of ECF. If the dye y is given, for a normal person then the value would come around 14L

• Thus if dye y is given in place of x, then the value would be 14 instead of 3 which is a false and the obtained value is high when compared to normal value

• Therefore the answer is falsely high.

questions.question: Interstitial fluid volume is best measured using a combination of which two dyes?
questions.explanation:
Interstitial fluid volume is best measured using a combination of inulin and Evans blue.

Insterstitial fluid is measured indirectly. ECF minus plasma volume gives the interstitial fluid value.

• Best measure of ECF - Inulin

• Best measure of Plasma Volume - Evans Blue (T1824)

questions.question: Which of the following is higher in the ECF compared to ICF?
questions.explanation: The pH of ECF is 7.4 while the pH of ICF is 7.0. There is continuous generation of H+ ions in the ICF due to the various metabolic processes. So, the pH of ICF is a little lower compared to ECF.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most abundant intracellular anion?
questions.explanation:
Phosphate is the most abundant intracellular anion.

• ICF

• Major anion- Phosphate

• Major cation- K+

• ECF

• Protein content in ICF is ~8 times greater than plasma (ECF)

questions.question: How many grams of NaCl make 1 mole of NaCl?
questions.explanation:
1 mol of NaCl is 58.5 g

• A mole is the gram-molecular weight of a substance (molecular weight of a substance in grams)

• In this case, the molecular weight of Na-23 and Cl-35.5.

• 1 mol of NaCl = 23 g + 35.5 g = 58.5 g

Note

• Each mole consists of 6 X 10 23 molecules.

• The molecular weight of a substance is the ratio of the mass of 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Because molecular weight is a ratio, it is dimensionless.

• The Dalton (Da) is a unit of mass equal to the mass of 1/12th the mass of an atom of carbon-12. Thus molecular mass is expressed in units.

questions.question: How much is one equivalent of calcium (molecular weight = 40)?
questions.explanation:
1 equivalent of calcium is 20 g.

One equivalent is 1 mol of an ionized substance divided by its valency.

For calcium in solution, 1 mol is going to be 40g and its valency is 2. Therefore, 1 equivalent of calcium is 40/2 = 20g.

questions.question: The unit expressing the concentration of osmotically active particles is_____
questions.explanation:
The concentration of osmotically active particles is usually expressed in osmoles. Normal plasma osmolality is 280 to 290 mosmole/kg H2O

• Example

• NaCl dissociate into 2 particles- Na+ and Cl- in an ideal solution. Hence we can say that for every 1 mole of NaCl, there are 2 osmoles.

• If a solute is a non-ionizing compound such as glucose, the osmotic pressure is a function of the number of glucose molecules present.

• NOTE: The body fluids are not ideal solutions, and although the dissociation of strong electrolytes is complete, the number of particles free to exert an osmotic effect is reduced owing to the interaction between the ions. Thus, 1mol of NaCl per litre body fluids contribute somewhat less than 2 osmoles. The more concentrated the solution, the greater the deviation from the ideal solution.

questions.question: A female patient was infused with a solution which leads to rapid lysis of the RBCs. Which solution was most likely infused?
questions.explanation:
Urea is a highly permeable solute, 300mMol/L urea solution behaves as a hypotonic solution.

Urea diffuses to the inside of RBC's via UTB channels very rapidly, while the rest of the solutes in the ECF cannot enter the cell. So the ECF now becomes hypotonic. So, fluid enters the RBC and causes their lysis.

Other Options :

• Option A : The solution is iso-osmotic. (150mmol of NaCl contains 150mmol of Na+ and 150mmol of Cl- ions making the total osmolality 300 mOsm/L.This is equivalent to 0.9% NaCl which is isotonic.)

• Option B and C: The solutions are hyper-osmotic. This will lead to shrinking of the RBCs.

Note :

• If a cell is placed into a hypotonic solution that has a lower concentration of impermeant solutes (<282 mOsm/L), water will diffuse into the cell, causing it to swell.

• If a cell is placed in a hypertonic solution having a higher concentration of impermeant solutes, water will flow out of the cell leading to cell shrinkage.

questions.question: Normal osmolarity of plasma is mainly due to ________.
questions.explanation:
Normal plasma osmolarity (~290 mOsm/L) is mainly due to Na+ and its accompanying anions, principally Cl- and HCO3-

• Osmolarity (mOsm/L) = 2 [Na+] (mEq/L) + 0.055 [Glucose] (mg/dL) + 0.36 [BUN] (mg/dL)

• Because sodium and its associated anions (Cl- , HCO3- ) account for about 94 per cent of the solute in the extracellular compartment, plasma osmolarity (Posm) can be roughly approximated as

• Posm = 2.1 x Plasma sodium concentration

• With a plasma sodium concentration of 142 mEq/L, the plasma osmolarity would be estimated from the formula above to be about 298 mOsm/L.

• In conditions associated with renal disease, the contribution of two other solutes, glucose and urea, should be included.

• Because urea easily permeates most cell membranes, it exerts little effective osmotic pressure under steady-state conditions. (Ineffective osmoles)

• Contribution to plasma osmolarity:

• Na+ and associated anions: 270 mOsm/L

• Glucose : 5 mOsm/L

• Urea: 5 mOsm/L

• Plasma proteins: 2 mOsm/L

• Other ions: 8 mOsm/L

questions.question: Plasma proteins contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles because_____
options: High molar concentration, high molecular weight
Low molar concentration, low molecular weight
Low molar concentration, high molecular weight
High molar concentration, low molecular weight
questions.answer: C. Low molar concentration, high molecular weight
questions.explanation:
Proteins actually contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles (∼1 mOsm) because of their low molar concentration and high molecular weight.

Protein concentration measured as g/L may be high. However, as their molecular weight is high, the protein concentration in terms of moles per liter ( molar concentration) will be low. Thus, they contribute only slightly to the total number of osmotically active particles.

questions.question: Daily water loss in sweat during normal activities is (ml)_____
questions.explanation: The amount of water lost by sweating is highly variable, depending on physical activity and environmental temperature. The volume of sweat normally is about 100 ml/day, but in very hot weather or during heavy exercise fluid loss in sweat occasionally increase to 1 to 2 L/hour.

questions.question: Which type of disturbance of body fluids is observed in sweating?
questions.explanation:
Sweating→ loss of water→ Hyperosmotic volume contraction

• The osmolarity of ECF increases because sweat is hyposmotic (relatively more water than salt is lost).

• ECF volume decreases because of the loss of volume in the sweat.

• Water shifts out of ICF; as a result of the shift, ICF osmolarity increases until it is equal to ECF osmolarity, and ICF volume decreases.

• Plasma protein concentration increases because of the decrease in ECF volume. Although hematocrit might also be expected to increase, it remains unchanged because of the water shifts out of the RBCs, decreasing their volume and offsetting the concentrating effect of the decreased ECF volume.

• So,Loss of hypotonic fluid causes hypertonic volume contraction.

questions.question: A 73-year-old diabetic man is brought to the emergency with an altered sensorium. He is dehydrated and his blood glucose is 550mg/dl. A hyperosmolar, hyperglycemic state is suspected. Which of the given formulae can correctly evaluate his serum osmolality?
questions.explanation:
Calculated serum osmolality = 2 sodium + (glucose/18) + (BUN/2.8).

In the given clinical scenario, the patient with untreated type 2 diabetes mellitus has most likely developed a hyperosmolar, hyperglycemic state. His serum osmolality will be significantly raised.

The principal determinants of osmolality of serum are the concentrations of sodium, glucose and urea (blood urea nitrogen or BUN).

Osmolality is defined as a measure of the osmoles (Osm) of solute per kilogram of solvent (osmol/kg or Osm/kg). The osmolality of the intracellular and extracellular fluids is maintained between 290 and 310 mOsm in each compartment.

questions.question: Addition of 500 mL of hypertonic saline to the extracellular fluid leads to _______
questions.explanation:
The images shown in the figure are called Darrow Yannet Diagrams. They depict the change in plasma osmolality and plasma volume in various conditions.

If a hypertonic solution is added to the extracellular fluid, the extracellular osmolarity increases and causes osmosis of water out of the cells into the extracellular compartment

• ECF osmolality increases. ECF volume increases.

• As, ECF osmolality rises, fluid from ICF moves to ECF till osmotic equilibrium is established. So,

• ICF osmolality rises. ICF volume decreases.

Therefore, the net effect is an increase in extracellular volume (greater than the volume of fluid added), a decrease in intracellular volume, and a rise in osmolarity in both compartments.

Note : The dotted line in the diagram is the change after either addition or removal of fluid

questions.question:
The following Darrow Yannet diagram is suggestive of which condition?
( dotted line denotes the change caused by the condition)
questions.explanation:
In the given darrow yannet diagram, there is hypoosmostic volume expansion which is suggestive of SIADH.

• In SIADH there is excessive secretion of ADH. So, excess water is retained in the body.

• So, ECF volume rises. ECF osmolality decreases.

• ECF fluid enters ICF untill osmotic equilibrium is re-established.

• So, ICF volume rises. ICF osmolality decreases.
