questions.question: Various safety factors prevent excessive fluid accumulation in the interstitial spaces. Total safety factor against edema is (mmHg)_____
questions.explanation:
The total safety factor against edema is about 17 mmHg.

Summary of safety factors that prevent edema is:

• The safety factor caused by low tissue compliance in the negative pressure range is about 3 mm Hg

• The safety factor caused by increased lymph flow is about 7 mm Hg

• The safety factor caused by washdown of proteins from the interstitial spaces is about 7 mm Hg

 Therefore, the total safety factor against edema is about 17 mm Hg.

questions.question: Which among the following is embryologically and physiologically unrelated to other neural cells?
questions.explanation: Microglia are physiologically and embryologically unrelated to other neural cell types. They arise from macrophages outside the nervous system.

questions.question: In which of the following areas is a pseudo-unipolar type of neuron present?
questions.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion is a classic example of a pseudo-unipolar neuron.

questions.question: Where does the initiation of nerve impulse occur in a spinal motor neuron?
questions.explanation:
In a spinal motor neuron, initiation of nerve impulse occurs in the axon hillock and initial segment of the axon because it has a very high density of voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels. Hence, this region is also known as the trigger zone for the action potential.

Parts of a Neuron:

• Cell body/perikaryon: contains many Nissl bodies.

• Dendritic zone where multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated.

• Axon hillock: part of the cell body from which the axon arises.

• Initial segment: the first part of the axon where propagated action potentials are generated.

• An axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings. The unmyelinated regions of a myelinated axon are termed as nodes of Ranvier.

• Synaptic knobs/nerve endings where action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters.

Note: Action potentials are generated at the initial segment in spinal motor neurons and the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons.

questions.question: Which part of the neuron contains a maximum number of Na+ channels per square micrometer?
questions.explanation:
The maximum number of Na+ channels per square micrometer in myelinated neurons is present at the nodes of Ranvier. It contains 2000-12,000 channels per square micrometer.

Voltage-gated Na+ channels are highly concentrated in the nodes of Ranvier and the initial segment in myelinated neurons.

The spatial distribution of ion channels along the axon plays a key role in the initiation and regulation of action potential.

questions.question: In a cutaneous sensory neuron, at which of the following places is the propagated action potential generated?
questions.explanation:
In cutaneous sensory neurons, propagated action potentials are generated in the initial node of Ranvier.

From a functional point of view, neurons generally have four important zones :

1. A receptor, or dendritic zone, where multiple local potential changes generated by synaptic connections are integrated

2. A site where propagated action potentials are generated (the initial segment in spinal motor neurons, the initial node of Ranvier in cutaneous sensory neurons)

3. An axonal process that transmits propagated impulses to the nerve endings

4. The nerve endings, where action potentials cause the release of synaptic transmitters

The cell body is often located at the dendritic zone end of the axon, but it can be within the axon (eg, auditory neurons)

questions.question: What is the relationship between diameter of the nerve and conduction velocity?
questions.explanation:
The conduction velocity of a myelinated axon increases linearly with diameter.

Conduction velocity is increased by:

•

Increasing the fiber size: Increasing the diameter of a nerve fiber results in decreased internal resistance; thus, conduction velocity down the nerve is faster.

•

Myelination: Myelin acts as an insulator around nerve axons and increases conduction velocity. Myelinated nerves exhibit saltatory conduction. It is a rapid process that allows myelinated axons to conduct up to 50 times faster than the fastest unmyelinated fibers.

•

Activity of the Na+–K+ pump does not directly affect the formation or conduction of action potentials.

questions.question: What process is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3?
options: Movement of Na+ into the cell
Movement of Na+ out of the cell
Movement of K+ into the cell
Movement of K+ out of the cell
questions.answer: A. Movement of Na+ into the cell
questions.explanation:
The graph depicts action potential. The movement of Na+ into the cell is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3.

Once the membrane is depolarized to the threshold, local potential, the upstroke of the nerve action potential is caused by the opening of the Na+ channels. The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage-gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop. When the Na+ channels open, Na+ moves into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential.

The process responsible for repolarization is the opening of K+. The K+ permeability becomes very high and drives the membrane potential toward the K+equilibrium potential by the flow of K+ out of the cell.

questions.question: The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum at which of the following points in a nerve action potential?
questions.explanation:
The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum during repolarization (marked as point 3 in the above image).

Most of the increase in K+ conductance comes after the increase in Na+ conductance around the time of repolarization.

During the early portion of the action potential, the sodium conductance is 1000 times greater than potassium conductance. Therefore, far more sodium ions flow to the interior of the fiber than do potassium ions to the exterior. This causes the membrane potential to become positive at the action potential onset.

When the membrane potential rises from −90 millivolts toward zero, this voltage change causes a conformational change in the K+ channels which allows increased potassium efflux. Then, the sodium channels begin to close and the potassium channels begin to open, and potassium conductance begins to increase (and sodium conductance decreases).

The increased flow of K+ out of the cell causes membrane repolarization. The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state explains the after-hyperpolarization followed by a return to the resting membrane potential.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the upstroke of a nerve action potential?
options: There is net outward current and the cell interior becomes more negative
There is net outward current and the cell interior becomes less negative
There is net inward current and the cell interior becomes more negative
There is net inward current and the cell interior becomes less negative
questions.answer: D. There is net inward current and the cell interior becomes less negative
questions.explanation:
Regarding the upstroke of a nerve action potential, there is a net inward current and the cell interior becomes less negative. The direction of the current is either

1. same as the direction of positive charge ( eg, Na+ )

2. opposite to the direction of negative charge (eg, Cl- )

3. opposite to the direction of electrons

Since Na+ moves in, there is a net inward current.

Since the RMP increases, the cell interior becomes less negative.

In response to a depolarizing stimulus, some of the voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters the cell and the membrane is brought to its threshold potential. The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage-gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop. The rapid upstroke in the membrane potential ensues. So, there is a net influx of Na+, and the interior of the cell becomes positive during the upstroke of the action potential.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correctly matched?

Ionic Changes
Components of Action Potential

1
Slow closure of voltage-gated K+ channels
After-hyperpolarization

2
A decrease in extracellular Ca2+
Repolarization

3
Closing of voltage-gated Na+ channels
Depolarization

4
Rapid closure of voltage-gated Na+ channels
Resting membrane potential
questions.explanation:
The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state also explains the after-hyperpolarization.

In response to a depolarizing stimulus, some of the voltage-gated Na+ channels open and Na+ enters the cell. The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage-gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop. The rapid upstroke in the membrane potential ensues.

The membrane potential moves toward the equilibrium potential for Na+ (+60 mV) but does not reach it during the action potential, primarily because the increase in Na+ conductance is short-lived. The Na+ channels rapidly enter a closed state called the inactivated state and remain in this state for a few milliseconds.

In addition, the direction of the electrical gradient for Na+ is reversed during the overshoot because the membrane potential is reversed, and this limits Na+ influx; also the voltage-gated K+ channels open. These factors contribute to repolarization. The opening of voltage-gated K+ channels is slower and more prolonged than the opening of the Na+ channels. The net movement of positive charge out of the cell due to K+ efflux at this time helps complete the process of repolarization.

The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state also explains the after-hyperpolarization, followed by a return to the resting membrane potential.

Thus, voltage-gated K+ channels bring the action potential to an end and cause closure of their gates through a negative feedback process.

Note: Na+ channels: Positive feedback loop; K+ channels: Negative feedback loop.

questions.question: What is known as the time period in which a second stronger impulse can elicit action potential after the application of one stimulus?
questions.explanation:
The refractory period is the time period in which a second stronger impulse can elicit action potential after the application of one stimulus. It can be absolute or relative.

During the rising and much of the falling phases of the spike potential, the neuron is refractory to stimulation. This refractory period is divided into an

• Absolute refractory period, corresponding to the period from the time the firing level is reached until repolarization is about one-third complete

• Relative refractory period, lasting from this point to the start of after-depolarization

During the absolute refractory period, no stimulus, no matter how strong, will not excite the nerve. However, during the relative refractory period, stimuli that are stronger than normal can cause excitation.

The absolute refractory period for large myelinated nerve fibers is about 1/2500 second.

questions.question: From where does the relative refractory period start?
questions.explanation:
The relative refractory period starts from one-third of repolarization till the start of after-depolarization.

The refractory period is a period during which another normal action potential cannot be elicited in an excitable cell.

questions.question: Rheobase is an indicator of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The rheobase is an indicator of the magnitude of the current. It is the minimum intensity (strength/magnitude) of stimulation required to generate an action potential when the stimulation is of infinite duration.

Utilization time is the minimum time (duration) for which the rheobase has to be applied for the excitation of tissue.

Chronaxie is the minimum time (duration) for which a stimulus double the strength of rheobase has to be applied for excitation of tissue.

Strength-duration curve gives the idea of the excitability of a tissue.

Strength-duration relationship arises because the same minimum electrical charge necessary to excite an action potential can come from a current that is either brief but large or prolonged but small. It is the product of strength and duration that determines excitability, and thus these two parameters are inversely related in their effectiveness.

Note: Chronaxie is a better index than rheobase and utilization time for comparing the excitability of a tissue.

questions.question: A slowly rising stimulus fails to fire a nerve because of a process known as __________.
questions.explanation:
Slowly rising subthreshold currents fail to fire the nerve due to a process called accommodation, which is a type of adaptation.

Accommodation is due to inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels. Due to the slow rise of stimulus, only a few voltage-gated Na+ channels are activated at a time. These few channels are inactivated by the time more channels are activated. So, at no moment, are a sufficient number of channels activated to give an action potential.

When a membrane is depolarized rapidly, a large number of Na+ channels open at once, and an action potential is produced.

In contrast, decreased response to a long-lasting and sustained suprathreshold stimulus, in general, is called adaptation.

questions.question: Which of the following is true?
options: Type Aα fibre carry information related to pressure
Type Aβ fibre has the largest diameter
Type C fibre has the slowest conduction velocity
questions.answer: D. Type C fibre has the slowest conduction velocity
questions.explanation:
Type C fibers are the small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities.

Greater the diameter of a given nerve fiber, the greater its speed of conduction.

The nerve fibers are divided into types A (myelinated), B (myelinated), and C(Unmyelinated). The type A fibers are further subdivided into α, β, γ, and δ fibers.

questions.question: You are performing a CNS examination on a patient with a stroke. With his eyes closed, you move his big toe up or down while holding his toe joint. You ask him to state the position of the digit. Which of the following fibers are responsible for the transmission of the sensation tested here?
questions.explanation: The test performed here is used to check the proprioception. The large axons like Aα nerve fibers (12-20μm) carry information regarding proprioceptive sensation and somatic motor function.

questions.question: In the Erlanger and Gasser classification of peripheral nerve fibers, which type of signal is transmitted by the type B nerve fibers?
questions.explanation:
The type B fibers transmit the preganglionic autonomic fibers of both the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems.

Erlanger and Gasser classified the fibers into types A, B, and C, and the type A fibers are further subdivided into α, β, γ, and δ fibers.

• Type A fibers are the typical large- and medium-­sized myelinated fibers of spinal nerves.

• Type B fibers are smaller fibers with minimal myelination. They transmit impulses of the ANS including the bladder. (B for Bladder)

• Type C fibers are the small unmyelinated nerve fibers that conduct impulses at low velocities. They constitute more than one-half of the sensory fibers in most peripheral nerves, as well as all the postganglionic autonomic fibers.

questions.question: Spike duration is maximum in which of the following nerve fiber?
questions.explanation:
Spike duration is maximum is C fibers.

The spike duration in decreasing order: C > B > A

Absolute refractory period follows the same order: C > B > A

questions.question: Golgi tendon organ, being sensory is classified under which subtype of sensory nerve fibres?
questions.explanation: Golgi tendon organ, which contains the receptor for inverse stretch reflex, belongs to Class Ib sensory nerve fibres.

questions.question: Which sensory fibers are least susceptible to hypoxia?
questions.explanation: Susceptibility of nerve fibers to hypoxia is B >A>C, and in the general classification, type IV sensory nerves are Type C fibers.

questions.question: All of the following are true regarding a biphasic action potential except __________.
questions.explanation:
Biphasic Action Potential

• This type of record is obtained when both recording electrodes are placed on the surface of an axon that has been stimulated.

• The record shows an upward deflection followed by an isoelectric interval and then a downward deflection which denotes to the time taken for the electric potential to travel from one electrode to another.

Compound Action Potential

• It is a property of mixed nerves.

• The record shows multiple peaks in action potential because a mixed nerve is made up of families of fibres with various speeds of conduction. Therefore, when all the fibres are stimulated, the activity in the fast-conducting fibres arrives at the recording electrode sooner than the activity in slower fibers.

questions.question: End plate potential follows all of the following except?
questions.explanation:
End plate potential is a graded potential with the following characteristics:

• Magnitude is related to the magnitude of the initiating event

• Amplitude decreases over distance

• Can be summated

Graded Potential

Action Potential

Amplitude proportionate to strength of stimulus. It is graded.

Independent of stimulus intensity – all or none response

Can be depolarising or hyperpolarizing

Depolarizing

Is conducted decrementally - amplitude decreases with distance

Self-propagated unchanged in amplitude

Generated spontaneously or in response to stimuli- physical, chemical

Generated only in response to Membrane Depolarization

Can be summated

Cannot be summated

Has no threshold and refractory period

Has a threshold about 15 mv depolarized relative to the resting potential.

Has a refractory period

Not always followed by some action

Always followed by some action

questions.question: Which of the following can be used to measure a synaptic potential?
questions.explanation:
Instruments required for recording membrane potential/synaptic potential

• Stimulating electrodes: Cathode and anode

• Recording electrodes: Glass microelectrode (tip diameter <0.5μ)

• Display: Cathode ray oscilloscope (CRO)

• Squid giant axon: It is a large diameter neuron (up to 0.5 mm) from where the recording of potential is easier.

questions.question: A man who is fond of exotic cuisine develops perioral numbness after eating the Pufferfish. The given poisoning is due to which of the following toxins?
questions.explanation: Pufferfish poisoning is caused by the toxin tetrodotoxin. The sodium channels can be blocked by this toxin when it is applied to the outside of the cell membrane where the sodium activation gates are located.

questions.question: Conduction in the chemical synapses in CNS is
questions.explanation:
Conduction in the chemical synapses in CNS is always orthodromic.

When an action potential is set up in an axon, two impulses travelling in the opposite direction is set up by depolarization on either side of the initial current.

In the natural situation, impulses pass in one direction only- from synaptic junctions to axon terminals. Such conduction is called orthodromic. Conduction in the opposite direction is called antidromic. Under natural conditions, impulse conduction is normally only orthodromic. Antidromic conduction is usually only seen when a nerve fibre is stimulated under artificial conditions.

In a chemical synapse, conduction is always orthodromic. As the transmission in a chemical synapse is due to the release of neurotransmitters from the presynaptic membrane which activate receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, antidromic conduction (i.e. from the postsynaptic membrane to presynaptic membrane) is not possible. Any impulse travelling in such direction would die as it encounters the first synapse.

questions.question: Fast axonal transport is by all except______
questions.explanation:
Fast axonal transport is by all except neurofilaments.

Neurofilaments play no role in axonal transport. Fast axonal transport takes place along microtubules which are tubular polymers of protein tubulin.

AXONAL TRANSPORT

• Protein synthesis occurs in the cell body of neuron and proteins and polypeptides are transported to axonal endings by the axoplasmic flow.

• Axonal transport can be orthograde or retrograde.

• Orthograde transport

• Can be either fast or slow axonal transport and it occurs along microtubules that run along the length of the axon away from the cell body.

• Fast axonal transport occurs at about 400 mm/day, and slow axonal transport occurs at 0.5 to 10 mm/day.

• Molecular motor involved in orthograde transport is Kinesin.

• Retrograde transport,

• In the opposite direction (from the nerve ending to the cell body), occurs along microtubules at about 200 mm/day. Synaptic vesicles, nerve growth factor (NGF) and some viruses are transported back to the cell body.

• Molecular motor involed in retrograde transport is Dyenin.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding axonal transport?
options: Slow orthograde axonal transport occurs at 100 mm/day
Kinesins are required for orthograde axonal transport
Viruses exploit retrograde transport for invasion
questions.answer: B. Slow orthograde axonal transport occurs at 100 mm/day
questions.explanation:
Slow orthograde transport occurs at a speed of 0.5 to 10 mm/day.

AXONAL TRANSPORT

• Protein synthesis occurs in the cell body of neuron and proteins and polypeptides are transported to axonal endings by the axoplasmic flow.

• Axonal transport can be Orthograde or Retrograde.

• Orthograde transport

• Can be either fast or slow axonal transport and it occurs along microtubules that run along the length of the axon away from the cell body.

• Fast axonal transport occurs at about 400 mm/day, and slow axonal transport occurs at 0.5 to 10 mm/day.

• Molecular motor involved in orthograde transport is kinesin.

• Retrograde transport,

• In the opposite direction (from the nerve ending to the cell body), occurs along microtubules at about 200 mm/day. Synaptic vesicles, nerve growth factor (NGF) and some viruses (Eg: herpes simplex, rabies, and polio) are transported back to the cell body.

• Molecular motor involed in retrograde transport is dyenin.

questions.question: When a nerve is cut, which of the following takes place first?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, myelin degeneration would be the best answer.

However, the earliest change in Wallerian degeneration after nerve injury is the degeneration of the axon distal to the site of injury (axonal degeneration) where there is a disruption of the retrograde and anterograde flow of signals within the axon.

Wallerian degeneration

• If the axon is cut, the part distal to the cut degenerates; this process is called as Wallerian degeneration.

• Orthograde degeneration (Wallerian degeneration) occurs from the point of injury to the nerve terminal, interrupting neural transmission.

• After the injury, the membrane breaks down and the myelin sheath degenerates. The cell body of the injured neuron swells, the nucleus moves to an eccentric position, and the rough endoplasmic reticulum becomes fragmented (chromatolytic reaction).

• The nerve then starts to regrow, with multiple small branches projecting along the path the axon previously followed (regenerative sprouting).

• When the motor nerve to skeletal muscle is cut and allowed to degenerate, the muscle gradually becomes extremely sensitive to acetylcholine. This is called denervation hypersensitivity or supersensitivity.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding the resting membrane potential (RMP) in a nerve fibre?
options: It is equal to the RMP of inner hair cells of cochlea
It can be measured by surface electrodes
It becomes more positive as extracellular K+ increases
It depends on the equilibrium potential of Na+
questions.answer: C. It becomes more positive as extracellular K+ increases
questions.explanation:
The resting membrane potential is close to the equilibrium potential for K+. So, changes in the external concentration of this ion can have major effects on the resting membrane potential.

• If the extracellular level of K+ is increased (hyperkalemia), the resting potential moves closer to the threshold for eliciting an action potential, thus the neuron becomes more excitable.

• If the extracellular level of K+ is decreased (hypokalemia), the membrane potential is reduced and the neuron is hyperpolarized.

Option a: The RMP of a nerve fiber is -70 mV, while the RMP of inner hair cells is between -45 and -60 mV relative to the fluid that bathes the basal end of the cell.

Option b: The membrane potential can be measured only when one electrode is inserted into the interior of the cell.

Option d: It depends on the equilibrium potential of K+.

questions.question: Which of the following about sensory nerve fibers is not true?
questions.explanation:
Group III fibers carrying temperature, crude touch, and pricking pain sensations are δ-type A fibers, not A-gamma type .

Alternative Classification Used in Sensory Nerves

• Group Ia. Fibers from the annulospiral endings of muscle spindles are α-type A fibers in the general classification.

• Group Ib. Fibers from the Golgi tendon organs are also α-type A fibers.

• Group II. Fibers from most discrete cutaneous tactile receptors and from the flower-spray endings of the muscle spindles are β- and γ-type A fibers in the general classification.

• Group III. Fibers carrying temperature, crude touch, and pricking pain sensations are δ-type A fibers in the general classification.

• Group IV. Unmyelinated fibers carrying pain, itch, temperature, and crude touch sensations are type C fibers in the general classification

questions.question: All of the following are the connective tissue layers of the skeletal muscle except ______
questions.explanation:
Sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the muscle cell, while the remaining options are connective tissue layers surrounding the muscle.

A muscle is made up of individual muscle fibers. Each muscle fiber is a single cell that is multinucleated, long, cylindrical, and surrounded by a cell membrane, the sarcolemma.

Arrangement of the connective tissue is shown below.

questions.question: Which of the following is a regulatory muscle protein?
questions.explanation:
Tropomyosin is a regulatory muscle protein.

It extends over the entire actin filament and covers the myosin-binding sites on the actin molecules thus preventing the attachment of actin to myosin.

One molecule covers 7 active sites on actin

Troponin is another regulatory protein. Troponin molecules are small globular units located at intervals along the tropomyosin molecules. Each of the three troponin subunits has a unique function:

• Troponin T binds the troponin components to tropomyosin.

• troponin I inhibits the interaction of myosin with actin.

• troponin C contains the binding sites for the Ca2+ that helps initiate contraction.

questions.question: Which of the following does not belong to dystrophin-glycoprotein complex?
questions.explanation:
Perlecan is a large extracellular matrix proteoglycan that plays a crucial role in tissue development and organogenesis.

Dystrophin-glycoprotein complex

• The dystrophin-glycoprotein complex provides a structural link between the cytoskeleton of the muscle cell and the extracellular matrix, which appears to stabilize the sarcolemma, adds strength to the muscle by providing a scaffolding for the fibrils and prevents contraction-induced injury (rupture).

• Organisation of DG complex

• Dystrophin connects F-actin to the transmembrane protein β-dystroglycan via smaller proteins called Syntrophins.

• This β-dystroglycan, in turn connects to the merosin subunit of laminin 211 in the extracellular matrix via α-dystroglycan.

• The dystroglycans are also associated with a complex of four transmembrane glycoproteins, α-, β-, γ-, and δ-sarcoglycan and sarcospan.

APPLIED ASPECT

• Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy

• X-linked recessive disorder

• Deletion of DMD gene which codes for Dystrophin

• Becker muscular Dystrophy

• Dystrophin is present but altered or reduced in amount

• Limb Girdle Dystrophy

• Sarcoglycan is mutated

questions.question: Thin filaments consists of all of the following except _______
questions.explanation:
Myosin forms the thick filament, while actin, troponin, and tropomyosin form the thin filament.

Thin Filaments in Sarcomere

• The thin filaments are polymers made up of two chains of actin that form a long double helix.

• Tropomyosin molecules are long filaments located in the groove between the two chains in the actin.

• Each thin filament contains 300–400 actin molecules and 40–60 tropomyosin molecules.

• Troponin molecules are small globular units located at intervals along the tropomyosin molecules.

• Each of the three troponin subunits has a unique function:

• Troponin T binds the troponin components to tropomyosin.

• Troponin I inhibits the interaction of myosin with actin.

• Troponin C contains the binding sites for the Ca 2+ that helps to initiate contraction.

questions.question: Which of the following proteins is present in skeletal muscles, but absent in a smooth muscle?
questions.explanation: Actin, myosin, and tropomyosin are present in both skeletal muscle and smooth muscle. But troponin is absent and calmodulin is present in smooth muscle.

questions.question: Myosin filament has a fixed length of ______.
questions.explanation: The total length of each myosin filament is uniform, almost exactly 1.6 micrometers.

questions.question:
The thick filament is made up of ________.
1. Heavy chain of myosin
2. Light chain of myosin
3. Dystrophin
4. Titin
questions.explanation:
The thick filament or the myosin is made up of the heavy chain of myosin and light chain of myosin.

The myosin molecule is composed of six polypeptide chains- Two heavy chains, each with a molecular weight of about 200,000, and four light chains with molecular weights of about 20,000 each.

The two heavy chains wrap spirally around each other to form a double helix, which is called the tail of the myosin molecule.

One end of each of these chains is folded into a globular polypeptide structure called a myosin head. These heads contain an actin-binding site and a catalytic site that hydrolyzes ATP. Thus, there are two free heads at one end of the double-helix myosin molecule.

The four light chains are also part of the myosin head, two to each head. These light chains help control the function of the head during muscle contraction.

questions.question: Pseudo H zone in a sarcomere extends between the ______
questions.answer: C. Two sides of M line
questions.explanation:
Pseudo H-zone is the light area between the two sides of M line due to reversal of polarity of the myosin molecules in each of the thick filaments.

Sarcomere

• The sarcomere is the contractile unit of the skeletal muscle fibre.

• Z line: provides attachment to actin filaments. The area between two adjacent Z lines is called the sarcomere.

• It is composed of thick and thin filaments:

• Thick filament : Myosin

• Thin filaments : Actin, tropomyosin and troponin

• I band:

• Isotropic to light.

• Only thin filaments.

• Half lies in one sarcomere and half in the next.

• A band:

• Anisotropic to light.

• Myosin plus overlapped actin.

• H bands:

• lighter area in the centre of A band, when the muscle is relaxed, the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments.

• Only Myosin

• Pseudo H: light portion on two sides of M line because of absence of cross bridges (no myosin head).

• M line: centre of A band. Here there are slender cross-connections that hold the thick filaments in proper array.

questions.question: A cross-sectional view of a skeletal muscle fiber through the H zone would reveal the presence of _______
questions.explanation:
H zone is the central region of the A band which is lighter than the outer edges of the A band because the H zone is occupied by thick filaments only (No cross bridges)

In the figure, note the section through various levels and the myofilaments observed.

• Section through I band → only actin (thin filament)

• Section through A band (Exlcuding H zone) → Actin and Myosin

• Section through H zone → only myosin (thick filament)

• Section through M line → thick filament linked with accessory proteins

• Section at AI junction → both actin and myosin

questions.question: The titin protein present in the muscle fiber binds ______
options: The tail ends of actin filaments to Z disc
The head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc
The tail ends of myosin filaments to M disc
The myofibrils to each other, and also to the cell membrane
questions.answer: B. The head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc
questions.explanation:
The titin protein present in the muscle fiber binds the head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc

Several proteins other than actin and myosin are also present in the muscle. Some of them include:

1. Titin:

• It is the largest known protein.

• It runs between the M line and Z disc and binds the head ends of myosin filaments to the Z disc.

• It has a tethered portion in the A band, where it is attached to the myosin filament and an elastic portion in the I band.

• The elastic property of the titin causes elastic recoil of the sarcomere and prevents it from being overstretched.

2. Nebulin:

• It extends from the Z disc and runs along the full length of each actin filament.

• It regulates the length of the actin filaments.

3. α-actinin:

• It is a component of the Z discs

• It binds the plus ends of actin filaments to this disc.

4. Myomesin

• It is present in the region of the M line.

• It maintains the regular lattice arrangement of the myosin filaments in this region.

5. Desmin:

• It is an intermediate filament characteristic of the muscle

• It encircles the myofibrils near the Z disc and binds myofibrils to each other and also to the cell membrane.

6. Dystrophin:

• It is present in the periphery of the muscle fiber, towards the cytoplasmic face of the sarcolemma.

• It binds to the actin filaments and the glycoprotein complex, consisting of dystroglycan and sarcoglycan that spans the sarcolemma.

questions.question: Muscle myosin and actin filaments are kept in place by ______
questions.explanation:
The side-by-side relationship between the myosin and actin filaments is maintained by a large number of filamentous molecules of a protein called titin.

Titin is a filamentous and springy protein. These springy titin molecules act as a framework that holds the myosin and actin filaments in place so that the contractile machinery of the sarcomere will work.

One end of the titin molecule is elastic and is attached to the Z disk, acting as a spring and changing length as the sarcomere contracts and relaxes. The other part of the titin molecule tethers it to the myosin thick filament.

questions.question: Choose the true statement regarding the sarcomere in skeletal muscle.
options: Desmin binds Z line to sarcoplasmic reticulum
Actinin binds M line to actin
Titin binds M line to z line
The length of myosin changes with contraction
questions.answer: C. Titin binds M line to z line
questions.explanation:
Titin binds M line to Z line

Other options

Desmin binds Z line to sarcolemma ( not sarcoplasmic reticulum)

Actinin binds Z line to actin ( not M line; in fact, one of the two attachments of actin, desmin and titin, is always Z line)

Titin binds M line to z line, forms scaffolding, is responsible for muscle elasticity, is the largest known protein (Largest protein - titin; Largest gene - Dystrophin; Most abundant protein - Collagen )

The length of myosin or actin does not change with contraction; actually, the length of zones I and H get changed (i.e, gets decreased )

questions.question: Which of the following occurs during skeletal muscle contraction?
options: Both H and I band shorten
Both A and I band shorten
Both A and H band shorten
questions.answer: B. Both H and I band shorten
questions.explanation:
Sliding of thin filament over thick filament (cross bridge formation) reduces the length of I and H band.

• During contraction, the Z lines come closer to each other reducing the length of the sarcomere.

• The A band remains constant and M line becomes prominent.

questions.question: The cross-bridges of the sarcomere in skeletal muscle are made up of _______.
questions.explanation:
When the action potential reaches the muscle fiber, there is influx of Ca2+ ions. This Ca2+ binds to troponin C and tropomyosin is moved out of the way. Myosin heads can now bind to actin and form so-called cross-bridges.

When a head attaches to an active site, this attachment simultaneously causes profound changes in the intramolecular forces between the head and arm of its cross-bridge. This causes the head to tilt toward the arm and to drag the actin filament along with it. This tilt of the head is called the power stroke.

Immediately after tilting, the head then automatically breaks away from the active site.

Formation of cross-bridges is associated with hydrolysis of ATP and generation of force.

questions.question: ATPase activity is present in ______.
questions.explanation:
A feature of the myosin head that is essential for muscle contraction is that it functions as an adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) enzyme.

Chemical Events during Muscle Contraction

• Before contraction begins, the heads of the cross-bridges bind with ATP. The ATPase activity of the myosin head immediately cleaves the ATP but leaves the cleavage products, ADP plus phosphate ion, bound to the head. (Point A)

• When the troponin-tropomyosin complex binds with calcium ions, active sites on the actin filament are uncovered and the myosin heads then bind with these sites. (Point B)

• The bond between the head of the cross-bridge and the active site of the actin filament causes a conformational change in the head and the power stroke occurs. (Point C)

• Once the head of the cross-bridge tilts, the ADP and phosphate ion that were previously attached to the head are released and a new ATP moelcule binds in that place. (Point D)

• The binding of the new ATP molecule causes detachment of the head of myosin from the actin. (Point D)

• This cycle is then repeated.

questions.question: In human skeletal muscles, calcium ions are stored in?
questions.explanation:
In a skeletal muscle, calcium ions are majorly stored in the terminal cisterns of the Sarcoplasmic Reticulum.

Terminal cisterns are the lateral sacs of the sarcoplasmic reticulum. The spread of action potential triggers the release of Ca2+ from the terminal cisterns.

The sarcolemma is the cell membrane of the skeletal muscle. Transverse tubules are the internal extensions of the sarcolemma.

questions.question: All of the following are true about excitation-contraction coupling in skeletal muscle except that _____
options: Acetylcholine is released at the nerve terminal.
Ca2+ is released from sarcoplasmic reticulum during contraction.
Ca2+ is pumped back into sarcoplasmic reticulum during relaxation.
Ca2+ binds to tropomyosin to initiate muscle contraction.
questions.answer: D. Ca2+ binds to tropomyosin to initiate muscle contraction.
questions.explanation: Ca2+ binds to troponin C (not tropomyosin) to initiate muscle contraction.

questions.question: A skeletal muscle contraction ends when _______.
options: Ions move out of the cytoplasm
Ach is metabolised at the Neuromusclular junction (NMR)
Decreased calcium outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.answer: C. Decreased calcium outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation:
Once the Ca2+ concentration outside the sarcoplasmic reticulum has been lowered sufficiently, chemical interaction between myosin and actin ceases and the muscle relaxes.

• The SERCA pump uses energy from ATP hydrolysis to remove Ca2+ from the cytosol back into the terminal cisterns, where it is stored until released by the next action potential.

• Thus during relaxation

• Ca2+ concentration in cytoplasmic decreases.

• Ca2+ concentration in sarcoplasmic reticulum increases.

Option a: Calcium ions do not move out of the cytoplasm. They are taken up by the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.question: A bodybuilder is regularly working out in a gym. Which of the following is true regarding total heat production during muscle contraction?
options: Activation heat is produced when a muscle is contracting
Initial heat produced is due to the basal metabolic processes.
Relaxation heat is present in both isotonic and isometric contractions
Recovery heat of muscle is greater than the initial heat
questions.answer: A. Activation heat is produced when a muscle is contracting
questions.explanation:
Activation heat is the heat that muscle produces whenever it contracts.

Heat Production in Muscle

• Resting heat: The heat given off at rest due to the basal metabolic processes.

• Initial heat: The heat produced in excess of resting heat during contraction. It is made up two subtypes:

• Activation heat: The heat that muscle produces whenever it is contracting, and

• Shortening heat: The heat which is proportional in amount to the distance the muscle shortens. Shortening heat is apparently due to some change in the structure of the muscle during shortening.

• Recovery heat: this is the heat liberated by the metabolic processes that restore the muscle to its precontraction state. The recovery heat of muscle is approximately equal to the initial heat.

• Relaxation heat: Heat released in a muscle that has contracted isotonically to restore it to its previous length. This extra heat is in addition to recovery heat.

questions.question: The length of the muscle fiber at the onset of contraction which is required to attain the maximum active tension is known as
questions.explanation:
The length of the muscle fiber at the onset of contraction which is required to attain maximum active tension is known as resting length.

Resting length is also known as the optimum length. It is about 2μm. At this length, there is a maximal overlap between the actin and myosin fibers and therefore, the maximum number of cross-bridge binding sites are formed.

Passive tension is the tension in a muscle when it is not stimulated. Total tension is the tension developed when a muscle contracts isometrically in response to a maximal stimulus.

Active tension = Total tension - Passive tension

When the muscle fiber contracts, the active tension developed is proportional to the number of cross-bridges between the actin and myosin fibers. Hence, at the resting length, maximum active tension is produced and the muscle fiber contracts with a maximum force of contraction.

In the given image, the purple line represents the passive tension in the muscle (before contraction) and its relation with the muscle length, while the red line represents the total tension present (during contraction) and its relation with the muscle length.

questions.question: All of the following are true regarding the resting length of a muscle fiber except ________.
options: There are maximum cross-bridges between actin and myosin
The resting length is around 2μm in humans
The velocity of contraction is maximum for any given load
questions.answer: B. The passive tension is maximum
questions.explanation:
The passive tension is not maximum at resting length of a muscle fiber.

Passive tension is the tension in a muscle when it is not stimulated. Total tension is the tension developed when a muscle contracts isometrically in response to a maximal stimulus.

Active tension = Total tension - Passive tension

The active tension is maximum at the resting length of a muscle fiber. This is because there is a optimal overlap between the actin and myosin fibers at the resting length and therefore the maximum number of cross-bridges are formed. (Option A) This provides for the maximum force of contraction at this length. The active tension decreases as the muscle is stretched beyond its normal length. The resting length is around 2μm in humans. (Option C)

The velocity of muscle contraction varies inversely with the load on the muscle i.e. as the load on the muscle increases, the velocity of contraction decreases. At a given load, the velocity is maximal at the resting length and declines if the muscle is shorter or longer than this length. (Option D)

questions.question: Active tension in a muscle depends upon which of the following?
questions.answer: B. Number of motor units recruited
questions.explanation:
Active tension in a muscle depends upon the number of motor units recruited.

The greater the number of motor units recruited, the greater will be the active tension.

Factors affecting muscle tension

Tension developed by each fiber

• Action potential frequency

• Fiber length (length-tension relationship)

• Fiber diameter

• Fatigue

Number of active fibers

• Number of fibers per motor unit

• Number of active motor units (recruitment)

questions.question: Which of the following have the maximum density of white muscle fibers?
questions.explanation: Extra-ocular muscles have the maximum density of white muscle fibers (type IIB), which contract quickly with peak tension attained within 7.5 msec of stimulation.

questions.question: All are true about red muscle fibers except -
questions.explanation: The red muscle fibers are Type 1 muscle fibers with low/moderate glycolytic metabolism. Rest of the options are true regarding red muscle fibers.

questions.question: A motor unit is made up of _______________.
options: All the muscle fibers within a given muscle
A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates
All the neurons going into an muscle of the body
questions.answer: B. A motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates
questions.explanation:
Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates constitute a motor unit.

• The number of muscle fibers in a motor unit varies.

• In muscles concerned with fine, graded, precise movement, (eg. extraoccular muscles) each motor unit innervates very few (three to six) muscle fibers.

• On the other hand, in human leg and back muscles, number of muscle fibers per motor unit can be upto 600.

• Each spinal motor neuron innervates only one kind of muscle fiber, so that all the muscle fibers in a motor unit are of the same type.

• On the basis of the type of muscle fiber they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of their twitch contraction, motor units are divided into S (slow), FR (fast, resistant to fatigue), and FF (fast, fatigable) units.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct about the recruitment of fast fatiguable motor unit ?
questions.explanation:
The fast fatigable motor unit is recruited last.

Each single motor neuron and the muscle fibers it innervates constitute a motor unit. On the basis of the type of muscle fiber they innervate, and thus on the basis of the duration of their twitch contraction, motor units are divided into

• S (slow)

• FR (fast, resistant to fatigue)

• FF (fast, fatigable) units.

S fibers have a low innervation ratio (ie, small units) and FF fibers have a high innervation ratio (i.e., large units).

The recruitment of motor units during muscle contrac­tion follows a general scheme, the size principle.

• In general, a specific muscle action is developed first by the recruitment of S muscle units that contract relatively slowly to produce controlled contraction.

• Next, FR muscle units are recruited, resulting in more powerful response over a shorter period of time.

• Lastly, FF muscle units are recruited for the most demanding tasks.

questions.question: Twitch of a single muscle fiber is called _____
questions.explanation:
Twitch of a single muscle fiber is called fibrillation.

Fibrillation
Fasciculation

Twitch of a single muscle fiber
Jerky, visible contractions of groups of muscle fibers

Occurs due to the degeneration of a single α motor neuron or its axon.
Occur as a result of a pathologic discharge of spinal motor neurons (motor unit).

questions.question: A scientist found that the latent period of muscle twitch is 10 ms and the contraction period is 40 ms. What is the tetanizing frequency (Hz)?
questions.explanation:
Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1/40 ms = 25 Hz.

Tetanizing frequency

• As the contractile mechanism does not have a refractory period, on rapid stimulation of a muscle, each new contraction occurs before the preceding one is over. As a result, the second contraction is added partially to the first, and thus the total strength of contraction rises progressively with increasing frequency. Such a response is called a tetanus (tetanic contraction). It is a complete tetanus when no relaxation occurs between stimuli.

• Tetany occurs because enough calcium ions are maintained in the muscle sarcoplasm throughout the period of stimulation.

questions.question: Tetanic contraction is due to the accumulation of _______ ions.
questions.explanation:
Tetanic contraction occurs due to progressive accumulation of Ca2+ ions with rapidly repeated stimulation of skeletal muscle.

• With rapidly repeated stimulation, activation of the contractile mechanism occurs repeatedly before any relaxation has occurred, and the individual contractions fuse into one continuous contraction. Such a response is called a tetanus (tetanic contraction).

• A single action potential releases sufficient Ca2+ to cause a twitch contraction.

• However, the duration of this contraction is very short because Ca2+ is very rapidly pumped back into the SR.

• If the muscle is stimulated a second time before the muscle is fully relaxed, there is progressive accumulation of Ca2+ and the force of contraction increases. Thus, twitch forces are amplified as stimulus frequency increases.

• At a high level of stimulation, intracellular Ca2+ increases and is maintained throughout the period of stimulation, and the amount of force developed greatly exceeds that seen during a twitch. The response is termed tetany.

questions.question: Human cardiac muscle contains ________.
questions.explanation:
Human heart contains both alpha and beta isoforms of the myosin heavy chain. β isoform has a lower myosin ATPase activity than the α isoform.

• α isoform predominates in the adult atria.

• β isoform predominates in the adult ventricles.

• The spatial distribution contributes to the well coordinated contraction of the heart.

questions.question: Intercalated discs are seen in _______.
questions.explanation:
• Cardiac muscle fibres are made up of many individual cells connected in series and parallel with one another.

• The areas where the end of one muscle fiber abuts on another, which always occur at Z lines, are called intercalated discs.

• It provides a strong union between fibers, maintaining cell-to-cell cohesion, so that the pull of one contractile cell can be transmitted along its axis to the next.

• It contains Desmosomes to prevent pulling apart of the cells when strain

• At each intercalated disc, the plasma membrane fuses with one another forming gap junction which provide low resistance bridges for the spread of excitation from one fiber to another permitting the cardiac muscle to function as a syncytium.

questions.question: Activation of the sympathetic system increases the myocardial contractility of a patient. Which of the following is responsible for this positive inotropic effect?
questions.explanation:
Phosphorylation of phospholamban is responsible for the positive inotropic effect on the myocardium observed after the stimulation of the sympathetic nervous system.

Phospholamban is a protein that regulates Ca2+ATPase in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. When phosphorylated, phospholamban stimulates the Ca2+ ATPase, resulting in greater uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

Increased Ca2+ uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum has two effects:

It causes faster relaxation (i.e., briefer contraction).

it increases the amount of stored Ca2+ for release on subsequent beats.

This positive inotropic effect has three important features: increased peak tension, increased rate of tension development, and faster rate of relaxation.

Faster relaxation means that the contraction (twitch) is shorter, allowing more time for refilling.

This effect is mediated via activation of β1 receptors, which are coupled via a Gs protein to adenylyl cyclase.

Activation of adenylyl cyclase leads to the production of cAMP, activation of protein kinases, and phosphorylation of proteins that produce the physiologic effect of increased contractility.

questions.question: Which among the following is the function of phospholamban?
options: Regulates calcium entry into sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.answer: C. Regulates calcium entry into sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation:
• Phospholamban is a protein that regulates SR Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. In its dephosphorylated state, phospholamban inhibits the Ca2+ ATPase, resulting in diminished uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum, while in its phosphorylated state, there is disinhibition of the Ca2+ ATPase leading to increased uptake and storage of Ca2+ by the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

• Increased Ca2+ uptake by the sarcoplasmic reticulum has two effects:

• It causes faster relaxation (i.e., briefer contraction).

• it increases the amount of stored Ca2+ for release on subsequent beats.

• Phosphorylation of phospholamban is responsible for the positive inotropic effect effect on the myocardium observed after the stimulation of sympathetic nervous system.

• This effect is mediated via activation of β1 receptors, which are coupled via a Gs protein to adenylyl cyclase.

• This positive inotropic effect has three important features: increased peak tension, increased rate of tension development, and faster rate of relaxation.

• Faster relaxation means that the contraction (twitch) is shorter, allowing more time for refilling.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of cardiac muscle?
questions.explanation:
Cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized due to long refractory period.

In cardiac myocytes, depolarization proceeds rapidly and an overshoot of the zero potential is present. This is followed by a plateau before the membrane potential reaches the RMP (-90mV). This plateau phase lasts for 200 msec or more. Repolarization is therefore not complete until contraction is 50% completed.

Phases of cardiac action potential

• 0→ Depolarisation and overshoot

• Due to opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels

• 1→ Initial rapid repolarization

• Due to closure of Na+ channels and opening up of K+ channels

• 2→ Plateau phase

• Due to slow but prolonged opening of Ca2+ channels

• 3→ late rapid repolarization

• 4→ Baseline (RMP)

• Phases 3 and 4 are due closure of Ca2+ channels and a slow, delayed increase of K+ efflux through K+ channels.

• During phases 0 to 2 and about half of phase 3 of cardiac action potential, cardiac muscle cannot be excited again, that is, it is in its absolute refractory period. It remains relatively refractory until phase 4. Thus, cardiac muscle cannot be tetanized.

questions.question: The following graph displays which physiological law of the heart?
questions.explanation:
The diagram displays the Length-Tension relationship for a cardiac muscle explaining the Starling law of the heart.

In the body, the initial length of the fibers is determined by the degree of diastolic filling of the heart, and the pressure developed in the ventricle is proportional to the volume of the ventricle at the end of the filling phase (Starling law of the heart).

• The developed tension increases as the diastolic volume increases until it reaches a maximum, then tends to decrease.

• The decrease is due to beginning disruption of the myocardial fibers and not due to a decrease in the number of cross-bridges between actin and myosin as seen in skeletal muscle.

questions.question: Muscles in hollow viscera behave as ______
questions.explanation: Hollow viscera are primarily composed of single-unit smooth muscles.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding excitation-contraction coupling in smooth muscle?
options: Sustained contraction occurs with high calcium concentration
Phosphorylation of actin is required for contraction
Cellular calcium concentration is essential to cause contraction
questions.answer: D. Cellular calcium concentration is essential to cause contraction
questions.explanation:
Increased cytosolic Ca2+ is essential for contraction of smooth muscles.

Events in Excitation Contraction Coupling in Smooth Muscles.

A unitary smooth muscle is unique in that it can contract when stretched even in the absence of any extrinsic innervation. Stretch is followed by a decrease in membrane potential and an increase in the tone of the muscle.

Other options:

Option a: Troponin is absent in smooth muscle.

Option b: Sustained contraction of the smooth muscle occurs even when the calcium concentration falls. This is mainly because of the latch-bridge mechanism where the myosin cross-bridges remain attached to the actin. This mechanism allows for maintaining the contraction with less expenditure of energy and is particularly important in the vascular smooth muscle.

Option c: Unlike skeletal muscle where troponin binding is essential for contraction, the smooth muscle contraction requires phosphorylation of myosin (not actin).

questions.question: Calmodulin is mostly both structurally and functionally related to ______
questions.explanation:
Calmodulin is structurally and functionally related to troponin. In place of troponin, smooth muscle cells contain a large amount of the regulatory protein calmodulin.

Calmodulin is similar to troponin; it is different in the manner in which it initiates contraction. Calmodulin initiates contraction by activating the myosin light chain kinase. Troponin, on the other hand, initiates contraction by causing a conformational change in the tropomyosin molecule which then uncovers the active sites on the actin filament.

questions.question: A sustained contraction with little expenditure of energy is made possible by a latching mechanism in ________.
questions.explanation:
• Smooth muscles can maintain prolonged full tonic contraction with little use of energy (as little as 1/300 the energy required for comparable sustained skeletal muscle contraction) and with little continued excitatory signal due to this mechanism.

• This is due to the fact that even after dephosphorylation of myosin, the cross-bridges continue to cling on for some time.

• The excitation coupling mechanism occurring in smooth muscle is similar to the skeletal muscles but for a few features:

• The process is slow and a low energy mechanism.

• There is no fixed length tension relationship as it shows the property of plasticity (smooth muscles behaving like a viscous mass rather than a rigidly structured tissue).

• This mechanism is specially useful in vascular smooth muscles.

questions.question: The most distinguishing feature between skeletal muscle and smooth muscle is ______
questions.explanation: Actin, myosin, and tropomyosin are present in both skeletal muscle and smooth muscle. But, troponin is absent and calmodulin is present in smooth muscle.

questions.question: Which of the following acts to increase the release of calcium ions from the endoplasmic reticulum of a smooth muscle?
questions.explanation:
In response to a stimulus, the efflux of calcium from intracellular stores occurs through an Inositol triphosphate receptor (IP3R)- Ca+2 channel.

The source of Ca+2 in smooth muscle contraction can be different depending on the activating stimulus.

• The influx from the extracellular site through voltage or ligand-gated Ca+2 channels in the plasma membrane

• Efflux from intracellular stores (eg, sarcoplasmic reticulum) through the RyR and the inositol triosephosphate receptor (IP3R).

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding smooth muscle is false?
options: Unitary smooth muscle has an unstable membrane potential
Dense Bodies are present instead of Z lines
It can exert a variable tension at any given length
Sympathetic stimulation produces excitatory membrane potentials
questions.answer: D. Sympathetic stimulation produces excitatory membrane potentials
questions.explanation:
Sympathetic stimulation (norepinephrine) of a smooth muscle produces inhibitory potentials and relaxation.

Parasympathetic stimulation (or acetylcholine) causes depolarization and contraction in the smooth muscle.

Smooth muscle can be divided into:

• Unitary smooth muscle - has low-resistance gap junctions between individual muscle cells and functions in a syncytial manner

• Multiunit smooth muscle - made up of individual units with few or nil gap junctions.

Blood vessels have both unitary and multiunit smooth muscle in their walls.

Option A: Unitary smooth muscle has an unstable membrane potential with continuous irregular contractions independent of its nerve supply. This state of partial contraction is called tonus or tone.

Option B: Dense bodies are present instead of Z lines in smooth muscle. These are bound to actin filaments by α-actinin.

Option C: Smooth muscle can exert variable tension at any given length. This property is called plasticity. When a unitary smooth muscle is stretched, it first exerts increased tension. However, if it is held at this length after stretching, the tension gradually decreases. This is referred to as plasticity.

questions.question:
A synapse is a junction between _______.

1. Axon and dendrite

2. Axon and axon

3. Axon and muscle cell

4. Axon and soma
questions.explanation:
Impulses are transmitted from one nerve cell to another cell at junctions called synapse. These are the junctions where the axon or some other portion of one cell (the presynaptic cell) terminates on the dendrites, soma, or axon of another neuron or, in some cases, a muscle or gland cell (the postsynaptic cell).

There are two major types of synapses:

• Chemical

• Electrical

When a neuron terminates on a muscle , it is called a neuromuscular junction . This is an example of a chemical synapse .

questions.question: All of the following are true regarding chemical synapses except_____
options: These are the most common type of synapses
Neurotransmitter is produced by the presynaptic neuron
Protoplasmic continuity between pre- and post- synaptic membrane ensures faster conduction
questions.answer: C. Protoplasmic continuity between pre- and post- synaptic membrane ensures faster conduction
questions.explanation:
Chemical synapses are interneuronal junctions without protoplasmic continuity.

Most of the synapses used for signal transmission in the central nervous system of the human being are chemical synapses.

In these synapses, the first neuron (presynaptic neuron) secretes neurotransmitters at its nerve ending synapse. This transmitter, in turn, acts on receptor proteins in the membrane of the next neuron (post-synaptic neuron) to excite the neuron, inhibit it, or modify its sensitivity in some other way.

As neurotransmitters are released only by the pre-synaptic neuron, the synaptic conduction in the CNS is only orthodromic (unidirectional).

questions.question: In a typical chemical synaptic cleft, the extracellular distance between the presynaptic plasma membrane and the postsynaptic plasma membrane is approximately_____
questions.explanation: In a typical chemical synaptic cleft, the extracellular distance between the presynaptic plasma membrane and the postsynaptic plasma membrane is approximately 20-40nm.

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding neurotransmitters?
options: All neurotransmitter are derived from amino acids
Nitric oxide is a neurotransmitter in the CNS
They do not act on ionotropic receptors
They are released on repolarization of the nerve
questions.answer: B. Nitric oxide is a neurotransmitter in the CNS
questions.explanation:
Nitric oxide is a neurotransmitter in the CNS.

Neurotransmitters are the substances that mediate chemical signaling between neurons. They can be choline esters, biogenic amines, amino acids, and neuropeptides.

Two main classes of chemical substances that serve as neurotransmitters:

• small-molecule neurotransmitter (acetylcholine)

• large molecule neurotransmitter (enkephalin)

They can act on ionotropic receptors (ligand-gated ion channels) and/or metabotropic receptors on the postsynaptic membrane to produce a change in membrane potential to bring about their action.

Criteria for the substance to be neurotransmitter:

• the substance must be demonstrated to be present in the presynaptic terminal.

• the cell must be able to synthesize the substance.

• should be released on depolarization of the terminal.

• there should be specific receptors for it on the postsynaptic membrane.

• if the substance is applied exogenously to the postsynaptic membrane at physiologic concentration, the response of the postsynaptic cell must mimic the in vivo response.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a monoamine neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation:
GABA is not a monoamine neurotransmitter. It is an amino acid.

Biogenic amines are small, charged molecules that are synthesized from amino acids and contain an amino group (R—NH2). Amines known to act as neurotransmitters are dopamine, norepinephrine (noradrenaline), epinephrine (adrenaline), serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine [5-HT]).

Amino acids and their derived amines acting as neurotransmitters:

• Tyrosine - catecholamines : dopamine, norepinephrine, and epinephrine .

• Tryptophan - serotonin

• Histidine - histamine

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding metabotropic neurotransmitters?
options: They act through second messenger systems
They bind to cationic channels and increase influx of Na
They bind to anionic channels and increase influx of Cl
They inhibit the fusion of synaptic vesicle with the synaptic cleft
questions.answer: A. They act through second messenger systems
questions.explanation:
Neurotransmitter receptors that act through second messenger systems are called metabotropic receptors.

Neurotransmitters bind to receptors on the post-synaptic membrane to activate ion channels in one of the two ways:

• by gating ion channels directly (ionotropic receptors).

• by activating a second messenger (metabotropic receptor) for a prolonged postsynaptic neu­ronal excitation or inhibition. Most commonly activated is a G-protein coupled membrane receptor.

The following four changes can occur usually after binding to a G-protein coupled receptor:

• Opening specific ion channels through the post-synaptic cell membrane.

• Activation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) or cyclic guanosine monophosphate (cGMP) in the neuronal cell.

• Activation of one or more intracellular enzymes.

• Activation of gene transcription. Activation of gene transcription is one of the most important effects of activation of the second messenger systems because gene transcription can cause formation of new proteins within the neuron, thereby changing its metabolic machinery or its structure.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding the neurotransmitter glutamate in the brain?
options: It is involved in excitatory neurotansmission
It is a minor neurotransmitter in the brain
It acts via both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors
Glycine binding to the NMDA receptor is essential for the receptor to respond to glutamate
questions.answer: B. It is a minor neurotransmitter in the brain
questions.explanation:
Glutamate is a major excitatory neurotransmitter responsible for ~75% excitatory neurotransmission in the CNS.

Glutamate is the best-known example of excitatory amino acid neurotransmitters. It brings about its action via both ionotropic and metabotropic receptors.

 Glutamate Receptors :

Type

Mechanism of Action

Ionotropic Glutamate Receptors

AMPA, Kainate receptors

Primarily permits influx of Na+ and efflux of K+ →EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential)

NMDA receptors

Permits ↑ influx of Ca2+ along with Na+

→EPSP (excitatory postsynaptic potential)

(Glycine binding to the NMDA receptor is essential for the receptor to respond to glutamate)

Metabotropic Glutamate Receptor(mGluR)

Leads to either ↑ in IP3/DAG or ↓cAMP

questions.question: Which of the following is a well-known inhibitory brain neurotransmitter?
questions.explanation:
GABA (gamma-amino-butyric acid) is probably the best known inhibitory neurotransmitter in the brain, especially in the forebrain regions.

GABA mediates both presynaptic and postsynaptic inhibition

GABA Receptors :

Type

Mechanism of Action

GABA A and GABA C

Ionotropic receptors

Activation →↑Cl- influx into the neurons → IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential)

Benzodiazepines (diazepam), barbiturates and phenobarbital enhance/potentiate the effect of GABA A receptors (neuromodulation)

GABA B

Metabotropic receptors

G-protein coupled receptors

Gi→inhibits adenylyl cyclase to open K+ channels

G0→ inhibits or delays Ca2+ influx

Net effect=IPSP

Other options :

• Glutamate is a good example of an excitatory brain neurotransmitter.

• Acetylcholine and glycine have been known to play either excitatory or inhibitory neurotransmitter roles depending on the particular brain circuits under study.

Note:

Glycine sometimes potentiates the excitatory action of glutamate at NMDA receptors. So, it might act as an excitatory neurotransmitter as well.

questions.question: Correctly matched with its receptor is ______
questions.explanation:
GABA A is an ionotropic receptor.

GABA is the major inhibitory mediator both pre and postsynaptically in the brain.

GABA receptors :

Type

Mechanism of Action

GABA A and GABA C

Ionotropic receptors

Activation →↑Cl- influx into the neurons → IPSP (inhibitory postsynaptic potential)

Benzodiazepines (eg. Diazepam), barbiturates and phenobarbital enhance/potentiate the effect of GABA A receptors (neuromodulation)

GABA B

Metabotropic receptors

G protein coupled receptors

Gi→inhibits adenylyl cyclase to open K+ channels G

G0→ inhibits or delays Ca2+ influx

Net effect=IPSP

questions.question: Which is not true about neuromodulators?
options: Modify the postsynaptic neuron’s response to a specific neurotransmitter
May change the presynaptic neuron’s release of a transmitter
May be released by the presynaptic neuron along with the neurotransmitter
questions.answer: D. Actions are faster than neurotransmitters
questions.explanation:
Neuromodulators typically have actions that are slower than neurotransmitters.

Neuromodulators are chemicals released by neurons that have little or no direct effects on their own but can modify the effects of neurotransmitters.

They can modify the postsynaptic neuron’s response to a neurotransmitter and they can change how much of a neurotransmitter the presynaptic neuron synthesizes or releases.

Neuromodulators also can be released by the presynaptic neuron along with the neurotransmitter.

questions.question: A medical student was doing research in a laboratory that studies the neuromuscular junction. Which of the following events at the junction are listed in correct sequential order?
options: Motor neuron action potential, acetylcholine release, Ca2+ entry at the endplate
Ca2+ entry into the motor nerve terminal, acetylcholine release, Na+ entry at the endplate
Ca2+ entry into the motor nerve terminal, Na+ entry at the endplate, motor neuron action potential
Na+ entry at the endplate, acetylcholine release, muscle fiber action potential
questions.answer: B. Ca2+ entry into the motor nerve terminal, acetylcholine release, Na+ entry at the endplate
questions.explanation:
Events Occurring at the Chemical Synapse:

The action potential arriving at the end of the motor neuron increases the permeability of its endings to Ca2+

 ↓

Ca2+ enters the endings and triggers a marked increase in exocytosis of the acetylcholine-containing synaptic vesicles

 ↓

Binding of acetylcholine to nicotinic receptors increases the Na+ and K+ conductance

 ↓

Resultant influx of Na+ produces a local depolarizing potential, the endplate potential

 ↓

The current created by this local potential depolarizes the adjacent muscle membrane to its firing level

 ↓

Action potentials are generated on either side of the endplate and are conducted away from the endplate in both directions along the muscle fiber. This muscle action potential, in turn, initiates muscle contraction.

Acetylcholine is then removed from the synaptic cleft by acetylcholinesterase, which is present in high concentration at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.question: Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is due to the influx of ______.
questions.explanation:
Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) is due to the influx of sodium ions (Na+).

At the post-synaptic membrane, neurotransmitters binding to receptors generate responses that can be excitatory or inhibitory. If it generates an excitatory response (makes the membrane more electrically positive/ depolarized), it is an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) because it makes the cell more likely to reach an action potential.

EPSP may be due to

• The opening of sodium channels or calcium channels to allow large numbers of positive electrical charges to flow to the interior of the postsynaptic cell.

• Depressed conduction through chloride or potassium channels or both.

• Various changes in the internal metabolism of the postsynaptic neuron to increase the number of excitatory membrane receptors or decrease the number of inhibitory membrane receptors.

As seen in the figure, following the discharge of the sensory neuron, there is positivity in the motor neuron signifying a EPSP.

questions.question: Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential (IPSP) is due to influx of ______
questions.explanation:
Inhibitory Postsynaptic Potential (IPSP) is due to the influx of chloride ions (Cl-).

If, binding of a neurotransmitter causes the postsynaptic membrane to become more negative (hyperpolarized), it is called an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) because hyperpolarization moves the membrane potential farther from the threshold and makes the cell less likely to reach an action potential.

IPSP may be due to :

• Increase in Cl- influx. This action causes diffusion of negatively charged chloride ions from outside the postsynaptic neuron to the inside, thereby carrying negative charges inward and increasing the negativity inside. This leads to hyperpolarization.

• Increase in K+ efflux. This action causes positive ions to diffuse to the exterior, which causes increased negativity inside the neuron, which leads to hyperpolarization.

• Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors or decrease the number of excitatory receptors.

questions.question: The following effect in the motor neuron is due to:
options: Opening of chloride ion channels through the pre-synaptic neuronal membrane
Increase in conductance of potassium ions to the inside of the neuron
Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors
Increase in conductance of sodium ions inside the neuron
questions.answer: C. Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors
questions.explanation:
Activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors can cause the effect shown, namely, the generation of IPSP.

In the figure given, there is an increased negativity in the motor neuron following the action potential in the interneuron. So, the synaptic potential is IPSP. This can be caused at the postsynaptic membrane due to Cl- influx, K+ efflux or activation of receptor enzymes that increase the number of inhibitory synaptic receptors or decrease the number of excitatory receptors.

Other options:

• Opening of chloride ion channels through the post-synaptic neuronal membrane.

• Increase in conductance of potassium ions to the outside of the postsynaptic neuron.

• Increase in conductance of sodium ions inside the neuron causes the generation of an EPSP.

questions.question: Slow inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) is generated by all except _______
questions.explanation:
Slow EPSPs and IPSPs are not generated by skeletal muscles.

Slow excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) and inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSPs) are seen in autonomic ganglia, cardiac, and smooth muscle, and cortical neurons.

EPSPs and IPSPs occur after a latency of 0.5ms while slow EPSPs and IPSPs occur after a latency of 100–500 ms and last for several seconds. The slow EPSPs are due to a decrease in K+ efflux, and the slow IPSPs are due to an increase in K+ efflux.

questions.question: Which of the following physiologic processes is not correctly matched?
options: Presynaptic inhibition: GABA-B receptors decrease K+ conductance.
Presynaptic inhibition: GABA-A receptors increase Cl– conductance.
questions.answer: C. Presynaptic inhibition: GABA-B receptors decrease K+ conductance.
questions.explanation:
GABA-B receptors are present in the spinal cord and appear to mediate presynaptic inhibition via a G-protein that produces an increase in K+ conductance.

PRE-SYNAPTIC INHIBITION

• Presynaptic inhibition is a process mediated by neurons whose terminals are on excitatory endings, forming axoaxonal synapses.

• The first transmitter shown to produce presynaptic inhibition was GABA. On the pre-synaptic membrane

• Acting via GABA-A receptors, GABA increases Cl– conductance.

• GABA-B receptors appear to mediate presynaptic inhibition via a G-protein that produces an increase in K+ conductance.

• This leads to hyperpolarization of the pre-synaptic membrane and inhibition of release of the neurotransmittor from the pre-synaptic neuron.

POST-SYNAPTIC INHIBITION

• Postsynaptic inhibition occurs when an inhibitory transmitter such as glycine or GABA is released from a presynaptic nerve terminal onto the postsynaptic neuron to induce an IPSP in the postsynaptic neuron.

• In the figure shown below, an inhibitory transmitter such as GABA is released from the nerve terminals of an inhibitory interneuron (dark) that synapses on a postsynaptic neuron.

questions.question: Renshaw cell inhibition is ________
questions.explanation:
Renshaw cell inhibition is an example of feedback inhibition.

The axon of a spinal motor neuron has a recurrent collateral that synapses on an inhibitory interneuron that terminates on the cell body of the same and other motor neurons. The inhibitory interneuron is called a Renshaw cell and its neurotransmitter is glycine.

questions.question: Feedforward inhibition is seen in ________
questions.explanation:
Feedforward inhibition is seen in the cerebellum. In the cerebellum, stimulation of basket cells / stellate cells produces IPSPs in the Purkinje cells (i.e, inhibits Purkinje cells)
