questions.question: In which phase of sleep bruxism occurs?
questions.explanation:
Sleep-related bruxism is diagnosed when an individual grinds or clenches the teeth during sleep. Bruxism occurs more commonly during NREM 2.

Parasomnias refer to abnormal behavior or experiences that arise from or occur during sleep.

questions.question: Which of the following sleep disorder does not occur in stage 3 of NREM?
questions.explanation: Bruxism occurs in stage 2 of NREM, whereas other sleep disorders given in the option occur in stage 3 of NREM

questions.question: A 30-year-old male, who met with an RTA, regained consciousness after 36 hours. It was then discovered that the patient is unable to create new memories. Which of the following is the probable site of the lesion?
questions.explanation:
From the history, it is clear that the patient is suffering fron anterograde amnesia, most probably due to a lesion is hippocampus.

Hippocampus is the primary structure within the temporal lobe involved in conversion of short-term memory to long-term memory.

Hippocampal cognitive map is inappropriately reactivated during a deja vu experience.

Hippocampus does not store memory but only converts short-term memory to long-term memory. Hence, hippocampal lesions cause only anterograde amnesia.

questions.question: Which of the following is correctly paired to show the relationship between a brain area and a type of memory?
options: Medial temporal lobe and declarative memory
questions.answer: B. Medial temporal lobe and declarative memory
questions.explanation:
Declarative memory involves the hippocampus and the medial temporal lobe for retention.

Priming - neocortex.

Procedural memory - striatum.

Associative learning- amygdala for its emotional responses and the cerebellum for the motor responses.

Nonassociative learning - various reflex pathways.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man is severely injured in a road traffic accident. Brain MRI shows significant damage to the bilateral frontal lobes. Which of the following neurological features will be least likely seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Retained judgement will be least likely seen if the patient survives such a devastating injury.

Injury to the frontal lobe may lead to frontal lobe syndrome, which consists of poor judgment, slowed thinking, decreased curiosity, social withdrawal, and irritability.

Frontal lobe injury:

• Impairs the executive functions: motivation, attention, and sequencing of actions

• Aphasia, apraxia, constructional apraxia, neglect, and memory deficits can be seen

• Characterized by changes in personality

• Apathetic indifference and impulsive behaviour.

• Commonly urinary incontinence and faecal incontinence is seen

• Commonly produced by trauma, infarcts, tumours, lobotomy, multiple sclerosis, or Pick's disease.

Frontal lobe pathology may become apparent only under unstructured, stressful, real-life situations and are difficult to detect in intelligence scales, as IQ mostly requires parietal lobe activation.

questions.question: Emotion is regulated by:
questions.explanation:
Emotion is regulated by the frontal lobe.

There are two aspects of emotion:

• Genesis of emotion and rating of emotional importance –from the limbic system – amygdala.

• The limbic system houses the emotional association areas, which direct the hypothalamus to express the motor and endocrine components of the emotional state.

• The amygdala rates the emotional importance of an experience and activates the hippocampus (memory) accordingly. Thus an emotionally intense experience is etched in memory, which is the basis for learned fear responses.

• Damage to the amygdala ablates the ability to distinguish fear and anger in other persons' voices and facial expressions.

• Regulation of emotion - frontal lobe.

questions.question: The main stimulus for the carotid body is a fall in:
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond mainly to low PaO2.

questions.question: Where is the pneumotaxic centre located?
questions.explanation:
Pneumotaxic center is located in upper pons.

Neural regulation of respiration:

It involves set of neurons located in pons and medulla:

• Pons:

• Pneumotaxic centre

• Apneustic centre

• Medulla: Pre-Botzinger complex

• Dorsal respiratory group

• Ventral respiratory group

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the main respiratory control neurons?
options: Send out regular bursts of impulses to expiratory muscles during quiet respiration
Are unaffected by impulses from the cerebral cortex
Send out regular bursts of impulses to inspiratory muscles during quiet respiration
questions.answer: D. Send out regular bursts of impulses to inspiratory muscles during quiet respiration
questions.explanation:
The main respiratory control neurons called the pre- Bőtzinger complex (pre-BOTC), are located in the medulla.

Pre-Bötzinger complex (pre-BÖTC) is located on either side of the medulla, between the nucleus ambiguus and the lateral reticular nucleus

They send out regular bursts of impulses to inspiratory muscles via phrenic nerve during quiet respiration.

Option a: Expiration is passive during quiet breathing. There is no discharge of any neurons.

Option b: Pain stimulates respiration. There are NK1 receptors and μ-opioid receptors in Pre-Botzinger complex, and, in vivo, substance P stimulates and opioids inhibit respiration.

Option c: Impulses from cerebral cortex also influence the pre-Botzinger complex.

questions.question: The rate of inspiration is controlled by _______
options: Ventral group of neurons in medulla
questions.explanation:
The rate of inspiration is controlled by the pneumotaxic center.

Pneumotaxic centre:

Location: Upper pons (dorsally in nucleus parabrachialis)

Function:

• Transmits signals to the inspiratory area, i.e., it inhibits the apneustic center and thus the dorsal respiratory group of neurons, to stop inspiration.

• It thus helps limit duration of inspiration and switching between inspiration and expiration.

• This has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing because limiting the duration of inspiration also shortens the duration of expiration, and hence, the entire period of respiration.

questions.question: Depth of inspiration is increased by_____
options: Ventral group of neurons in medulla
questions.explanation:
Depth of inspiration is increased by the apneustic center.

The apneustic centre sends signals to prevent switching off of inspiration maintained by the dorsal respiratory group of neurons, thereby increasing depth of inspiration.

In contrast to this, the pneumotaxic center primarily limits inspiration by controlling the "switch off" point of the inspiratory ramp signal.

A note on inspiratory ramp signal:

The neural signals transmitted to the inspiratory muscle, mainly the diaphragm, is not the instantaneous burst of action potentials. Instead, it begins weakly and increases steadily in a ramped manner. The advantage of the ramp is that it causes a steady increase in the volume of the lungs during inspiration, rather than inspiratory gasps.

Control of the limiting point at which the ramp suddenly ceases is the mechanism by which the respiratory centers control depth and rate of respiration.

Option A: Pneumotaxic center of the pons regulates the rate and depth of breathing.
Option B: Ventral group of neurons regulate expiration.
Option C: Dorsal group of neurons regulate inspiration.

questions.question: A young couple was spending their afternoon on a picnic. Suddenly, the woman got down on her knee, pulled out a ring, and proposed. The man was taken aback and began to hyperventilate. The overdrive mechanism observed is due to_____
options: Dorsal group of neurons (DRG) in the medulla
Ventral group of neurons (VRG) in the medulla
questions.answer: D. Ventral group of neurons (VRG) in the medulla
questions.explanation:
The ventral respiratory group contributes to the extra respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism)

• During quiet breathing: Expiration is a passive process and the neurons from the ventral respiratory group remain almost totally inactive during quiet respiration. Unlike the dorsal respiratory group (DRG; dorsal group of neurons), VRG (the ventral group of neurons) does not appear to participate in the basic rhythmic oscillations that control respiration.

• Extra-respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism): When the respiratory drive for increased pulmonary ventilation becomes greater than normal, for example, during exercise, respiratory signals spill over to VRG from DRG. So, VRG contributes to the extra respiratory drive (overdrive mechanism).

• The neurons of VRG contribute to both inspiration and expiration; especially, they are important in providing powerful expiratory signals to the abdominal muscles during very heavy expiration.

Dorsal and ventral respiratory group:

Dorsal respiratory group
 Ventral respiratory group

Location
Nucleus Tractus Solitarius in medulla
Nucleus Retro Ambigualis in medulla

Function
Inspiratory ramp signals - Stimulates inspiration
Inactive during quiet breathing; Active during forced expiration

questions.question: Stimulation of the apneustic centre causes______
options: Decrease in the inspiratory ramp signal
questions.answer: B. Marked increase in inspiratory activity
questions.explanation:
The apneustic center is located in the lower pons and it stimulates the inspiratory center to increase inspiratory activity.

The apneustic center of pons send signals to the DRG in medulla to delay the ‘switch off’ signal of the inspiratory ramp provided by pneumotaxic center of pons. It gets feedback from vagal afferents and also from other respiratory centers.

The apneustic center is inhibited by vagal afferents from pulmonary stretch receptors aroused by inspiration so that stimulatory effect on the inspiratory neurons is switched off allowing expiration to supervene.

questions.question: A few nights before the respiratory physiology exam, a student was suffering from a recurring nightmare. In this nightmare, a knife-wielding horse was chasing him through the streets and threatening to cut off his brainstem at the mid-pontine level. Assuming the horse was proficient in its threat, and performed a bilateral vagotomy as well, which of the following outcomes would occur?
questions.explanation:
Transection of the brain stem at the mid-pontine level with bilateral vagotomy causes apneusis.

At mid pontine level lesion, the apneustic centre is intact while the pneumotaxic centre is separated. Concurrent removal of vagus inputs causes this kind of abnormal pattern of breathing characterized by deep, gasping inspiration with a pause at full inspiration followed by a brief insufficient release.

questions.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors _____
options: Respond minimally to changes in PO2 under normoxic conditions
Respond to changes in arterial PO2 but not pH
Respond to changes on PCO2 slower than the central chemoreceptors
Are most important receptors causing an increased ventilation in response to a rise in PCO2
questions.answer: A. Respond minimally to changes in PO2 under normoxic conditions
questions.explanation:
Peripheral chemoreceptors respond minimally to changes in PO2 under normoxic conditions.

Because of the enormous blood flow per unit of tissue to the carotid bodies, the receptors are not stimulated in conditions such as anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, in which the amount of dissolved O2 in the blood reaching the receptors is generally normal, even though the combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased.

Peripheral chemoreceptors are responsive to changes in arterial O2, CO2, and H+ ions.

They are excited by a decrease in arterial O2. However, a graph plotted between the rate of firing of afferent neurons in the chemoreceptor vs. arterial pO2 shows they are most sensitive to changes in pO2 of less than 60mmHg. Thus, ventilation is driven by pCO2 and H+ under normoxic conditions.

Other options :

• Option B: Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to changes in blood pH. They are excited by an increase in H+ ions (i.e decrease in pH)

• Option C: The response of peripheral chemoreceptors to changes in Pco2 is faster than that of central chemoreceptors. Increase in arterial pCO2 stimulates respiration. However, the stimulation by way of peripheral chemoreceptors occurs 5 times as rapidly as that from central chemoreceptors. This helps increase the rapididty of response to CO2 at the onset of exercise.

• Option D: Central chemoreceptors are more important than the peripheral chemoreceptors in the ventilatory response to increased CO2.

Note:

• Most potent stimulus for central chemoreceptor in blood: CO2

• Most potent stimulus for central chemoreceptor in CSF: H+ ions

• Most potent stimulus for respiration: CO2

questions.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors are primarily sensitive to_____
questions.explanation:
The peripheral chemoreceptors, located in the carotid and aortic bodies, are primarily sensitive to decrease in arterial PO2, although high PaCO2 and low pH also stimulates them and enhance their sensitivity to hypoxia.

Carotid body is more sensitive than aortic body.

questions.question: Peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated maximally by____
questions.explanation:
Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia, and thus, by preventing the O2 utilization at the tissue level; it acts as the powerful stimulus for peripheral chemoreceptors. Even though Po2 level of blood is normal in case of cyanide poisoning the sensors in carotid and aortic bodies are not able to sense oxygen in blood because of blockade of cellular respiration and hence, they go in for hypoxic state and gets stimulated.

• Option a: Acidosis (Increased H+ ions) stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors.

• Option b: Increased pCO2 mainly stimulates central chemoreceptors.

• Option c: The peripheral chemoreceptors have an enormous blood flow per unit tissue (2000mL/100g of tissue/min) because of which the O2 needs of the cells can be met by dissolved O2 Therefore, Carbon monoxide poisoning does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors because the amount of dissolved O2 is generally normal, even though the combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased.

questions.question: Carotid body chemoreceptors are stimulated by all of the following types of hypoxia except_____
questions.explanation:
Anemic hypoxia does not stimulate carotid body chemoreceptors.

In anemia,

• Amount of dissolved O2 reaching the receptors is generally normal

• Combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased.

• The blood flow per unit tissue of carotid body chemoreceptors is enormous (2000mL/100g of tissue/min). Hence, O2 needs of the tissue can be met largely by dissolved O2 alone. Therefore, the receptors are not stimulated by conditions such as anemia or carbon monoxide poisoning, in which the amount of dissolved O2 reaching the receptors is generally normal, even though combined O2 in the blood is markedly decreased. These peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated when arterial pO2 is low.

questions.question: Central chemoreceptors_____
options: Respond to both pCO2 and pO2 of blood
Are activated by changes in pH of the CSF
For a given rise in pCO2, the pH of the CSF falls less than that of blood
HCO3- concentration in CSF doesnt affect output of central chemoreceptors
questions.answer: B. Are activated by changes in pH of the CSF
questions.explanation:
Central chemoreceptors are stimulated by changes in pH of the CSF. They are located on the ventral surface of medulla

Option A: Central chemoreceptors do not respond to pO2 of the blood.

Option C: For a given rise in pCO2, the CSF pH falls more than that of the blood because the CSF has less buffering. CO2 combines with H2O to form H2CO3 which dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. H+ is buffered by combining with Hb. This buffering is less in CSF and hence pH falls.

Option D: The HCO3- concentration of the CSF can affect the output of the central chemoreceptors by buffering the changes in pH. HCO3- can combine with H+ and thus neutralise it and alter pH and thus alter output of central chemoreceptors.

questions.question: Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to the following change in the blood:
questions.explanation:
Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased Pco2 in the blood.

Central chemoreceptors are most sensitive to increased Pco2 in the blood because CO2 moves into the CSF, where it is promptly hydrated to form H2CO3 that dissociates to increase the CSF H+ concentration. This stimulates the central chemoreceptors, which monitor CSF H+ concentration (not blood H+ concentration).

Other options:

• H+ in arterial blood penetrates the blood-brain barrier very slowly and hence has little effect on central chemoreceptors.

• Arterial Po2 has no effect on central chemoreceptors.

questions.question: The primary direct stimulus for excitation of central chemoreceptors which regulate ventilation is______
questions.explanation:
The central chemoreceptors are primarily stimulated by an increase in the H+ in the CSF.

CO2 readily penetrates the blood-brain barrier and is promptly hydrated in the CSF to form H2CO3 that dissociates so that local H+ concentration rises. The H+ concentration in the CSF parallels the arterial Pco2. So the effect of arterial Pco2 and CO2 in CSF is indirect or secondary.

Arterial Po2 has no effect on central chemoreceptors.

questions.question: Peripheral and central chemoreceptors may both contribute to increased ventilation that occurs as a result of decreased______
questions.explanation:
Both peripheral and central chemoreceptors contribute to increased ventilation that occurs as a result of decreased arterial blood pressure.

• Decrease in arterial blood pressure → hypoperfusion → hypoxia → stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors.

• Decrease in arterial blood pressure → CO2 retention → increased arterial PCO2 → ↑ H+ concentration in the CSF → stimulation of central chemoreceptors

Option a : Decreased arterial Pco2 doesnt stimulate chemoreceptors. It is increased Pco2 that stimulates central chemoreceptors.

Option b : Decreased arterial Po2 stimulates peripheral chemoreceptors but has no influence on central chemoreceptors.

Option d : Increased (not decreased) H+ ions stimulate both peripheral and central chemoreceptors.

questions.question: Which of the following do not stimulate either central or peripheral chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation:
Hypercapnia is a stimulus for central and peripheral chemoreceptors and not hypocapnia.

Option b: The peripheral chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypoxia (hypoxic, stagnant and histotoxic but NOT anemic hypoxia)and exercise (increased K+ levels).

Option c: The central chemoreceptors are stimulated by hypercapnia and resultant acidosis.

Option d: Low perfusion pressure produces hypoxia because the amount of O2 delivered to the receptors per unit time is decreased. This stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors.

questions.question: The most important stimulus controlling the level of resting ventilation is_____
options: pH of CSF on central chemoreceptors
questions.answer: A. pH of CSF on central chemoreceptors
questions.explanation:
The most important stimulus comes from the pH of the CSF on the central chemoreceptors. The CO2 that enters the brain and CSF is hydrated to H2CO3 and dissociates, leading to rising H+ levels. The CSF H+ concentration hence parallels the arterial CO2 levels.

The effect of pO2 on peripheral chemoreceptors under normoxic conditions is very small. Changes in pCO2 do affect the peripheral chemoreceptors, but the magnitude is less than that for the central chemoreceptors.

The effect of changes in the pH on peripheral chemoreceptors under normal conditions is small: and the changes in pO2 do not affect the central chemoreceptors.

questions.question: Which of the following occurs after hyperventilation with 6% CO2 in inspired air?
questions.explanation:
Hyperventilation with 6% CO2 is followed by continued hyperventilation till alveolar Pco2 drops towards normal.

Ventilatory responses to CO2

There is a linear relationship between increase in % of CO2 in inspired air and respiratory minute volume.

• The upper limit for this linearity is 6% of alveolar PCO2.

• When the CO2 content of the inspired gas is >7%, the alveolar and the arterial PCO2 begin to rise abruptly in spite of hyperventilation leading to hypercapnia.

• Hypercapnia depresses the central nervous system, including respiratory centers leading to CO2 narcosis (a headache, confusion and eventually coma).

Mechanism:

Increased CO2 in inspired air ⇒ Increased Alveolar PCO2 ⇒ Increased arterial PCO2 ⇒ Stimulation of central chemoreceptors ⇒ Stimulation of ventilation ⇒ Alveolar PCO2 drops toward normal

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the ventilatory response?
options: CO2 major factor controlling the normal level of ventilation
Is not related to respiratory minute volume
Is increased if alveolar PO2 is raised
questions.answer: A. CO2 major factor controlling the normal level of ventilation
questions.explanation:
The normal level of ventilation is controlled by the ventilatory response to CO2.

Option b: There is linear relationship between respiratory minute volume and the alveolar Pco2, i.e. as alveolar Pco2 increases respiratory minute volume increases.

Option c: The ventilatory response depends on peripheral chemoreceptors in addition to central chemoreceptors.

Option d: The ventilatory response to CO2 is increased if the alveolar PO2 is reduced

The ventilatory response is reduced also during sleep.

questions.question: Hering-Breuer reflexes are mediated by ____________ .
questions.answer: A. Slowly adapting myelinated vagal fibers
questions.explanation:
Hering-Breuer reflexes are mediated by slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers.

Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: "Prolonged inspiration inhibits further inspiration"

• Hyperinflation of lungs stimulates slowly adapting pulmonary stretch receptors and the impulses travel in the vagus nerve via large myelinated fibers.

• This signal inhibits the inspiratory ramp signals of the dorsal respiratory group of neurons (DRG), thus, inspiration is quickly inhibited and expiration follows.

• Advantages of Hering-Breuer inflation reflex: It cuts down the inspiration time, and therefore,

• It prevents overinflation of the lungs.

• Lungs operate at lower lung volumes, thereby preventing wastage of energy.

• The Hering-Breuer reflex is activated when the lung volume increases to more than three times the normal tidal volume (tidal volume = 0.5 liters/breath; So, lung volume > 1.5 liters per breath activates the reflex).

• It signifies that the reflex plays a protective role preventing the overinflation of the lung rather than regulating the normal ventilation.

questions.question: All of the following statements about Hering-Breuer inflation reflex are true except_____
options: The impulses travel to the brain via vagus nerve
It results in further inspiratory efforts if the lung is maintained inflated
It is seen in adults at high tidal volumes
Abolishing the reflex in many animals causes slow deep breathing
questions.answer: B. It results in further inspiratory efforts if the lung is maintained inflated
questions.explanation:
Hering-Breuer inflation reflex inhibits further inspiratory efforts if the lungs are maintained inflated.

Mechanism- Stretch receptors ⇒ Vagus ⇒ Inhibit Dorsal Respiratory Group ⇒ Phrenic & Intercostal Nerves ⇒ Inspiration shortened, Expiration prolonged

Option a: The impulses travel to the brain via the vagus nerve.

Option c: HB Reflex activated when TV > 1.5L. The reflex is seen in adults at high tidal volumes.

Option d: Abolishing the reflex by cutting the vagal nerves in experimental animals causes slow deep breathing.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about Head’s paradoxical reflex?
options: Plays an important role in normal respiration
questions.answer: B. Stimulated by hyperinflation of lung
questions.explanation:
Head’s paradoxical reflex is stimulated by hyperinflation of lungs. It refers to prolonged inspiration stimulating further inspiration. Hyperinflation of the lungs causes strong and long-lasting inspiratory effort (an effect opposite to the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex).

Physiological role:

• Occasional deep breaths which are thought to counteract any tendency to atelectasis in quiet breathing and possibly in reinforcing the gasps or inspiratory efforts.

• First cry after birth.

• The possible explanation for this could be the inhibition of vagus nerve at cold temperatures (due to the presence of pulmonary fluid in the unaerated newborn lungs).

• Lack of inhibitory impulses from the pulmonary stretch receptors and vagus has an effect opposite to Hering-Breuer’s inflation reflex.

questions.question: The immediate response of J receptor stimulation is
questions.explanation:
The immediate reflex response of J receptor stimulation is apnea. It is followed by rapid breathing, bradycardia, and hypotension (pulmonary chemoreflex).

Juxtacapillary receptors are the C fiber endings located close to the pulmonary vessels in the alveolar interstitium. They are not involved in quiet or normal respiration. They are stimulated by

• Hyperinflation of the lung

• Intravenous or intracardiac administration of chemicals like capsaicin P

questions.question: Moderate exercise being one of the most powerful stimulators of ventilation works by the way of_____
options: Low PO2 in mixed venous blood
questions.explanation:
Moderate exercise does not reduce the arterial Po2, increase the arterial Pco2, or reduce the arterial pH.

Option A: The brain, upon transmitting motor impulses to the exercising muscles, is believed to transmit collateral impulses into the brainstem at the same time to excite the respiratory center. This action is analogous to the stimulation of the vasomotor center of the brain stem during exercise that causes a simultaneous increase in arterial pressure.

Option B: The Po2 of mixed venous blood does fall, but there are no known chemoreceptors that are stimulated as a result.

Option C:

Two points are important regarding pH during moderate exercise:

• pH = pK+ log ([HCO3-)/ [CO2])

• The pH of the blood is dependent only on the ratio of the amount of CO2 to the amount of HCO3-. The concentrations of both buffer components (HCO3- and CO2) are very large compared to the amount of H+ added to the blood during moderate exercise. Thus, any change in HCO3- due to the addition of H+ during moderate exercise is very tiny compared to the amount of HCO3- already present in the blood. Thus, the pH of blood during moderate exercise remains constant.

• When sufficient oxygen is not available during exercise, there is increased accumulation of lactic acid, which initially leads to an increase in PaCO2. However, this is counteracted by the stimulation of ventilation and as a result, PaCO2 is decreased. This provides some respiratory compensation for further lactic acid production and prevents a decline in blood pH. Thus, blood pH remains constant in moderate exercise.

questions.question: The exercise-induced hyperventilation during vigorous exercise is produced due to the receptors present in ______
questions.explanation:
The exercise-induced hyperventilation during vigorous exercise is produced due to the receptors present in carotid bodies.

When exercise becomes more vigorous, buffering of the increased amounts of lactic acid that are produced liberates more CO2, and this further increases ventilation. The additional increase in ventilation produced by the acidosis depends on the carotid bodies and does not occur if they are removed.

Note: The abrupt increase at the start of exercise is presumably due to psychic stimuli and afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.

questions.question: In moderate exercise, the respiratory rate is increased at the beginning due to the response of______
options: Decrease in PO2 in arterial blood
questions.explanation:
In moderate exercise, the respiratory rate is increased at the beginning due to the response of joint proprioceptor stimulation.

Respiratory responses to exercise

• During exercise, there is an increase in ventilatory rate that matches the increase in O2 consumption and CO2 production by the body. The stimulus for increased ventilation rate is the activation of joint proprioceptors at the beginning of the exercise.

• The mean values for arterial Po2 and Pco2 do not change during exercise. Arterial pH does not change during moderate exercise, although it may decrease during strenuous exercise because of lactic acidosis.

• On the other hand, venous Pco2 increases during exercise because the excess CO2 produced by exercising muscle is carried to the lungs in venous blood.

• Pulmonary blood flow increases because cardiac output increases during exercise. As a result, more pulmonary capillaries are perfused, and more gas exchange occurs. The distribution of V/Q ratios throughout the lung is more even during exercise than when at rest, and there is a resulting decrease in the physiologic dead space.

The abrupt increase at the start of exercise is presumably due to

• Psychic stimuli

• Afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, and joints.

The more gradual increase in ventilation is presumably due to

• Increase in O2 consumption (Proportional increase)

• Increase in body temperature

• Increases in the plasma K+ level (Stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors).

• Sensitivity of the neurons controlling the response to CO2 is increased or that the respiratory fluctuations in arterial PCO2 increase so that, even though the mean arterial PCO2 does not rise, it is CO2 that is responsible for the increase in ventilation.

questions.question: Which among the following is not a function of pneumotaxic centre ?
options: Increase in the rate of breathing
questions.explanation:
Respiratory rhythm generation is a function of dorsal respiratory group of neurons (and not pneumotaxic center).

Pneumotaxic center:

• It is located dorsally in the nucleus parabrachialis of the upper pons and it transmits signals to the inspiratory area.

• Primary effect of this center is to control the switch­off point of the inspiratory ramp, thus controlling the duration of the filing phase of the lung cycle.

• Function of the pneumotaxic center is primarily to limit inspiration, which has a secondary effect of increasing the rate of breathing, because limitation of inspiration also shortens expiration and the entire period of each respiration.

questions.question: What is the total number of airway divisions present in between trachea and alveolar sacs?
questions.explanation:
The total number of airway generations present in between the trachea and alveolar sac is 23.

The tracheobronchial tree is divided into multiple generations based on Weibel’s lung model. It begins at the trachea (designated as zero) and ends with alveoli (last generation). There are 2 zones:

• Conducting zone

• Consists of the first 16 generations

• Incapable of gas exchange

• Respiratory zone

• Consists of the last 7 generations (17-23)

• Capable of gas exchange

 Terminal bronchiole is the transition point between the conducting and respiratory zone.

questions.question: A 14-year-old boy with shortness of breath was diagnosed with chronic inflammation of conducting airways. Which of the following is not a feature of the affected structure?
options: Includes first 16 generations starting from trachea
Secrete variety of molecules that aid in lung defence
Membrane bound organelles namely lamellar bodies are present
questions.answer: D. Membrane bound organelles namely lamellar bodies are present
questions.explanation:
Chronic inflammation of conducting airways is suggestive of asthma. Lamellar bodies are storage bodies of surfactant present in the alveoli and not the conducting airway.

The conducting airways form the first 16 generations from the trachea to the terminal bronchial. It is lined by pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium. It also consists of smooth muscles which are responsible for bronchoconstriction and dilatation. It also consists of other specialized cells such as:

• Basal cells - stem cells

• Clara/Club cells - specialized epithelial cells (non-ciliated cuboidal cells) that:

• Functions as stem cells

• Helps in lung defense.

The conducting airways secrete several substances that in lung defense such as:

• Secretory immunoglobins - IgA

• Collectins - surfactant protein(SP)-A and SP-D

• Defensins

• Reactive oxygen species

• Reactive nitrogen species.

questions.question: Maximal smooth muscle relative to wall thickness is seen in _______.
questions.explanation: Smooth muscle is maximum in terminal bronchioles.

questions.question: An elderly smoker who presented with an acute exacerbation of COPD is administered salbutamol. Which one of the following substances has a similar mechanism of action?
questions.explanation:
Salbutamol, a short-acting beta (adrenergic) agonist (SABA) is a bronchodilator. Similarly, vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP) is also a bronchodilator. Along with dynorphin, it is part of the non-adrenergic non-cholinergic (NANC) inhibitory system.

Bronchial innervation:

Site
Type of receptor
Effect

Sympathetic system

Tracheal and bronchial smooth muscle

Bronchial glands

β2

Increase secretion

Parasympathetic system (more predominant)

Tracheal and bronchial smooth muscle

Contraction

Bronchial glands
M2, M3
Stimulation

Other potent bronchoconstrictors are histamine and leukotrienes.

Clinical relevance:

• Methacholine sensitivity test or Airway hyperresponsiveness test: Methacholine which is similar to acetylcholine causes exaggerated bronchoconstriction in case of bronchial asthma.

• 5-Lipoxygenase inhibitor (5-LOX inhibitor-Zileuton), selective CysLT-receptor antagonists (Cys leukotriene receptor antagonist-zafirlukast, pranlukast, and montelukast), and β2 receptor agonists are used in the treatment of asthma.

questions.question: Which of the following cells secrete surfactant in lungs?
questions.explanation:
Type 2 pneumocytes secrete surfactant in the lungs.

Alveolar Lining Epithelial Cells

Two types

• Type I cells – The primary lining cells of the alveoli (squamous epithelium); Helps in gas exchange

• Type II cells – Granular pneumocytes produce surfactant

Type II cells make 60% of epithelial cells in alveoli but type I cells form 95% of the total surface area because of its flat surface.

Type II cells are stem cells which help in replenishing damaged Type 1 pneumocytes in conditions like drug-induced pulmonary toxicity by amiodarone, bleomycin etc.

Other cells – Pulmonary alveolar macrophages (PAMs/type 3 alveolar cells), lymphocytes, plasma cells, neuroendocrine cells (APUD cells-Amine precursor uptake and decarboxylation), and mast cells.

questions.question: Surfactant is composed mainly of_____
questions.explanation:
Major surfactant is dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine i.e Lecithin. Sphingomyelin is a minor surfactant.

The surfactant is a surface-active agent in water, which means that it greatly reduces the surface tension of water.

Pulmonary surfactant is produced by type 2 pneumocytes.

Most important components are

• Phospholipid - dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) also known as Dipalmitoyl Lecithin. Lecithin is the most abundant lipid in surfactant.

• Phosphatidylglycerol- minor component

• Surfactant apoproteins

• Calcium ions.

• 4 unique apoproteins of surfactant: surfactant protein (SP)-A, SP-B, SP-C, and SP-D.

Clinical relevance:

• Tests to assess fetal lung maturity:

• L/S ratio i.e. Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio: Ratio ≥ 2 is considered normal.

• Shake test/Bubble test/Clement test: Formation of stable foam in the presence of surfactant.

• Phosphatidylglycerol levels in Amniotic fluid

• Autosomal dominant familial interstitial lung disease has absent surfactant protein SP-C.

• Pulmonary alveolar proteinosis - Autoantibody against GM-CSF which is involved in clearance of surfactant.

questions.question: All are true of surfactant except_____
options: Deficiency of surfactant causes Infant Respiratory Distress Syndrome
Helps prevents alveolar collapse according to Bernoulli's principle
Decrease in surfactant increases the work of breathing
questions.answer: C. Helps prevents alveolar collapse according to Bernoulli's principle
questions.explanation:
Surfactant helps to prevent alveolar collapse according to Law of Laplace.(Not Bernoulli's)

Physiologic advantages of surfactant

• By reducing surface tension it increases lung compliance

• Reduces the lung's tendency to recoil

• Helps to keep the alveoli dry

• Helps to prevent pulmonary edema (Option A)

The surface tension generates a pressure that tends to collapse the sphere.

In accordance with Law of Laplace - P=2T/r, where
P - Collapsing pressure on alveolus (dynes/cm2) or Pressure required to keep alveolus open (dynes/cm2)
T = Surface tension (dynes/cm)
r = Radius of the alveolus (cm).

Collapsing pressure is inversely related to radius i.e. large alveolus (one with a large radius) will have a low collapsing pressure and therefore will require only minimal pressure to keep it open. On the other hand, a small alveolus (one with a small radius) will have a high collapsing pressure and require more pressure to keep it open.

By reducing surface tension, surfactant reduces the collapsing pressure for a given radius.

Option B: Surfactant deficiency is an important cause of infant respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) also known as hyaline membrane disease, the serious pulmonary disease that develops in infants born before their surfactant system is functional.

• In IRDS, there is high surface tension in the lungs resulting in atelectasis

• Also, there is retention of fluid in the lungs.

• During fetal life, Cl- is secreted with fluid by the pulmonary epithelial cells. At birth, there is a shift to Na+ reabsorption by these cells via ENaC and fluid is absorbed along with Na+. Prolonged immaturity of ENaC contributes to pulmonary edema in IRDS.

Option D: Surfactant increases lung compliance, which reduces the work of expanding the lungs during inspiration. Increasing the compliance of the lungs reduces the collapsing force at any given volume so that it is easier for the lungs to expand.

questions.question: A young lady at 35 weeks of gestation is at high risk of preterm delivery in the next 7 days. She is started on antenatal corticosteroid therapy to increase surfactant production in the fetus. What is the mechanism of action of this substance?
options: Breaks the structure of water in alveoli
Lubricate the flow of CO2 diffusion
questions.answer: A. Breaks the structure of water in alveoli
questions.explanation:
The mechanism of action of surfactant is by breaking the structure of water in alveoli.

When water forms a surface with air, the water molecules on the surface of the alveoli have a strong attraction for one another. This pulls the molecules together, leading to high surface tension.

The surfactant is amphipathic in nature (i.e., hydrophobic on one end and hydrophilic on the other). They align themselves on the alveolar surface, with their hydrophobic portions facing the alveolar lumen.

The cohesive force between a water molecule and an adjacent pulmonary surfactant molecule is very low. So, they break up the attracting forces between water molecules lining the alveoli (which had been responsible for the high surface tension). Thus, they reduce surface tension.

questions.question: Stability of alveoli is maintained by______.
options: Increased alveolar surface area by surfactant
questions.answer: C. Increased alveolar surface area by surfactant
questions.explanation:
Stability of alveoli is maintained by increased alveolar surface area by surfactant.

Surfactant reduces the lung's tendency to recoil so that they do not collapse easily and so the stability of the alveoli is maintained.

Factors that maintain alveolar stability

• Pulmonary surfactant: ↓ surface tension within alveoli

• Mechanical interdependence: prevents alveolar collapse

Interdependence

The tendency of one alveolus to collapse is opposed by the traction exerted by the surrounding alveoli. Thus, the collapse of a single alveolus stretches and distorts the surrounding alveoli, which in turn are connected to other alveoli. This support offered to lung units by those surrounding them is termed Interdependence.

questions.question: A woman at risk for preterm delivery is planned for assessment of fetal lung maturity. At what gestational age will the surfactants be detectable in the amniotic fluid?
questions.explanation:
Surfactant appears in the amniotic fluid between 28 and 32 weeks of gestation.

By week 20-24, primitive alveoli form and surfactant production begins but it does not reach the surface of the lungs until later.

Mature levels of pulmonary surfactant are present usually after 35 wk of gestation.

Clinical aspects :

• Preterm infants develop respiratory distress syndrome or hyaline membrane disease due to surfactant deficiency.

• Antenatal corticosteroids are given to increase the production of surfactants.

• Lecithin/Sphingomyelin ratio is a test for fetal lung maturity. L/S ratio > 2 is suggestive of a mature fetal lung.

questions.question: A woman on multiple medications came for an antenatal check-up. Which among the following medications that she takes decreases surfactant production?
questions.explanation:
Inadequate Insulin intake in diabetic pregnant causes inadequate glucose control. This causes excess glucose in maternal plasma, crossing Placenta. Excess glucose in fetal plasma causes fetal pancreas to hypersecrete fetal Insulin.

Excess insulin in fetal plasma decreases surfactant production. This is the reason for the increased incidence of hyaline membrane disease in infants of diabetic mothers.

Factors increasing surfactant synthesis:

• Glucocorticoids

• Thyroxine

• Stretching of lungs in infancy

• Beta adrenergic agonist

• Calcium

• Regular exercise.

Factors decreasing surfactant synthesis:

• Smoking

• Long term inhalation of 100% oxygen

• Occlusion of main bronchus/pulmonary artery.

questions.question: Which is the best metabolic function of the lung?
options: Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
questions.answer: D. Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II
questions.explanation:
Conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II is the most significant metabolic function of the lungs.

This is mediated by angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE), located on the surface of endothelial cells in the pulmonary capillaries.

• Synthesized and used in the lungs

• Surfactant

• Synthesized or stored and released into the blood

• Prostaglandins

• Histamine

• Kallikrein

• Partially removed from the blood

• Prostaglandins

• Bradykinin

• Adenine nucleotides

• Serotonin

• Norepinephrine

• Acetylcholine

• Activated in the lungs

• Angiotensin I → Angiotensin II

questions.question: A healthy 25-year-old software engineer participates in a 10-km charity run. Which of the following muscle does this person use during expiration?
questions.answer: B. Internal intercostals and abdominal recti
questions.explanation:
In this scenario, the person has performed a strenuous exercise, so he will be using accessory muscles of respiration along with primary muscle of respiration. Internal intercostals and abdominal recti are the muscles involved.

Muscles involved in Respiration

Primary inspiratory muscles

• Diaphragm

• External intercostal muscles

Accessory inspiratory muscles

• Sternocleidomastoid

• Scaleni

• Alae nasi

• Small muscles of the head & neck

Accessory expiratory muscles

• Internal intercostal muscles

• Rectus Abdominis

• Internal & external obliques

• Transversus abdominis

Clinical correlation:

• The diaphragm is the chief muscle of inspiration.

• It is supplied by the phrenic nerve ( C3-C5 )

• Hence transection of the spinal cord above the third cervical segment is fatal without artificial respiration, but transection below the fifth cervical segment is not fatal because, it leaves the phrenic nerves that innervate the diaphragm.

questions.question: The intrapleural pressure is______
options: Negative at apex but positive at base
questions.answer: C. Negative except in forced expiration
questions.explanation:
Intrapleural pressure is usually negative. (normally -2.5 mmHg)

During inspiration, it becomes more negative. (-6 mmHg).

During forced expiration, contraction of the expiratory muscles raises intrapleural pressure to a positive value.

Intrapleural pressure is the pressure of the fluid in the thin space between the visceral and parietal pleura.

questions.question: The intrapleural pressure is negative both during inspiration and expiration because______
options: Thoracic cage and lung recoil in opposite direction
questions.answer: B. Thoracic cage and lung recoil in opposite direction
questions.explanation:
The intrapleural pressure is negative both during inspiration and expiration because the thoracic cage and lung recoil in opposite direction.

The 2 factors that lead to a negative or subatmospheric intrapleural pressure are:

• The lungs, with their elastic properties, tend to collapse, and the chest wall, with its elastic properties, tends to spring out. When these two opposing forces pull on the intrapleural space, a negative pressure, or vacuum, is created.

• The continuous suction of excess fluid into the lymphatic channels.

Applied aspect:

In cases of pneumothorax, intrapleural pressure suddenly becomes equal to atmospheric pressure. Thus instead of its normal negative value, intrapleural pressure becomes zero. Hence lungs collapse and the chest wall spring out.

questions.question: The intrapleural pressure (cm of H2O) at the beginning of inspiration is around
questions.explanation:
The normal intrapleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration is about -3.4 cm H2O (-2.5 mmHg).

Intrapleural pressure is the pressure of the fluid in the thin space between the lung pleura and the chest wall pleura. During normal inspiration, expansion of the chest cage pulls outward on the lungs with greater force and creates more negative pressure.

At the peak of normal inspiration, it is about -8.15 cm H2O (-5.4 mm Hg).

Note: 1mm Hg = 1.36 cm H2O

questions.question: With reference to atmospheric pressure, what is the alveolar pressure at the end of normal inspiration (in cms of H2O)?
questions.explanation:
At the end of inspiration, the alveolar pressure is zero with reference to the atmospheric pressure.

Whenever alveolar pressure equals atmospheric pressure, alveolar pressure is said to be zero. This happens when no air is moving in or out of the lungs.

During inspiration, the diaphragm contracts, causing the volume of the thorax to increase. As lung volume increases, the pressure in the lungs must decrease. (Boyle’s law states that P × V is constant at a given temperature.) Halfway through inspiration, the alveolar pressure falls below atmospheric pressure (−1 cm H2O). The pressure gradient between the atmosphere and the alveoli drives airflow into the lung. Air flows into the lungs until, at the end of inspiration, alveolar pressure is once again equal to the atmospheric pressure; the pressure gradient between the atmosphere and the alveoli has dissipated, and airflow into the lungs ceases.

During expiration, alveolar pressure rises to about +1 cm of H2O.

questions.question: The transpulmonary pressure is the pressure difference between _______
questions.answer: B. Intra alveolar and intrapleural pressure
questions.explanation:
Transpulmonary pressure is intra-alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure. (Mnemonic TAP: Transpulmonary pressure = Alveolar pressure - Pleural pressure)

It is the pressure difference between that in the alveoli and that on the outer surfaces of the lungs, and it is a measure of the elastic forces in the lungs that tend to collapse the lungs at each instant of respiration, called the recoil pressure.

questions.question: A man inspires 1000ml from a spirometer. The intrapleural pressure was -4cm H2O before inspiration and -12cm H20 at the end of inspiration. What is the compliance of lungs?(ml/cm H20)?
questions.explanation:
Compliance is change in volume per unit change in pressure.

• C= ΔV/ΔP

In this case,

ΔV= 1000 mL

ΔP= -12-(-4) = -8 cm of H2O

The minus sign indicates that the pressure has fallen by 8cms of H20 at the end of inspiration

Therefore the compliance is,

C= 1000/8= 125 mL/cm of H2O

questions.question: A 22-year-old woman has pulmonary compliance of 0.2 L/cm H2O and an alveolar pressure of 4 cmH2O and an intrapleural pressure of -5 cmH2O at the beginning of inspiration. What is the transpulmonary pressure (in cmH2O) when this woman inhales 600mL of air ?
questions.explanation:
The transpulmonary pressure would be 12 cmH2O when she inhales 600mL of air.

Transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) is the difference between alveolar pressure (Palv) and intrapleural pressure (Pip). It is given by the formula: Ptp = Palv-Pip. Inspiration causes a negative change in both the Palv and Pip. Lung compliance is the extent to which the lungs will expand for each unit increase in transpulmonary pressure.

In a normal adult, the pulmonary compliance is 0.2 L/cmH2O or 200 mL/cmH2O of both lungs together. Hence, expanding the lungs by 200 mL of inspired air will require an increase in Ptp by 1 cm H2O.

Given:
Pulmonary compliance = 0.2 L/cm H2O = 200 ml/cm H20
Alveolar pressure at the beginning of inspiration = 4 cmH2O
Intrapleural pressure at the beginning of inspiration = -5 cmH2O
Volume of air inhaled = 600mL (0.6L)

Step 1: Calculate the initial transpulmonary pressure (Ptp).

Transpulmonary pressure = Alveolar pressure - Intrapleural pressure; Initial transpulmonary pressure = 4 cmH2O - (-5 cmH2O) = 9 cmH2O

Step 2: Use the lung compliance formula to find the change in transpulmonary pressure.

Lung compliance = Change in volume / Change in transpulmonary pressure.

Pulmonary compliance is 0.2 L/cmH2O or 200 mL/cmH2O. Hence, to expand the lungs by 200 mL of inspired air, it will require an increase in Ptp by 1 cm H2O. So, for 600 ml inspired air, the compliance is = 600 mL / 200 mL/cm H2O = 3 cmH2O

Step 3: Calculate the transpulmonary pressure (Ptp) after inhaling 600mL of air.

During inspiration, the alveolar pressure (Palv) decreases, and the intrapleural pressure (Pip) becomes more negative.

Final transpulmonary pressure = Initial transpulmonary pressure + change in transpulmonary pressure; Final transpulmonary pressure = 9 cmH2O + 3 cmH2O = 12 cmH2O.

questions.question: Compared to a gas-ventilated lung, a liquid-ventilated lung _____
questions.explanation:
A liquid-ventilated lung is more compliant compared to a gas-ventilated lung.

Compliance is a measure of distensibility. In a gas-filled lung, surface tension and elastic recoil forces act to collapse the lung and thus reduce compliance.

• When the lungs are filled with air, there is an interface between the alveolar fluid and the air in the alveoli; so, there is surface tension.

• But, in the case of the saline solution-filled lungs, there is no air–fluid interface and there is no surface tension, making it more compliant.

• Hence, the pressure–volume curve obtained with saline measures only the tissue elasticity.

• The difference in the curves generated during inflation and deflation, termed hysteresis, is not present in the saline-generated curves.

questions.question: The factor responsible for hysteresis is _______
questions.explanation:
Surfactant is the factor responsible for hysteresis.

Difference between the curve of inflation (inspiration) and deflation (expiration) in a pressure–volume curve of the lung is termed as hysteresis.

The alveolar environment and, specifically, the secreted factors that help reduce surface tension and keep alveoli from collapsing, contribute to hysteresis.

Inspiration curve:

Expiration curve:

questions.question: In the pressure–volume graph shown below, compliance of lung is represented by _________.
questions.explanation:
In the given pressure–volume graph:

• A – Compliance of chest

• B – Compliance of lung

• C – Compliance of lung and chest wall

The equilibrium position is at functional residual capacity (FRC), where the expanding force on the chest wall is exactly equal to the collapsing force on the lungs. FRC is also known as relaxation volume and represents the amount of air remaining in the lungs at the end of normal expiration.

At the point where volume= FRC,

• Intraalveolar pressure is equal to atmospheric pressure and considered as zero.

• Intrapleural pressure is negative (-2.5 mmHg)

• Transpulmonary pressure = Intraalveolar pressure – intrapleural pressure = 0 – (-2.5 mmHg) = +2.5 mmHg.

For compliance of lung – Pressure considered is Transpulmonary pressure. So at FRC, Transpulmonary pressure is positive (+2.5 mmHg). Hence, B indicates compliance of lung.

For compliance of chest wall – Pressure considered is intrapleural – atmospheric pressure. At FRC, this value is -2.5 mmHg. Hence, A represents compliance of the chest wall.

When the volume is FRC, the combined lung and chest-wall curve intersects the X-axis at an airway pressure of zero. Hence, C represents the combined chest wall and lung compliance.

questions.question: What is specific compliance of lung?
questions.explanation:
Specific compliance is obtained by dividing compliance by functional residual capacity.

Types of compliance:

• Static compliance: It is measured at rest.

• Dynamic compliance: It is measured during breathing. It considers airflow resistance or impedance into account. It is maximum in medium-sized bronchi.

• Specific compliance:

• Lung compliance is volume-dependent.

• It is greater at low lung volumes than at high lung volumes. For this reason, the term specific compliance is often used to denote compliance with reference to the original lung volume.

• The total compliance of a normal person near the normal end-expiratory lung volume (functional residual capacity [FRC]) is about 0.1 L/cm H2O.

• The compliance of the lungs is about 0.2 L/cm H2O.

Applied aspect:

In case of emphysema, compliance is increased but specific compliance decreases (because FRC is severely elevated).

questions.question: Work done in quiet breathing is (kg-m/min)______
questions.explanation:
Work done in quiet breathing is 0.5 kg-m/min.

Estimates of the total work of quiet breathing range from 0.3 up to 0.8 kg-m/min.

The work of breathing can be calculated from the pressure-volume curve.

The value rises markedly during exercise, but the energy cost of breathing in normal individuals represents less than 3% of the total energy expenditure during exercise.

Applied aspect:

In the case of COPD, airway resistance increases (obstruction to outflow). Hence, the patient should take slow, deep breathing.

In the case of restrictive lung disease, viscous resistance increases. Hence, the patient is advised rapid, shallow breathing.

questions.question: Work of breathing is mostly due to____
questions.explanation:
Most of the work of breathing is due to surface tension elasticity.

Work of Breathing:

• Elastic/Compliance work (65%): Surface tension (2/3rd) + Tissue elasticity (1/3rd)

• Non elastic work (35%): Tissue/Viscus resistance (7%) + Airway resistance (28%)

Work of quiet breathing = 0.3 - 0.8 kg-m/min

Maximum work of breathing = 10kg-m/min

questions.question: The following diagram shows the depth of respiration of a 45-year old man who suffered a head injury in an automobile accident. Identify the pattern of breathing.
questions.explanation:
The pattern of breathing seen in the image is Cheyne–Stokes breathing. In this case, the person breathes deeply for a short interval and then breathes slightly or not for an additional interval. This pattern repeats itself about every minute.

It is the most common type of periodic breathing seen most commonly in patients with heart failure and uremia, also seen in patients with brain disease and during sleep in normal individuals.

This increased response occurs apparently due to the disruption of neural pathways that normally inhibit respiration. In such an individual, increased sensitivity to CO2 causes relative hyperventilation, lowering the arterial Pco2. During the resultant apnoea, the arterial Pco2 rises again to normal, but the respiratory mechanisms again over-responds to CO2. Breathing ceases, and the cycle repeats.

questions.question: Oxygen comes from alveoli to blood by ______.
questions.explanation:
Oxygen diffuses from alveoli to blood along the concentration gradient i.e. passive process (ATP is not used).

It diffuses across respiratory membrane

It is governed by Fick’s law of diffusion which is given in equation:

Where

• D is the diffusion rate

• ΔP is the partial pressure difference between the two ends of the diffusion pathway

• A is the cross-sectional area of the pathway

• S is the solubility of the gas

• d is the distance of diffusion

• MW is the molecular weight of the gas.

(Diffusion coefficient of the gas, which is proportional to S/√MW ).

questions.question: What is the time taken (in seconds) for blood to traverse the pulmonary capillaries at rest?
questions.explanation: Time taken by a red cell is about 0.75 seconds to traverse the pulmonary capillaries at rest and 0.3 seconds or less during exercise.

questions.question: What is the percentage of systemic cardiac output which bypasses the pulmonary circulation (physiological shunt)?
questions.explanation:
The percentage of cardiac output that bypasses the pulmonary circulation or physiological shunt is 2%. The fraction of mixed venous blood that does not become oxygenated as it moves from the right atrium to the left ventricle is called physiologic shunt.

Causes of physiological shunt:

• Extrapulmonary R->L Anatomic Shunt (normally ~ 1% of cardiac output)

• Intrapulmonary “True” Shunt

• Flow past unventilated or collapsed alveoli (e.g., due to edema, pneumonia, atelectasis)

• Anatomic arterio-venous pathways - Mixing of unoxygenated blood in bronchial veins with oxygenated blood in pulmonary capillaries or vein reduces the final partial pressure of O2 in the arterial blood (PaO2).

• Intrapulmonary regions with low ventilation/perfusion ratio: Alveolar ventilation is not zero, but blood is not completely oxygenated (A virtual shunt, not a “true” shunt).

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with shortness of breath is undergoing tests to assess lung function. Which of the following is used to measure lung diffusion capacity?
questions.explanation:
The diffusing capacity for CO (DLCO) is measured as an index of the diffusing capacity of the lung because its uptake is diffusion-limited.

The diffusing capacity of the lung for a given gas is directly proportional to the surface area of the alveolo-capillary membrane and inversely proportional to its thickness.

The normal value of DLCO at rest is about 25 mL/min/mm Hg.

It increases up to threefold during exercise because of capillary dilation and an increase in the number of active capillaries.

questions.question: The partial pressure of H2O at the body temperature (37° C) is (in mm Hg)_______
questions.explanation:
The partial pressure of water vapor at a normal body temperature of 37°C is 47 mm Hg.

Humidification of air:

• When dry air enters respiratory system it is humidified i.e. water molecules are continually escaping from the water surface (tissues) into the gas phase.

• The partial pressure that the water molecules exert to escape through the surface is called the vapor pressure of the water.

• The vapor pressure of water depends entirely on the temperature of the water.

• The greater the temperature, the greater the kinetic activity of the molecules and, therefore, the greater the likelihood that the water molecules will escape from the surface of the water into the gas phase.

• For instance, the water vapor pressure at 0°C is 5 mm Hg, and at 100°C it is 760 mm Hg.

• The most important value to remember is the vapor pressure at body temperature 47 mm Hg. (Once the equilibrium is attained after diffusion, vapour pressure is called partial pressure).

questions.explanation:
The partial pressure of O2 in the alveolus is 100 mmHg.

questions.question: If the tidal volume is 500 mL, PeCO2 is 30 mmHg and PaCO2 is 45 mmHg, calculate the dead space?
questions.explanation:
The Bohr-enghoff equation is used to calculate physiological dead space/total dead space.

The original Bohr equation required measurement of the alveolar partial pressure of CO2 (PACO2).

Later Enghoff modified the equation and replaced the PACO2 with PaCO2 (partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood). Enghoff's modification of Bohr equation is:

Where,

• VD is the physiological dead space

• VT is the tidal volume

• PaCO2 is the partial pressure of CO2 in the arterial blood

• PeCO2 is the average partial pressure of CO2 in the entire expired air.

Vd=(45-30/45) x 500=166.66 ml

questions.question: Which of the following is true regarding dead space volume in a healthy individual?
options: Anatomical dead space> physiologic dead space
Anatomical dead space< physiological dead space
Anatomical dead space and physiologic dead space are almost equivalent
Anatomical dead space is not related to physiologic dead space
questions.answer: C. Anatomical dead space and physiologic dead space are almost equivalent
questions.explanation:
In healthy individuals, anatomical dead space and physiologic dead space are almost equivalent, and can be estimated by body weight.

Dead space is the volume of the airways and lungs that do not participate in gas exchange.

Types

• Anatomic dead space- Volume of the air-occupying conducting zone where no exchange of gases takes place.

• Alveolar/functional dead space- the volume of gas not equilibrating with blood (wasted ventilation)

• Total dead space/Physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar dead space.

In healthy individuals:

• Anatomical dead space = 150 mL.

• Alveolar dead space is usually zero (increased in diseased conditions).

Hence,

• Physiological dead space = Anatomical + Alveolar = 150 + 0 = 150 mL.

• Physiological dead space = Anatomical dead space.

• Radford's formula: Anatomical dead space in mL is approximately equal to the body weight in pounds.

• Dead space can be measured by the following:

• Single Breath N2 method (Fowler’s method)

• Bohr’s equation

questions.question: From base to the apex of the lung during standing, all the following decrease except ______
options: Intrapleural pressure (with respect to atmospheric pressure)
questions.explanation:
V/Q ratio does not decrease from the base to apex of the lung while standing.

• Normal differences in ventilation and perfusion of the lung in the upright position (refer figure).

Blood flow distribution in the lung

Zones of lung
Blood flow

PA > Pa > Pv

Zone 2
Medium
Pa > PA > Pv

Zone 3

PA: Alveolar pressure
Pa: arterial pressure
PV: venous pressure

Ventilation–perfusion ratio is not the same in all part of the lungs because of the effect of gravity.

At the apex (Against gravity):

Both ventilation and perfusion decrease since the flow is against gravity. But, a decrease in perfusion is higher than the decrease in ventilation. Hence, ratio increases (3.2).

At the base of lung:

Both ventilation and perfusion increase since the flow is towards gravity. Increase in perfusion is more than increase in ventilation, i.e., denominator increases. Hence, ratio decreases to 0.6.

The average value of V/Q ratio throughout lungs is 0.8.

Important points:

• If the effect of gravity is eliminated, as in the supine position, the value is the same in all parts of the lung = 0.8.

• V/Q ratio is infinity when perfusion is zero as in case of pulmonary embolism.

• V/Q ratio is zero when ventilation is zero like in case of foreign body obstruction.

• High V/Q ratio at apex leads to high pAO2 which favors the growth of microorganisms like tubercle bacilli.

Intra-pleural pressure decreases as we move from the base to the apex of the lung i.e- becomes more negative as we move from the base to the apex of the lung.

questions.question: Waterfall effect is seen in ____
options: Lower and middle portions of the lung
questions.answer: C. Middle portion of the lung
questions.explanation:
Water fall effect has been used to describe the blood flow in the middle portion of lung.

In this region blood flows in pulses. At first there is no flow because of obstruction at the collapsed venous end of the capillary bed. Pressure from the arterial side builds up until it exceeds alveolar pressure and flow resumes. This dissipates the capillary pressure and returns to the start of the cycle.

The blood flow in this region is determined by the pulmonary artery–alveolar pressure difference. Blood “falls” into the pulmonary veins, which are compliant and take whatever amount of blood can flow into them. This has been called the waterfall effect.

questions.question: The O2-CO2 diagram shown below shows a ventilation-perfusion ratio curve for the normal lung. Which of the following options best describes the effect of decreasing the ventilation-perfusion ratio on the alveolar Po2 and Pco2?
questions.explanation:
Decreased ventilation-perfusion ratio implies decreased oxygenation due to decreased ventilation with respect to perfusion. Hence, PAO2 decreases and Pco2 increases.

A decrease in the ventilation-perfusion ratio (VA/Q) is depicted by moving to the left along the normal ventilation-perfusion line as shown in the figure (Zones here refer to the zones of variation in pulmonary blood flow and alveolar ventilation under influence of gravity)

• Zone 1 - Zone 1 has the lowest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 3 but, in Zone 1 Ventilation (V)>>Perfusion (Q) hence V­/Q­ is high

• PAO2 is highest

• PACO2 is lowest

• Zone 2 - Ventilation (V) almost equal to Perfusion (Q) but slightly lower so V/Q is average (~0.8)

• Zone 3 - Zone 3 has the highest ventilation compared to Zones 2 and 1 but, in Zone 3 Perfusion (Q) >> Ventilation (V) hence V­/Q­ is low

• PAO2 is lowest

• PACO2 is highest.

*PAO2 - Alveolar partial pressure of oxygen

*PACO2 - Alveolar partial pressure of CO2

questions.question: A person with normal lung at sea level (760 mm Hg) is breathing 50% oxygen. With a normal respiratory quotient of 0.8, what is the approximate alveolar Po2 (in mmHg)?
questions.explanation:
Alveolar gas equation is used to calculate partial pressure of O2 in alveolar air.

It is given by the formula:

Where

• PAO2 = Alveolar PO2 (mm Hg)

• PIO2 = PO2 in inspired air (mm Hg)

• PACO2 = Alveolar PCO2 (mm Hg), which is normally 40mmHg

• R = Respiratory exchange ratio or respiratory quotient (CO2 production/O2 consumption)

• Correction factor is usually negligible.

Step 1: In the question PO2 in inspired air is not given directly. It has to be calculated using the formula:

PIO2 = FIO2 (PB - PH20)

Where

• PIO2 = PO2 in inspired air (mm Hg)

• FIO2 = Fraction of inspired O2 (50% or 0.5)

• PB = Barometric pressure (760 mmHg)

• PH2O = Water vapour pressure (47 mmHg)

Substituting the values:

PIO2 = 0.5 (760 - 47) = 0.5 × 713 = 356.5 mmHg

Step 2:

PAO2 = PiO2 – (Pco2/R) = 356.5 – (40/0.8) = 356.5 – 50 = 306.5 mmHg.

questions.question: Which of the following decreases in a patient with emphysema?
questions.explanation:
In emphysema, the destruction of the alveolar walls brings down the diffusion area.

Changes in Emphysema

• Due to the destruction of the alveolar walls, there is a decrease in surface/diffusion area.

• Cardiac output will be normal.

• Pulmonary artery pressure may be elevated because the destruction of alveoli leads to loss of surrounding capillaries which forces blood into remaining capillaries, which tends to increase pulmonary artery pressure.

• Alveolar Pco2 will tend to increase due to difficulty in expiration.

Diffusion capacity of Lung for CO (DLCO):

• In case of emphysema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of decreased surface area (trypsin destroys respiratory membrane)

• In case of fibrosis or pulmonary edema – Decreased diffusion (DLCO) because of increased thickness of membrane

• In case of anemia – Decreased DLCO

• Polycythemia, pulmonary hemorrhage – Increased DLCO.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the mean arterial oxygen tension (pO2), carbon dioxide tension (pCO2) and pH in a healthy athlete during moderate exercise?
options: ↓ Arterial pO2, ↓ Arterial pCO2, ↓ Arterial pH
↓ Arterial pO2, ↑ Arterial pCO2, ↓ Arterial pH
No change in Arterial pO2, Arterial pCO2 or Arterial pH
questions.answer: D. No change in Arterial pO2, Arterial pCO2 or Arterial pH
questions.explanation:
During moderate exercise, there is no change in arterial pO2, arterial pCO2 or arterial pH.

Ventilation increases abruptly at the onset of exercise due to psychic stimuli and afferent impulses from proprioceptors in muscles, tendons, and joints. This is followed by a brief pause and then a gradual increase in ventilation. This gradual increase in ventilation is believed to be due to multiple factors such as an increase in body temperature, increase in plasma K+ level stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors, or the sensitivity of the neurons controlling the response to CO2.

In strenuous exercise, at a certain point, the O2 uptake reaches its maximum levels, beyond which it cannot increase further. This leads to a rise in blood lactate levels. Buffering of lactic acid liberates CO2 which further increases ventilation. The increased production of lactic acid, increase in ventilation and CO2 production are proportional, and alveolar and arterial CO2 changes little to nil. This is called isocapnic buffering.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
questions.explanation:
Boyle’s law states that, at a given temperature, the product of pressure time’s volume for a gas is constant.

PV = nRT

Boyle's law:

• At a given temperature, the product of pressure times volume for a gas is constant

• PV=nRT

Charles law:

• At constant pressure, the volume occupied by a fixed mass of gas is proportional to temperature

• V/T = constant

Dalton's Law:

• It states that the partial pressure of a gas in a mixture of gases is the pressure that gas would exert if it occupied the total volume of the mixture.

• Partial pressure is the total pressure multiplied by the fractional concentration of dry gas.

Henry's Law:

• The amount of gas dissolved is directly proportional to the partial pressure of the gas with which it is in equilibrium.

Graham's Law:

• The rate of diffusion of a gas is inversely proportional to molecular weight.

questions.question: Transport of CO is diffusion limited because_____
options: Alveolar membrane is less permeable to CO
High affinity of CO to hemoglobin
questions.answer: B. High affinity of CO to hemoglobin
questions.explanation:
Transport of CO is diffusion limited because of the high affinity of CO to hemoglobin.

Diffusion across the alveolocapillary membrane:

• Blood takes 0.75s to traverse pulmonary capillaries.

• CO diffuses into blood and combines with Hb with very high affinity. Thus the partial pressure of CO doesn't rise (Only dissolved form of gas can increase the partial pressure, Gas which combines with Hb or plasma proteins cannot). Partial pressure gradient necessary for diffusion of CO is maintained for the whole 0.75s and hence it is Diffusion limited.

• In the case of N2O it does not react and reaches equilibrium in about 0.1s. The amount of N2O taken up is not limited by diffusion but by the amount of blood flowing through the pulmonary capillaries; that is, it is Flow-limited.

• O2 is intermediate between N2O and CO; it is taken up by haemoglobin, but much less avidly than CO, and it reaches equilibrium with capillary blood in about 0.3 s. Thus, its uptake is Perfusion-limited.

In the case of perfusion limited gases, an increase in pulmonary blood flow increases the amount of gas transferred. Hence O2 transport increases with an increase in pulmonary blood flow.

questions.question: What is the percentage of O2 carried, chemically bound to Hb?
questions.explanation:
Percentage of O2 carried chemically (bound to Hb) is 97%.

Oxygen is transported in the blood in two forms:

• physically 3% - dissolved in plasma

• chemically 97% - bound to hemoglobin.

Remember:

Gases are transported in 3 forms:

• Dissolved gas - This is the form which contributes to partial pressure. Nitrogen is carried only in dissolved form in blood.

• Bound gas - O2, CO are bound to Hb in RBC; CO2 is bound to Hb in RBC as well as plasma protein.

• Chemically modified gas - CO2 in the form of HCO3-.

Total gas concentration in solution is the sum of dissolved gas plus bound gas plus chemically modified gas.

questions.question: The presence of hemoglobin in normal arterial blood increases its O2 concentration approximately by how many times?
questions.explanation:
The presence of hemoglobin in normal arterial blood increases its O2 concentration approximately by 70 times

• Normal arterial blood has Po2 of about 100 mm Hg.

Amount of O2 transported in dissolved form (Calculated by using Henry's law):

• Concentration of dissolved O2 = Partial pressure of O2 × solubility of O2 = 100 mmHg × 0.003 mL O2/100 mL blood per mm Hg = 0.3 mL O2/100 mL

• Hence 1L of plasma has 3mL of 02 in dissolved form.

• 5L of plasma can carry maximum 15mL of 02.

• At rest, O2 demand is around 250mL/min.

• Hence dissolved O2 alone is not sufficient to meet body demands.

Amount of O2 transported bound to Hb:

• Concentration of Hb is 15g/100 mL

• Each gram of Hb binds to 1.34 mL of O2

• Hence, 15 g binds to 20.1mL of O2/100 mL

• On average, the 15 g of hemoglobin in 100 mL of blood can combine with a total of about 20 mL of O2.

Thus, this value (20.1) in the presence of Hb is about 70 times the value (0.3) in the absence of Hb.

questions.question: O2 delivery to tissues depends on all except_____
questions.explanation:
Oxygen delivery is the volume of oxygen delivered to the systemic vascular bed per minute. It is the product of the cardiac output and the arterial oxygen concentration.

Oxygen delivery to tissue depends on (refer flow chart)

questions.question: Each molecule of hemoglobin carries ______ molecules of O2.
questions.explanation:
Hemoglobin has 4 subunits each of which has heme molecule and polypeptide chain. Ferrous in heme binds to a molecule of O2. Hence, hemoglobin binds to 4 molecules of O2.

• Hemoglobin is a protein made up of four subunits.

• Each subunit contains a heme moiety attached to a polypeptide chain.

• Heme is a porphyrin ring complex that includes one atom of ferrous iron.

• In normal adults, most of the hemoglobin molecules contain two α and two β chains.

• Each of the four iron atoms in hemoglobin can reversibly bind one O2. The iron stays in the ferrous state so that the reaction is oxygenation (not oxidation).

questions.question: Most of the CO2 transported in the arterial blood is in the form of_____
questions.explanation:
CO2 is carried in the blood in three forms:

• Bicarbonate (HCO3−) - Quantitatively the most important(70%)

• Carbaminohemoglobin (23%)

• Dissolved CO2 (7%)

questions.question: Which of the following statements about hemoglobin is false?
options: The T configuration of Hb does not favor O2 binding
The R configuration of Hb does not favor O2 binding
The R configuration of Hb favors O2 binding
Each Hb molecules carries 4 oxygen molecules
questions.answer: B. The R configuration of Hb does not favor O2 binding
questions.explanation:
A relaxed (R) configuration, exposes more O 2 binding sites.

The quaternary structure of hemoglobin determines its affinity for O2.

In deoxyhemoglobin, the globin units are tightly bound in a tense (T) configuration, which reduces the affinity of the molecule for O2.

When O 2 is first bound, the bonds holding the globin units are released, producing a relaxed (R) configuration, which exposes more O2 binding sites. The net result is a 500-fold increase in O2

In tissues, these reactions are reversed, resulting in O2 dissociation .

questions.question: The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid shape because_____
options: Binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules
Binding of one O2 molecule decreases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules
questions.answer: A. Binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules
questions.explanation:
The oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid shape because binding of one O2 molecule increases the affinity of binding of subsequent O2 molecules.

The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve relates per­centage saturation of the O2 carrying power of hemoglobin (abbreviated as SaO2) to the Po2. It has a characteristic sigmoid shape due to the T–R interconversion. Combination of the first heme in the Hb molecule with O2 increases the affinity of the second heme for O2 and oxygenation of the second increases the affinity of the third, and so on, such that the affinity of Hb for the fourth O2 molecule is many times that for the first (Positive Co-operative Effect).

Option C: The effect of PCO2 and pH on the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve is called the Bohr effect.

Option D: O2 bound to hemoglobin changes its affinity for CO2, such that when less O2 is bound, the affinity of hemoglobin for CO2 increases. This is referred to as the Haldane effect.

questions.question: Hb would be expected to become 100% saturated with oxygen at Po2 of (in mmHg)_____
questions.explanation:
When blood is equilibrated with 100% O2, the normal hemoglobin becomes 100% saturated.

• In vivo, the hemoglobin in the blood at the end of the pulmonary capillaries is about 97.5% saturated with O2 (Po2 = 100 mm Hg).

• Because of a slight admixture with venous blood that bypasses the pulmonary capillaries (i.e, physiologic shunt), the hemoglobin in systemic arterial blood is only 97% saturated.

• Graph relates the percentage of saturated hemoglobin (SaO2) to PO2 and dissolved O2.
