questions.question: The normal value of P50 in an adult is(mm Hg)______
questions.explanation:
Normal P50 is about 27 mm of Hg for adult Hb.

P50 is the partial pressure of O2 at which Hb is 50 % saturated. P50 is an index of the affinity of Hb with O2.

Higher the P50 value, lower is the affinity: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve shifts to right.

Lower the P50 value, the higher is the affinity: Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve shifts to left.

questions.question: Decrease in pH shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to_____
options: On either side depending on other factors
questions.explanation:
The pH decreasing from the normal value shifts the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, to the right.

Oxygen-Hb dissociation curve (OHDC)

• This is a plot of the partial pressure of O2 and the % saturation of Hb with O2.

• It is normally sigmoid-shape.

• If OHDC is shifted to the right, it means that affinity of Hb for O2 has become less (which favors O2 delivery) i.e. Higher the P50. (R - Right shift Releases oxygen)

Shift to the right is caused by: (Conditions with increased requirement of O2 - metabolically active tissues)

• Hypoxia and Hypercarbia - Metabolically active tissues utilise O2 and tissues produce CO2

• ↓ pH - Secondary to increased CO2 production

• ↑ in temperature, heat

• ↑ in 2,3-DPG - increased anaerobic glycolysis

• Growth hormone, thyroid hormone, androgen - by increasing 2,3 DPG

• Sickle cell anaemia - reduced affinity for O2

questions.question: Four molecules of myoglobin will bind how many molecules of oxygen?
questions.explanation:
4 molecules of myoglobin will bind 4 molecules of oxygen.

• Myoglobin: This is present in skeletal muscles.

• 1 molecule of myoglobin binds 1 molecule of O2. Thus, 4 molecules of myoglobin will bind 4 molecules of oxygen

• The shape of O2-myoglobin dissociation curve is the rectangular hyperbola. It lies to the left of Oxygen-Hemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC)(refer figure).

questions.question: Bohr effect
questions.explanation:
Facilitation of oxygen transport depends on the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, explained by the Bohr effect.

When the metabolic activity of tissues increases, the production of CO2 increases. This CO2 diffuses into the blood and in turn, raises the blood H2CO3 and causes an increase in the H+ concentration and a decrease in pH. This decreases the affinity of Hb for O2, shifting the O2- hemoglobin dissociation curve to the right. This facilitates the unloading of O2 in the tissues. The effect of Pco2 and pH on O2 hemoglobin dissociation curve is called the Bohr Effect.

Conversely, in the lungs, CO2 diffuses from the blood to the alveoli and the H+ concentration decreases and theO2 hemoglobin dissociation curve shifts to the left increasing the affinity of Hb to O2.

Note:

Double Bohr effect occurring in the placenta: Oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve of fetal blood and maternal blood move in opposite directions.

 Mechanism:

• The fetal blood entering the placenta carries large amounts of carbon dioxide, but most of it diffuse from the fetal blood into the maternal blood.

• Fetal blood - loss of CO2 - reduced H+ - shift to left - loading of O2 i.e. oxygenation of fetal Hb.

• Maternal blood - increase in CO2 - increase in H+ - shift to the right - Release of oxygen.

questions.question: The level of 2,3 –DPG is decreased in______
questions.explanation:
The level of 2,3–DPG is decreased in acidosis.

2,3-DPG is produced from 3-phosphoglycerate which is a product of glycolysis. Acidosis inhibits red cell glycolysis which decreases the levels of 2,3-DPG.

questions.question: High affinity of HbF to O2 is due to_____
questions.explanation:
Increased affinity of HbF to O2 is due to decreased affinity of γ chains of HbF to 2,3DPG.

HbF is the fetal variant of hemoglobin.

The β chains of adult hemoglobin (hemoglobin A) are replaced by γ chains in HbF. This modification results in increased affinity of hemoglobin for O2, a left shift of the O2-hemoglobin dissociation curve, and decreased P50.
The mechanism of the left shift is based on the binding of 2,3-DPG. 2,3-DPG does not bind as avidly to the γ chains of HbF as it binds to the β chains of hemoglobin A. When less 2,3-DPG is bound, the affinity for O2 increases and facilitates the movement of O2 from the mother to the fetus.

This increased affinity is beneficial to the fetus, whose PaO2 is low (approximately 40 mm Hg).

questions.question: Haldane effect is _______
options: Binding of O2 to Hb favours release of CO2
Binding of CO2 to Hb favours release of O2
HCO3- leaving RBC in exchange for Cl-
questions.answer: A. Binding of O2 to Hb favours release of CO2
questions.explanation:
Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This effect is called the Haldane effect. (Remember - Haldane effect occurs in lungs and causes left shift of O2-Hb dissociation curve)

Haldane Effect

• Binding of O2 with hemoglobin tends to displace CO2 from the blood. This effect, called the Haldane effect, is important in promoting CO2 transport.

• The Haldane effect results from the simple fact that the combination of O2 with hemoglobin in the lungs causes the hemoglobin to become a stronger acid. This displaces CO2 from the blood and into the alveoli.

questions.question: You are comparing the packed cell volume (PCV) obtained from an arterial and venous blood sample of the same patient. Why is PCV higher in venous blood?
questions.explanation:
Hematocrit (PCV) of venous blood is normally 3% greater than that of the arterial blood because of 2 reasons:

• Chloride shift

• A small amount of fluid in the arterial blood returns via the lymphatics rather than the veins.

Chloride shift:

• Upon entering the red blood cell, CO2 is rapidly hydrated to H2CO3 by carbonic anhydrase.

• H2CO3 is in equilibrium with H+ and its conjugate base, HCO3-.

• H+ can interact with deoxyhemoglobin, whereas HCO3- can be transported outside of the cell via anion exchanger 1 (AE1 or Band 3).

• In effect, for each CO2 molecule that enters the red cell, there is an additional HCO3- or Cl- in the cell.

• Because of this chloride shift, the Cl – content of the red cells in venous blood is significantly greater than that in arterial blood.

• Note that for each CO2 molecule added to a red cell, there is an increase of one osmotically active particles in the cell - either a HCO 3 – or a Cl – ion. Consequently, the red cells take up water and increase in size.

chapters.chapter: Lung Volumes And Lung Function Tests

questions.question: Tidal volume is_____
options: Inspiratory capacity minus inspiratory reserve volume
Total lung capacity minus residual volume
Functional residual capacity minus residual volume
Vital capacity minus expiratory reserve volume
questions.answer: A. Inspiratory capacity minus inspiratory reserve volume
questions.explanation: The tidal volume = inspiratory capacity - inspiratory reserve volume.

questions.question: A 27-year-old man is breathing quietly. He then inhales as much air as possible and exhales as much air as he can, producing the spirogram shown in the figure. What is his expiratory reserve volume (in liters)?
questions.explanation:
Expiratory Reserve Volume = Functional Residual Capacity - Residual Volume

In the given spirogram,

• Functional Residual Capacity = 3L

• Residual Volume = 1L

Therefore,

Expiratory Reserve Volume = Functional Residual Capacity – Residual Volume = 3-1 = 2

Note:

The residual volume is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after the most forceful expiration.

The functional residual capacity equals the expiratory reserve volume plus the residual volume. This capacity is the amount of air that remains in the lungs at the end of normal expiration

The expiratory reserve volume is the maximum extra volume of air that can be expired by forceful expiration after the end of a normal tidal expiration.

questions.question: A nurse in the pulmonology clinic administered a test using the following instrument. Which of the following parameters cannot be measured?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows spirometry. All of the given parameters can be measured by a spirometer except residual volume.

Residual volume is measured by:

• N2 washout method

• Helium-dilution method

• Body plethysmography

Other parameters which cannot be measured by spirometry are:

• Functional residual capacity

• Total lung capacity

questions.question: Total lung capacity depends on____
questions.explanation:
Total lung capacity depends on the distensibility of lungs (compliance).

Determinants of Lung Compliance

• Stretchability of the lung tissues, particularly their elastic connective tissue.

• Surface tension at the air-water interfaces within the alveoli, which is markedly reduced in the alveoli by pulmonary surfactant preventing their collapse.

Option b: The Closing Volume is the lung volume above Residual Volume at which airways in the lower, dependent parts of the lungs begin to close off because of the lesser transmural pressure in these areas.

questions.question: Calculate the alveolar ventilation in a young man if the respiratory rate is 10/min and tidal volume is 600ml.
questions.explanation:
Alveolar ventilation = RR X (VT –V D)

In the given case,

• Respiratory rate (RR)= 10/min

• Tidal volume (VT) = 600 mL

• Dead space volume (VD) = 150 mL in a young man

Thus, Alveolar ventilation = 10 X (600-150) = 4500 mL/min = 4.5 L/min

questions.question: Normal VD(Dead space volume)/ VT (Tidal volume) is_____
questions.explanation:
• Dead space volume = VD = 150ml

• Tidal volume = VT = 500ml

• Normal VD/VT = 150/500 = 0.3

questions.question: A patient has a dead space of 150 mL, a functional residual capacity of 3L, tidal volume of 650 mL, expiratory reserve volume of 1.5 L, a total lung capacity of 8L, respiratory rate of 15 breaths/min. What is the rate of alveolar ventilation?
questions.explanation:
The rate of alveolar ventilation in this patient is 7.5 L/min.

Alveolar ventilation per minute is the total volume of new air entering the alveoli and adjacent gas exchange areas each minute. It is equal to the respiratory rate times the amount of new air that enters these areas with each breath.

Alveolar ventilation=Respiratory rate X (Tidal volume – Physiologic dead space)

 = 15 X (650-150)

 = 7500mL/min or 7.5L/min.

questions.question: Closing volume of the lung is_____
options: Above residual volume in upper portions of the lungs
Above the residual volume in dependent portions of the lungs
Above tidal volume in dependent portions of the lungs
Above tidal volume in upper portions of the lungs
questions.answer: B. Above the residual volume in dependent portions of the lungs
questions.explanation:
The closing volume (CV) is the lung volume above the residual volume (RV) at which the airways in the lower dependent parts of the lung begin to close off because of the lesser transmural pressure in these areas.

In young adults, the closing volume is about 10% of the vital capacity (VC). It increases steadily with age and is equal to about 40% of the VC. It equals FRC, at about the age of 65 years.

Diseases of the small airways apparently increase the closing volume

• Normal young adult: CV << FRC

• At 65 years of age: CV=FRC

• Small airway disease: CV >>FRC

• In case of hyaline membrane disease, FRC is smaller than closing volume.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man presented with gradually progressive dyspnea and a non-productive cough. On examination, he has bi-basilar inspiratory crackles and clubbing. Which of the following pulmonary function tests will be true if he is to be diagnosed with interstitial pulmonary fibrosis?
questions.explanation:
Interstitial pulmonary fibrosis is a restrictive lung disease that shows ↑FEV1/FVC, ↓Compliance when performing pulmonary function tests.

In a healthy normal adult male, FVC is approximately 5.0 L, FEV1 is approximately 4.0 L, and thus, the calculated FEV1/FVC is 80%.

Obstructive disorders result in a marked decrease in both FVC and FEV1/FVC, whereas restrictive disorders result in a loss of FVC without loss in FEV1/FVC.

Compliance is reduced in cases of restrictive lung diseases. For example - interstitial lung diseases, fibrosis, sarcoidosis, asbestosis, and radiation exposure.

questions.question: Flow volume given below indicates_____
questions.explanation:
The inspiratory flow-volume curve is truncated in patients with variable extrathoracic obstructions.

• During a forced expiration, the cross-sectional area of a variable extrathoracic obstruction increases as the pressure inside the airway increases.

• The expiratory flow-volume curve is therefore nearly normal or not affected.

• However, during a forced inspiration, the pressure inside the upper airway decreases below atmospheric pressure, and unless the stability of the upper airway is maintained by reflex contraction of the pharyngeal muscles or by other structures, the cross-sectional area of the upper airway will decrease. Therefore, the inspiratory flow-volume curve is truncated in patients with variable extrathoracic obstructions.

• Flow-volume curves are very useful in assessing obstructions of upper airways and the trachea (refer figure and flowchart).

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the changes in lung volume and thoracic volume in a case of pneumothorax, compared to normal?
questions.explanation:
In pneumothorax, lung volume is decreased and thoracic volume is increased.

Both lungs and the chest wall (thoracic cage) are elastic structures. Under normal conditions, the elastic tendency of the lungs to collapse is exactly balanced by the elastic tendency of the chest wall to expand.

In pneumothorax, air is introduced into the pleural space, so the pleural pressure, which is normally subatmospheric, becomes equal to atmospheric pressure. The chest wall springs outward and the lungs collapse. This increases the thoracic volume and decreases the lung volume.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man inhaled as much air as possible and then expired with a maximum effort until no more air could be expired. This produced the maximum expiratory flow-volume curve shown in the following diagram. What is the forced vital capacity of this man (in liters)?
questions.explanation:
The forced vital capacity of this man is 4.5 liters.

The forced vital capacity (FVC), the largest amount of air that can be expired after a maximal inspiratory effort, is frequently measured clinically as an index of pulmonary function.

Forced vital capacity(FVC) = Total lung capacity (TLC) – Residual volume(RV)

• In the flow-volume curve, the point of intersection between abscissa and flow-volume curve gives the TLC and RV.

• From the given flow-volume curve we can note that:

• Total Lung Capacity (TLC) = 5.5 L

• Residual volume (RV)= 1.0 L

• Thus,

• FVC = TLC – RV = 4.5 L

questions.question: A 71-year-old woman presents with cough and shortness of breath. The physician conducts a pulmonary function screening test in his office, and the patient generates the maximum expiratory flow–volume curve shown to the right of the normal curve in the diagram below. These findings are consistent with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
This is a case of asbestosis.

Asbestosis is a restrictive lung disease characterized by diffuse interstitial fibrosis. In restrictive lung disease, the maximum expiratory flow volume (MEFV) curve begins and ends at abnormally low lung volumes.

Note: In obstructive lung diseases, the airways are narrowed or radial traction of the airways is reduced, allowing them to close more easily. The lung volumes in these cases are higher than normal.

questions.question: The maximum expiratory flow-volume (MEFV) curves shown in the figure below were obtained from a healthy man (purple curve) and a 57-year-old man with shortness of breath (green curve). What is the most probable diagnosis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The green curve in the above image and the case scenario denotes that the diagnosis is likely to be emphysema.

Maximum expiratory flow volume (MEFV): When a person expires with great force, the expiratory airflow reaches a maximum flow beyond which the flow cannot be increased anymore, even with greatly increased additional force.

In obstructive airway disease like Emphysema, it is usually much more difficult to expire than to inspire because the closing tendency of the airways is greatly increased by the extra positive pressure during expiration. Due to the obstruction of the airways and because they collapse more easily than normal airways, the maximum expiratory flow rate is greatly reduced (But, total lung capacity and residual volume is increased) which is shown in the green curve below.

Other options given above will cause constricted lungs where the lungs cannot expand to a normal maximum volume. Hence, even with the greatest possible expiratory effort, the maximum expiratory flow rate will be reduced. (Note: here both the total lung capacity and the residual volume are reduced), which is shown as the blue curve in the graph below.

Following graph shows the MEFV of restrictive and obstructive lung diseases.

questions.question: Which of the following factors is most likely to stimulate ventilation after strenuous exercise?
options: Collateral impulses from higher than brain centres
questions.explanation:
The stimulus to ventilation after strenuous exercise is increased mean arterial H+.

The respiratory rate after exercise does not reach a basal level until the O2 debt is repaid. The stimulus for ventilation is increased mean arterial H+ due to an increase in blood lactic acid levels. Most of the lactic acid is converted to glycogen and some amount is converted to CO2 and H2O.

chapters.chapter: Respiratory Adaptations In Hypoxia, Anemia And With Pressure Changes

questions.question: Which is the best parameter to analyze hypoxic hypoxia?
options: Partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (Paco2)
Partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (Pao2)
questions.answer: B. Partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (Pao2)
questions.explanation:
Hypoxic hypoxia is characterized by low partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (Pao2), while other parameters like partial pressure of CO2 in arterial blood (Paco2) may remain normal.

Ventilation–Perfusion Imbalance:

• The patchy ventilation–perfusion imbalance is the most common cause of hypoxic hypoxia or hypoxemia.

• If alveoli are not ventilated but perfusion is present - blood passing through that alveoli remains unoxygenated.

• When this unoxygenated blood mixes with blood from normal or overventilated alveoli, there is a right to left shunt created.

• This results in reduced partial pressure of O2 in arterial blood (PaO2) i.e., hypoxemia and consequently hypoxia.

Note:

• Hypoxemia can be defined as a condition where arterial oxygen tension or partial pressure of oxygen (PaO2) is below normal.

• Hypoxia is defined as the reduction of oxygen supply at the tissue level, which is not measured directly by a laboratory value.

Scenario 1:

• Generally, the presence of hypoxemia suggests hypoxia i.e. if there is less oxygen in blood, O2 supply to tissues will also be reduced.

• But, in case of cyanide poisoning, there is hypoxia in the absence of hypoxemia, i.e., arterial O2 content is normal but tissues are not able to utilize it because cyanide interferes with aerobic metabolism in the tissues.

Scenario 2:

• Hypoxia may not be present in patients with hypoxemia if the patient compensates for a low PaO2 by increasing oxygen delivery. This is typically achieved by increasing cardiac output (by raising the heart rate) or decreasing tissue oxygen consumption.

• Nevertheless, hypoxemia is definitely the most common cause of tissue hypoxia, and the correct diagnosis should be made because it is readily treatable.

questions.question: Which type of hypoxia does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors?
questions.explanation:
In the case of anemic hypoxia, O2 content is low but dissolved O2 is within normal limits, so it does not stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors.

Peripheral chemoreceptors located in the carotid and aortic arteries sense changes in Po2(<60mm Hg), pH, and Pco2 and they respond to changes in dissolved O2(PaO2).

Histotoxic hypoxia will lead to metabolic acidosis that will lead to an increase in H+ concentration, which in turn will stimulate the peripheral chemoreceptors.

Hemorrhage that produces hypotension leads to chemoreceptor stimulation due to decreased blood flow to the chemoreceptors and consequent stagnant anoxia of these organs.

Note: In case of stagnant hypoxia, chemoreceptors can be stimulated if the resultant decreased oxygen delivery causes a significant drop in local tissue oxygen levels, which eventually can lower the PaO2 detectable by chemoreceptors. Therefore, they may not be significantly stimulated unless the reduction in oxygen levels is severe. Therefore, anaemic hypoxia is a better answer.

questions.question: Which of the following is most likely in a patient with cyanosis?
questions.explanation:
In stagnant hypoxia, blood flow is very low; so, more oxygen is extracted causing an increase in reduced hemoglobin → cyanosis.

Cyanosis - Cyanosis is the dusky bluish discoloration of the tissues occurring when the reduced hemoglobin concentration is more than 5g/dL.

• Its occurrence depends upon

• The total amount of hemoglobin in the blood

• Degree of hemoglobin unsaturation

• The state of capillary circulation

Option a: In the case of anemia, the total hemoglobin content is low, so enough reduced hemoglobin cannot be formed.

Option b: In histotoxic hypoxia, the amount of reduced hemoglobin formed is very less because the defect is in the tissue O2.

Option c: In CO poisoning, there is the formation of carboxyhemoglobin, which is red in color obscure the color of reduced hemoglobin.

questions.question: Administration of O2 has maximum benefit in:
questions.explanation:
Administration of oxygen has maximum benefit in hypoxic hypoxia.

Hypoxic hypoxia refers to a condition in which there is low atmospheric Po2, leading to low arterial Po2. Hence, supplemental O2 can be very beneficial when the cause of hypoxia is due to limited oxygen availability.

Administration of oxygen-rich gas has limited value in anemic, histotoxic, and stagnant hypoxia because:

Anemic hypoxia- Oxygen delivery is not beneficial because despite increasing the exogenous oxygen delivery, an anemic person will not have the capacity to carry more oxygen due to the hemoglobin/ red blood cell deficit in anemia.

Histotoxic hypoxia- The most common example is cyanide poisoning. Cyanide inhibits important enzymes in the oxidative phosphorylation process, which is essential to the survival of our cells. Additional oxygen supplementation will not be able to overcome this inhibition, and so it will have limited benefit. Hyperbaric oxygen may be helpful to some extent.

Stagnant hypoxia- Stagnant hypoxia refers to ischemic hypoxia that results from inadequate circulation due to conditions such as heart failure and hypoxia in the setting of shock. In such conditions, administering intravenous fluids can improve the patient's condition because it is the circulation that is affected. If the shock is prolonged it can result in acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), which can be treated with positive pressure ventilation and not simply by increasing oxygen administration.

questions.question: In which of the following situations is oxygen therapy most beneficial provided the lung function is normal?
questions.explanation:
With O2 therapy, increasing the inspired Po2 will result in an increased amount of dissolved O2. At high altitudes, there is low barometric pressure and so less Po2, hence, supplemental O2 will help.

Option A: With anemia, the hemoglobin is fully saturated and O2 will have minimal effect. Treatment of anemia is more beneficial than providing oxygen to an anemic patient.

Option B: With COPD there is CO2 retention due to difficulty in the expiration, and there will be a decreased Po2. So, there is a change in the regulation of respiration (drive for ventilation) from being under CO2 control to being driven by the decrease in O2. Giving supplemental O2 to such a person will increase arterial Po2, thus decrease the stimulus to breathe, resulting in patient stopping breathing.

Option C: Cyanide poisoning results in decreased O2 utilization by the tissues and so additional O2 would be of no benefit.

questions.question: Which of the points on the following figures represent arterial blood in a severely anemic person?
questions.explanation: When a person is anemic, there is decrease in O2 content of the blood (Fig 1-E) because of decreased number of RBCs and hence hemoglobin content in the blood. The oxygen saturation (Fig 2-D) of the available hemoglobin in the arterial blood is however normal and, the pO2 is also not affected by the hemoglobin concentration.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman is anemic with hemoglobin concentration of 6 g/dL. Which of the following set of changes have occurred in this case, compared to normal?
questions.answer: D. Normal Arterial Po2, ↓Mixed venous Po2, ↑2,3-DPG
questions.explanation:
Normal Arterial Po2, ↓Mixed venous Po2, ↑2,3-DPG are the set of changes that will be seen in the above patient.

The oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood is reduced in an anemic person, but the arterial Po2 and oxygen saturation are both normal.

The decrease in arterial O2 content is compensated for by an increase in the extraction of oxygen from hemoglobin, which reduces the Po2 of the venous blood.

The unloading of oxygen at tissue level is enhanced by an increased level of 2,3-DPG in an anemic patient because 2,3-DPG causes a right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve.

questions.question: Which of the following oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curves corresponds to blood from an adult (dark blue line) and blood from a fetus (light blue line)?
questions.explanation:
Curve C corresponds to blood from an adult (dark blue line) and blood from a fetus (light blue line). The fetal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is shifted to the left relative to the adult curve.

The fetal hemoglobin (Hb F) has a greater affinity for O2 than adult hemoglobin (Hb A). This facilitates the movement of O2 from the mother to fetus. The cause of this greater affinity is the poor binding of 2,3-DPG by ɣ polypeptide chains that replace β chains in Hb F. The fetal oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve is thus shifted to the left relative to the adult curve. Typically, fetal arterial Po2 is low, hence leftward shift enhances placental uptake of O2.

questions.question: Which of the following oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curves corresponds to blood during resting conditions (dark blue line) and blood during exercise ( light blue line)?
questions.explanation:
The right shift of the oxygen-hemoglobin curve allows more oxygen to be released to the muscle at a given Po2 in the blood. The oxygen dissociation curve shifts to the right when factors like:

1. Increased temperature resulting from heat generated by the exercising muscle,

2. Higher carbon dioxide levels released from the muscle tissue,

3. Elevated 2,3-Bisphosphoglycerate (2,3-BPG), and

4. Increased hydrogen ions concentration in the muscle capillary blood

Above factors decrease hemoglobin's oxygen affinity. This shift promotes easier oxygen release to muscles and other tissues.

Note: Despite the rightward shift, the maximum hemoglobin oxygen saturation at high oxygen levels remains unchanged. The plateau on the curve represents the maximal saturation achievable under optimal conditions, ensuring hemoglobin can still be fully saturated with oxygen.

questions.question: Decompression sickness is seen in_____
questions.explanation:
Decompression sickness is seen in pilots, mountaineers, and divers.

Decompression sickness (DCS) or diver’s disease, the bends, or Caisson disease is the name given to a variety of symptoms experienced by a person exposed to a reduction in the pressure surrounding their body.

It can be seen in

• Divers ascending rapidly from deep-sea (high pressure) to the surface of the earth (low pressure)

• Pilots traveling in unpressurized aircraft or mountaineers, rapidly ascending from the surface of the earth (high-pressure zone) to a high altitude (low-pressure zone).

Under high-pressure, gases get compressed and their solubility increases. When a person is in a high-pressure zone like the deep sea for a long time, an increased amount of nitrogen gets dissolved in his or her body. If the person suddenly comes back to an area of atmospheric pressure or a low-pressure zone, the gases escape from a dissolved state and form bubbles. These bubbles are almost entirely made of nitrogen. The bubbles can plug many small blood vessels in different tissues.

questions.question: Nitrogen narcosis is due to_____
options: Increased solubility of nitrogen in nerve cell
questions.answer: C. Increased solubility of nitrogen in nerve cell
questions.explanation:
Nitrogen narcosis is due to increased solubility of nitrogen in the nerve cell.

Concept:

• Below the sea level, atmospheric pressure increases at the rate of 1 atm for every 33 feet depth.

• According to Boyle’s law, as pressure increases, volume decreases. Hence, lungs tend to collapse. To prevent this and to keep lung expanded, gas is delivered at high pressure to the lungs.

• According to Dalton’s law, nitrogen contributes the maximum to barometric pressure and hence the amount of nitrogen entering alveoli increases.

• Henry’s law: As the partial pressure of nitrogen in alveoli increases, its concentration in blood also increases (dissolved form). Nitrogen is 5 times more soluble in fat compared to water.

• As a result, nitrogen dissolves in the fatty substances in neuronal membranes, and because of its physical effect on altering ionic conductance through the membranes, it reduces neuronal excitability and produces the narcotic effect.

questions.question: During acclimatization at higher altitude, all of the following changes take place except ______.
options: Shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve to left
questions.answer: D. Shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve to left
questions.explanation:
A shift of Oxygen Haemoglobin Dissociation Curve (OHDC) to the right is seen in acclimatization.

On ascension to higher altitudes over a period of days rather than a period of hours, the ability to breathe much more deeply and withstand lower atmospheric O2 concentrations is improved. This phenomenon is called acclimatization.

Variation of pH in Acclimatization:

Immediate exposure to low pO2 stimulates the arterial chemoreceptors. This increases alveolar ventilation. This immediate increase in pulmonary ventilation upon rising to a high altitude blows off large quantities of CO2, reducing the pCO2 and increases the pH of the body fluids.

These changes inhibit the brain stem respiratory center and thereby oppose the effect of low PO2 to stimulate respiration through the peripheral arterial chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.

There is a reduction of bicarbonate ion concentration in the cerebrospinal fluid, as well as in the brain tissues. This reduction, in turn, decreases the pH in the fluids surrounding the chemosensitive neurons of the respiratory center, thus increasing the respiratory stimulatory activity of the center. An important mechanism for the gradual decrease in bicarbonate concentration is compensation by the kidneys for the respiratory alkalosis. Gradually, the metabolic compensation of the kidney will shift the pH towards normal.

questions.question: Which phase of the cardiac cycle has all four valves closed?
questions.explanation: Ventricular pressure rises with AV and semilunar valves closed.

questions.question: The basal cardiac output in adults is around ________
questions.explanation:
The basal cardiac output in adults is around 5.5 litres.
Cardiac output is given by, Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.
In a resting, supine man cardiac output averages about 5.0 L/min (70 mL × 72 beats/min).

questions.question: The cardiac output can be determined by all except:
questions.explanation:
V/Q ratio not used to determine cardiac output.
Measurement of cardiac output:

• Fick principle

• Dye dilution/thermodilution

• Doppler plus echocardiograph

• MRI

questions.question: Cardiac output in litre per minute divided by heart rate gives ______
questions.explanation:
Cardiac output in litre per minute divided by heart rate gives stroke volume.
Cardiac output is given by, Cardiac Output = Heart Rate X Stroke Volume.
The stroke volume is the amount of blood pumped out of each ventricle per beat, is about 70 mL from each ventricle in a resting man in the supine position.

questions.question: Ejection fraction is
questions.explanation:
Ejection fraction is SV/EDV.
The amount of blood ejected by each ventricle per stroke at rest is 70–90 mL. The end-diastolic ventricular volume is about 130 mL. The ejection fraction is the percentage of the end-diastolic ventricular volume that is ejected with each stroke, is about 65%.

questions.question: A patient with cardiac output 5L/min and body surface area 1.7m2. What will be the cardiac index (L/min/m2)?
questions.explanation:
Cardiac index is the cardiac output per minute per square meter of body surface.

Cardiac Index = Cardiac output / body surface area.

Therefore Cardiac index = 5L/min /1.7m2= 2.94 L

questions.question: Volume determining preload is
questions.explanation:
Volume determining preload is End diastolic volume.
Preload is the initial stretch on muscle at the end of diastole. Preload is equal to End diastolic volume (EDV) and is determined by venous return to heart.

questions.question: Starling's law implies:
options: Increased heart rate leads to increased cardiac output
Increased discharge leads to increased cardiac output
Increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output
Increased blood pressure leads to increased cardiac output
questions.answer: C. Increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output
questions.explanation:
Starling's law implies increased venous return leads to increased cardiac output.

Frank-Starling law: The energy of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fiber.
The length of the muscle fibers is proportional to the end-diastolic volume, which is determined by venous return.

questions.question: Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is facilitated by all of the following factors except _____.
options: Increased arterial pressure due to gravitation.
questions.answer: D. Increased arterial pressure due to gravitation.
questions.explanation:
Venous return to the heart during quiet standing is not facilitated by increased arterial pressure.

Factors that facilitate venous return to the heart:

• Calf muscles contract and pump blood through veins.

• Valves don't allow the retrograde flow of blood through veins.

• Deep fascia by forming a supporting structure to veins.

Note: The pulsations of artery helps in increasing lymph flow .

questions.question: When a person changes position from standing to supine, _______
options: Venous return to heart rises immediately
Decrease in blood flow to the lung apices
questions.answer: B. Venous return to heart rises immediately
questions.explanation:
When a person changes position from standing to supine, venous return to heart rises immediately. On standing, Gravitational pull causes venous pooling of blood in the legs. On supine position, this gravitational pull equalizes over body, causing the pooled blood to return back to heart.

Other options:

Option A: Heart rate decreases because of increased cardiac output and increased BP via baroreceptor reflex.
Option C: Cerebral blood flow will remain constant due to autoregulation.
Option D: Blood flow to the apex of lung will be high due to high cardiac output.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman has a resting heart rate of 70-beats/min. Her pressure-volume diagram of the left ventricle is given below. What is her cardiac output (in mL/min)? (Point 2 corresponds to 120 ml)
questions.explanation:
In this case, the patient has a heart rate of 70-beats/min and the stroke volume can be determined from the given pressure-volume diagram.

Point 2 corresponds to the EDV(End diastolic volume) = 120 mL
Point 1 corresponds to the ESV(End systolic volume) = 50 mL

Thus, stroke volume (SV) = EDV – ESV = 120 – 50 = 70 mL

Therefore, Cardiac output = HR X SV = 70 X 70 = 4900 mL/min.

questions.question: A sister donated one of her kidneys to her brother. What would be the effect on her cardiac output?
questions.explanation:
Surgical removal of kidney leads to decrease in cardiac output.

Amputation of a limb or surgical removal of organs like kidney removes a parallel circuit thus increasing total peripheral vascular resistance. As the resistance increases, afterload increases hence decreasing stroke volume.
CO= HR × SV, therefore decrease in stroke volume leads to decrease in cardiac output.

questions.question: The duration of atrial diastole is _____
questions.explanation:
The duration of atrial diastole is 0.7 sec.

questions.question: The indication of the end of the isovolumetric relaxation phase is when ____
options: Ventricular pressure raise above atrial pressure
Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
Ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure
ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure
questions.answer: B. Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure
questions.explanation:
The indication of the end of the isovolumetric relaxation phase is when ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.

Events of the Cardiac Cycle

Diastole

• Protodiastole
Before the semilunar valve closes, even though ventricular muscle is relaxed, blood flow into great vessels is due to momentum of blood.

• Iso-volumetric Relaxation
The ventricular muscle continues to relax, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.

• Ventricular Filling
Isovolumetric relaxation ends when the ventricular pressure falls below the atrial pressure and the AV valves open, permitting the ventricles to fill.

• Atrial Systole
During the last third of diastole, the atria contract and give additional thrust to the inflow of blood into the ventricles. It correlates with 'a' wave in JVP.

Systole

• Isovolumetric Contraction
The ventricular muscle continues to contract, even though the ventricular volume does not change, with all valves closed.
It correlates with the ‘c’ wave of JVP.

• Ventricular Ejection
When the ventricular pressures rise above aortic and pulmonary pressures the valves open, and ventricular ejection begins. Peak pressures in the left and right ventricles are about 120 and 25 mmHg, respectively.

questions.question: During the cardiac cycle, the opening of the aortic valve takes place at the ______
questions.explanation:
Opening of the aortic valve takes place at the end of the isovolumetric contraction.

When the ventricular pressures rise above aortic and pulmonary pressures the semilunar valves (aortic and pulmonary valves) open, and ventricular ejection begins.

questions.question: The effect of increased heart rate on cardiac cycle is that it____.
options: Decrease the duration of systole and diastole.
Increase the duration of systole and diastole.
Decrease the duration of systole more than diastole.
Decrease the duration of diastole more than systole.
questions.answer: D. Decrease the duration of diastole more than systole.
questions.explanation:
The effect of increased heart rate on cardiac cycle is that it decreases the duration of diastole more than systole.
The duration of systole is much more fixed than that of diastole, so when the heart rate is increased, diastole is shortened to a much greater degree. Coronary blood flow and ventricular filling occur in diastole.

questions.question: Electromechanical systole is the time interval between _______
options: R wave and first heart sound
Q wave and second heart sound

questions.question: The windkessel effect is seen in___.
questions.explanation:
The windkessel effect is seen in large elastic vessels.

The aorta, the pulmonary artery, and their major branches have a large amount of elastin in their walls. Hence, they have a high elastic recoil effect. This property of elastic recoil is called windkessel effect (windkessel is a German word for the elastic reservoir).

This recoil of the vessels that have been stretched during systole helps to propel the blood forward during diastole thus maintaining a continuous flow throughout the cardiac cycle.

questions.question: Which of the following factors tends to increase the lymph flow?
questions.explanation:
The factor tend to increase lymph flow is increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure.

Since the lymph is derived from interstitial fluid, any factor that increases interstitial fluid pressure also increases lymph flow provided, the lymph vessels are functioning normally. The factors which increase interstitial fluid pressure include:

• Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure

• Increased interstitial fluid colloid osmotic pressure

• Increased permeability of the capillaries

• Decreased plasma colloid osmotic pressure

All of the above factors increase the filtration at the capillary-interstitium interface and therefore increase the interstitial fluid volume and pressure.

questions.question: What is the most powerful activator of sympathetic vasomotor system?
options: Posture of the body against gravity
questions.explanation:
The most powerful activator of the sympathetic vasomotor system is CNS ischemic response.

CNS ischemic response:

When blood flow to the vasomotor center in lower brainstem (medulla) is severely decreased, the local concentration of CO2 increases greatly and has a potent effect in stimulating the sympathetic vasomotor nervous control areas in the brain’s medulla. Blood pressure may increase till 250 mmHg. The strong activation may cause some peripheral vessels to occlude.

It doesnt activate till arterial pressure drops to 60mmHg or less, hence it is principally a emergency mechanism.

Note: Baroreceptors are the most common activators, but not the most powerful.

questions.question: An elderly man, with congestive cardiac failure, complains of shortness of breath when lying down. What is the mechanism behind this symptom?
options: Reservoir function of veins in lower limbs.
questions.answer: A. Reservoir function of pulmonary veins.
questions.explanation:
The given scenario describes orthopnea in congestive heart failure. It is due to reservoir function of pulmonary veins.

Orthopnea is dyspnea occurring in the recumbent position.

It results from redistribution of fluid from the splanchnic circulation and lower extremities (increased venous return) into the heart during recumbency. This increased venous return is not put out by the left ventricle and hence pools in the pulmonary veins that acts as capacitance vessels (reservoir function) adding to the already congested pulmonary vasculature resulting in breathing difficulty.

questions.question: The interstitial fluid pressure is negative in ______.
questions.explanation:
The interstitial fluid pressure is negative in the lungs.

The interstitial fluid pressure is slightly negative in the body except in the encapsulated organs.

It is positive in

• Rigid closed compartments- bone marrow, brain

• Encapsulated organs - kidney, skeletal muscle

This is due to the fact that in the kidneys, high-pressure vessels push the interstitial fluid against an unyielding fibrous capsule raising the pressure. The same principle applies to skeletal muscle surrounded by layers of fascia.

questions.question: Blood flow per minute in pulmonary circulation is

Blood flow per minute in the pulmonary circulation is equal to flow through the systemic circulation so as to provide continuous blood supply to the body.

If the flow rate is slower in the pulmonary circulation than systemic, then the left ventricle would soon empty completely. If the flow rate is faster in the pulmonary circulation then the left ventricle would be soon overloaded.

Please note that because some blood flows into the bronchial arteries, the actual flow through the pulmonary circulation is slightly lesser than the flow through the systemic circulation. However, this question aims to state that the blood flow through both pulmonary and systemic circulation is largely equal.

questions.question: A patient was receiving a red cell transfusion following hip arthroplasty. Midway through the transfusion, she developed signs and symptoms of shock. What is the type of shock seen in her?
questions.explanation:
The shock due to a transfusion reaction is distributive shock.

During transfusion reaction, there is decreased systemic vascular resistance due to system-wide vasodilation mediated by release of histamine by mast cells in response to antigen bound IgE, leading to distributive shock.

Types of circulatory shock:

• Hypovolemic shock: due to decreased blood in vascular compartment. E.g., haemorrhage, dehydration.

• Cardiogenic shock: due to decreased capacity of heart to pump. E.g., any pathology of heart decreasing its ability to maintain cardiac output.

• Obstructive shock: due to conditions causing obstruction to blood flow in lungs and heart.E.g:pulmonary embolism.

• Distributive/vasculogenic shock: excessive vasodilation leading to impaired organ perfusion. E.g: septic shock, SIRS, transfusion reaction, Addisonian crisis, neurogenic shock.

Three stages of shock:

• Non-progressive: also called compensated shock, where normal compensatory mechanism eventually causes full recovery without help from outside therapy.

• Progressive: also called non-compensated, without therapy it gets steadily worse.

• Irreversible: even therapy is inadequate to save life.

In progressive hemorrhagic shock, there is increased lysosomal activity, decreased active transport of sodium and tissue acidosis.

questions.question: Thin-walled and delicate vessels like capillaries are less prone to rupture. This can be explained by _______.
questions.explanation:
Thin-walled and delicate vessels like capillaries are less prone to rupture and this can be explained by Laplace law.

The principal reason for these vessels' relative invulnerability is their small diameter. The protective effect of small size, in this case, is an example of the law of Laplace.

Laplace law states that tension in the wall of a cylinder (T) is equal to the product of the transmural pressure (P) and the radius (r) divided by the wall thickness (w):

T = Pr/w

As the tissue pressure is low, P is equated to the pressure inside the blood vessel.
W can be ignored as well as capillaries are thin walled. Hence:

P = T/r

In a thin-walled viscus, P = T divided by the two principal radii of curvature of the viscus: P = T (1/r1+1/r2)

In a cylinder such as a blood vessel, one radius is infinite, so P = T /r

Hence, smaller the radius, lower is the tension necessary in the wall to balance the distending pressure.

questions.question: Mayer waves are due to ____.
options: Variation of arterial pressure during each systole.
Variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control of blood pressure
Variation of arterial pressure with changes in respiration.
Variation of arterial pressure with postural change.
questions.answer: B. Variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control of blood pressure
questions.explanation:
Mayer waves are due to the variation of arterial pressure due to reflex changes in nervous control of blood pressure.

The most important mechanisms are as follows:

I: Baroreceptor and chemoreceptor reflex:

High pressure excites the baroreceptors -->inhibits sympathetic nervous system and lowers the pressure -->The decreased pressure, in turn, reduces the baroreceptor stimulation -->elevating the pressure to a high value (the response is not instantaneous, it is delayed until a few seconds later). This high pressure then initiates another cycle, and the oscillation continues.

II: Oscillation of the CNS Ischemic Response:

The cerebrospinal fluid pressure is raised to 160 mm Hg --> causes compression of cerebral blood vessels --> cerebral ischemia--> CNS ischemic pressure response raises the arterial pressure up to 200mm Hg -->the brain ischemia is relieved and the sympathetic nervous system becomes inactive -->the arterial pressure falls rapidly back to a much lower value, causing brain ischemia once again -->initiates another rise in pressure. This chain of events repeats itself cyclically as long as the cerebrospinal fluid pressure remains elevated.

Blood usually does not flow continuously through the capillaries. Instead, it flows intermittently, turning on and off every few seconds or minutes. This is vasomotion, which is responsible for flow of blood in capillaries .

The main regulatory factor for vasomotion is tissue oxygen concentration.

questions.question: The relation between ventricular stroke volume and end-diastolic volume is explained by ________
questions.explanation:
The relation between ventricular stroke volume and end-diastolic volume is explained by Frank Starling's law.

Length–tension relationship in cardiac muscle is similar to that in skeletal muscle. when the muscle is stretched, the developed tension increases to a maximum and then declines as stretch becomes more extreme. Starling stated that “energy of contraction is proportional to the initial length of the cardiac muscle fibre”.

When cardiac output is regulated by changes in cardiac fibre length, this is referred to as heterometric regulation.

Conversely, regulation due to changes in contractility independent of length is called homometric regulation.

questions.question: If the SA node discharges at 0.00 sec, when will the action potential normally arrive at the epicardial surface at the base of the left ventricle?
questions.explanation:
The duration of action potential to arrive at the epicardial surface at the base of the left ventricle is 0.22sec.

Impulse initiated from SA node at 0.00s

 ↓

Impulse reaches AV node at 0.03s

 ↓

Delay of impulse at AV node by 0.13s resulting in a total time of 0.16s (0.03+0.13) to reach the beginning of Purkinje fibres

Impulse travels from endocardial to epicardial surface in 0.03s (due to arrangement of myocardial fibres)

 ↓

Hence, a total time of 0.22s (0.19+0.03) is taken for the impulse to travel from SA node to epicardial surface of the base of ventricles

questions.question: The order of depolarization after stimulation of Purkinje fibers is:

The order of depolarization is from septum → endocardium→ epicardium.

The spread of Cardiac Excitation:

Atrial depolarization is initiated from SA node spreads radially through atria, then converges on the AV node. A delay of about 0.1s (AV nodal delay) occurs before excitation spreads to the ventricles.
Ventricular depolarization starts at the left side of the interventricular septum and moves first to the right across the midportion of the septum. It moves along the ventricular walls to the AV groove, proceeding from the endocardial to the epicardial surface.

questions.question: Phases of the ventricular muscle action potential are shown below. At which phase of the below image, the action potential is most dependant on sodium permeability?

questions.question: Phase 0 of pacemaker potential is initiated by:
options: Opening of voltage gated Ca2+ channel
Inactivation of voltage gated Ca2+ channel
Inactivation of voltage gated Na+ channel
questions.answer: B. Opening of voltage gated Ca2+ channel
questions.explanation:
Phase 0 of pacemaker potential is initiated by opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels.

The pacemaker potential consists of:

• Phase 0 - this is upstroke seen due to the opening of voltage-gated Ca2+ channels. This causes an influx of calcium leading to the upstroke.

• Phase 3 - This is followed by inactivation of the calcium channels and simultaneous activation of K+ channels. This leads to efflux of K+ bringing about repolarization.

• Phase 4- As the K+ efflux declines, a channel permeable to both Na+ and K+ opens leading to an influx of both Na+ and K+. This is the If channel. This is responsible for slow spontaneous diastolic depolarization. This accounts for the automaticity of SA and AV node.

The slope of Phase 4 in the SA node determines the heart rate.

Note: Fast voltage-gated Na+ channels seen in myocyte potential are permanently inactivated because of the less negative resting potential of the pacemaker cells.
