Sympathetic stimulation causes faster conduction, therefore decreased refractory period.

Effects of sympathetic stimulation:

• Chronotropic- It increases the rate of sinus nodal discharge.

• Dromotropic- It increases the rate of conduction.

• Bathmotropic- It increases the level of excitability in all portions of the heart.

• Inotropic- It increases the force of contraction of all the cardiac musculature.

questions.question: The AH interval on His Bundle Electrocardiogram (HBE) corresponds to the conduction of _____ on ECG.
options: From AV node to bundle of His
questions.answer: B. From AV node to bundle of His
questions.explanation:
The AH interval corresponds to conduction from AV node to bundle of His on an ECG.

His bundle electrogram (HBE)

The record of the electrical activity obtained with the catheter passed through a vein to the right side of the heart and placed close to the tricuspid valve is HBE.

It shows 3 deflections as shown in the figure:

His bundle waves

Description

A

Denotes AV node activation

H

Denotes His bundle activation

V

Denotes ventricular depolarization

With HBE and standard ECG leads, 3 intervals can be timed accurately

Interval

Recording

Corresponding event

PA interval

Time from the first appearance of atrial depolarization to the A wave in HBE

Conduction time from SA node to AV node

AH interval

From A wave to start of H spike

AV nodal conduction time

HV interval

Time from start of H spike to start of QRS deflection in ECG

Conduction in Bundle of His and bundle branches

questions.question: What is blood pressure?
questions.answer: D. Cardiac output X peripheral resistance
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is defined as cardiac output X peripheral resistance.

questions.question: What is the SI unit of blood pressure?
questions.explanation:
The SI unit of blood pressure is Pascal (Pa). It is conventionally expressed in mm of Hg.

Note: 1 mmHg = 133 Pa.

questions.question: What is mean arterial pressure?
questions.explanation:
Mean arterial pressure is diastolic + 1/3rd pulse pressure.

The mean pressure is the average pressure throughout the cardiac cycle. It is not equal to the average of systolic and diastolic pressure because, at normal heart rates, a greater fraction of the cardiac cycle is spent in diastole than in systole. The mean arterial pressure is therefore determined by about 60 percent by the diastolic pressure and 40 percent by the systolic pressure.

Mean BP= DBP + 1/3 Pulse pressure
 = DBP +1/3(SBP- DBP)
 = (3DBP+SBP- DBP)/3
 = 2/3 DBP + 1/3 SBP

questions.question: Korotkoffs sounds are due to ______.
options: Increased laminar flow on application of pressure
Closure of aortic valve in diastole
Arterial turbulence on occlusion of vessel
Normal sound that exist even without application of cuff
questions.answer: C. Arterial turbulence on occlusion of vessel
questions.explanation:
Korotkoffs sounds are due to arterial turbulence on occlusion of the vessel.

The streamline flow in the unconstricted artery is silent. But when the artery is narrowed, the velocity of flow through the constriction exceeds the critical velocity and turbulent flow results. Turbulent flow in the partly occluded brachial artery sets up the vibrations (oscillations) of the vessel wall which are heard through the stethoscope and are known as Korotkoffs sounds.

questions.question: When measuring blood pressure, which of the following is unlikely to show a spuriously high BP?
questions.explanation:
The auscultatory gap may give a falsely low recording of systolic BP and overestimation of diastolic blood pressure not spuriously high BP.

In older patients with wide pulse pressure and in some hypertensive patients, the Korotkoff sounds may become inaudible between SBP and DBP, and reappear as cuff deflation continues, this is known as auscultatory gap.

Small cuff size, obesity, and thick calcified arteries can give rise to falsely high BP as in these conditions, vessels are difficult to compress and higher cuff pressure is required to compress them.

questions.question: The systolic pressure in the right ventricle is _______
questions.explanation: The systolic pressure in the right ventricle is about 25 mmHg.

questions.question: During diastole, the arterial pressure is maintained by:
questions.explanation:
During diastole, the arterial pressure is maintained by the elastic recoil of aorta.

There is stretching of aorta and arteries during systole due to ejection of blood from ventricle. During diastole, the previously stretched aorta and arteries recoil. The volume of blood that is displaced by the recoil furnishes continuous capillary flow throughout diastole.

questions.question: The shape of arterial pulse is influenced by _____
questions.explanation:
The shape of arterial pulse is influenced by arterial wall expansion.

Arterial Pulse

• The blood forced into the aorta during systole not only moves the blood in the vessels forward but also sets up a pressure wave that travels along the arteries. The pressure wave expands the arterial walls as it travels and the expansion is palpable as the pulse.

• The two major factors that influence arterial pulse are- stroke volume of the heart and distensibility (compliance) of the vessels.

questions.question: Carotid sinus baroreceptor is most sensitive to _____
questions.explanation:
The carotid sinus baroreceptor is most sensitive to pulse pressure. They fire more rapidly to a constantly changing pressure than a stationary one.

Baroreceptors

1. Stretch receptors located in the heart and adventitia of the blood vessels

2. Types based on location

• Carotid sinus and aortic arch receptors (high-pressure regions)

• Cardiopulmonary receptors (low-pressure regions)

3. Afferents

• Carotid sinus – a branch of Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX CN) – the carotid sinus nerve (sinus nerve of Hering)

• Aortic arch receptor – a branch of the Vagus nerve (X CN) – aortic depressor nerve

4. Center for Reflex

• Medulla (Nucleus Tractus solitarius)

5. Efferents

• Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons to heart and vasculature

• Most sensitive to pulsatile pressure: They work to maintain BP in the range of mean BP, but it is the changes in the pressure they are the most sensitive to.

• The threshold for excitation: 50 mmHg

• Maximal activity: 180 mmHg

6. Responses when one carotid sinus is isolated and perfused and the other baroreceptors are denervated

• Perfusion pressure <30mm Hg:no response

• 70–110mm Hg: the linear relationship between perfusion pressure and the fall in systemic BP and HR

• >150mm Hg: no further increase in response to the degree of inhibition of the sympathetic nerve is maximal.

questions.question: Baroreceptor stimulation would result in _______
questions.answer: C. Decreased sympathetic discharge to heart
questions.explanation:
Baroreceptor stimulation would result in decreased sympathetic discharge to heart.

The baroreceptors are stretch receptors in the walls of the heart and blood vessels.
Baroreceptor stimulation, by distension of the structures they are located in, inhibits the tonic discharge of sympathetic nerves and excites the vagal innervation of the heart. Thus leading to:

• Vasodilation and venodilation

• Hypotension

• Bradycardia

• Decrease in cardiac output

questions.question: The maximum blood pressure to which carotid baroreceptors respond is
questions.explanation:
The maximum blood pressure to which carotid baroreceptors respond is 180 mmHg (arterial pressure here and not MAP).
The blood pressure range to which carotid baroreceptors respond is 70- 150 mmHg of mean arterial pressure.

questions.question: Discharge from Baroreceptors cause inhibition of:
questions.explanation:
Discharge from Baroreceptors cause inhibition of Rostral ventrolateral medulla.

The baroreceptors are stimulated by distension of the structures in which they are located. Their afferent fibers pass via the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves to the medulla. These fibers release glutamate to excite neurons in the nucleus of the tractus solitarius (NTS). These NTS neurons then excite neurons in the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM). These CVLM neurons release the inhibitory neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) into the RVLM to reduce the firing rate of these. Thus, reducing the sympathetic outflow.

questions.question: The low pressure receptors are ______
options: Stimulated by atrial systole and diastole
questions.answer: B. Stimulated by atrial systole and diastole
questions.explanation:
The low-pressure receptors are stimulated by atrial systole and diastole

The low-pressure receptors are those in the great veins, right and left atria and pulmonary vessels.
Atrial stretch receptors are of two types:

• Type A: discharge primarily during atrial systole

• Type B: discharge primarily during late diastole

Distension of the atrial walls→stimulation of atrial receptors → Vasodilation, fall in BP and increased heart rate.

questions.question: Occlusion of common carotid arteries on both sides leads to _____
options: Increase in heart rate and BP
Increase in BP and decrease in heart rate
Decrease in heart rate and BP
No effect on heart rate and BP
questions.answer: A. Increase in heart rate and BP
questions.explanation:
Occlusion of both common carotid arteries causes an increase in HR and BP.

Reduced sinus pressure → response carried to nucleus tractus solitarius via glossopharyngeal and vagus nerve → less inhibitory effect on the vasomotor center.
This leads to:

• Decreased parasympathetic activity to the heart - Increases heart rate

• Increased sympathetic activity to the heart and blood vessels - Increases heart rate, contractility, constricts arterioles - Increases TPR, constricts veins - increases venous return

Note: The carotid baroreceptors are located in the walls of the carotid sinus, which is located at or slightly above the bifurcation of the common carotid arteries. So, the occlusion of common carotid arteries is occlusion proximal to the carotid sinus.

If the occlusion is distal to the carotid sinus →increase in sinus pressure → activation of baroreceptor reflex → decrease in BP and HR.

questions.question: The hormone involved in the regulation of blood pressure is _____
questions.explanation:
The hormone involved in the regulation of blood pressure is Angiotensin II.

Angiotensin II is a powerful vasoconstrictor that increases the total peripheral resistance and decreases Na+ and H2O excretion by kidney, thereby causing an increase in arterial BP.

questions.question: Marey’s law states that _____
options: Heart rate varies directly with blood pressure
Heart rate varies inversely with blood pressure
Heart rate do not have any relation with blood pressure
Heart rate is directly proportional to cardiac output
questions.answer: B. Heart rate varies inversely with blood pressure
questions.explanation: Marey’s law states that the heart rate varies inversely with blood pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT caused by sympathetic stimulation?
questions.explanation:
Increased venous capacitance is NOT caused by sympathetic stimulation.

Important effects of increased sympathetic stimulation:

• Arteriolar vasoconstriction

• Increased stroke volume

• Increased heart rate

• Venoconstriction and decrease in venous capacitance

• The increase in mean systemic filling pressure is caused mainly by venous contraction.

All these effects together bring about an increased arterial pressure.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding nitric oxide?
questions.answer: B. Acts by increasing cAMP levels
questions.explanation:
Nitric oxide acts by increasing cGMP not by increasing cAMP.

Nitric Oxide

• Also known as Endothelium-derived relaxing factor (EDRF).

• Synthesized in endothelial cells from arginine in a reaction catalyzed by nitric oxide synthase (NOS).

• Mechanism of action:
NO causes activation of guanylyl cyclase → ↑ cGMP → relaxation of vascular smooth muscle → vasodilation.

• Effects of NO:

• Vasodilation.

• Neuromodulator in brain.

• Antimicrobial and cytotoxic activity of various inflammatory cells.

• In GIT, relaxation of smooth muscle.

• Penile erection.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man comes to his primary-care clinician complaining of erectile dysfunction. He is given a prescription for sildenafil, and on follow-up, reports that his ability to sustain an erection has been improved markedly by this treatment. The action of which of the following vasoactive mediators would primarily be prolonged in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The action of nitric oxide would primarily be prolonged in this patient.

Sildenafil: It is used for the treatment of erectile dysfunction, which inhibits cGMP-specific phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5), an enzyme that degrades cGMP, thereby effectively prolonging the action of NO.

Penile erection is produced by release of nitric oxide (NO), with consequent vasodilation and engorgement of the corpora cavernosa.

questions.question: A 45-year-old male met with a road traffic accident and suffered a head injury. On examination, he was drowsy and his blood pressure is high. Which reflex is responsible for elevated blood pressure in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The reflex responsible for elevated blood pressure(BP) in head injury patients is the Cushing reflex.

When intracranial pressure is increased, the blood supply to rostral ventrolateral neurons is compromised, and the local hypoxia and hypercapnia increase the discharge of the central chemoreceptors. The resultant rise in systemic arterial pressure (Cushing reflex) tends to restore the blood flow to the medulla.

Cushing reflex causes a triad of symptoms:

• Reflex bradycardia (via arterial baroreceptors)

• Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure)

• Irregular respiration (bradypnea)

questions.question: All of the following are rapidly acting blood pressure control mechanisms except:
questions.explanation:
Renin-angiotensin vasoconstrictor mechanism is not a rapidly acting pressure control mechanism, it is an intermediate-acting mechanism.

Regulation of Arterial Blood Pressure:

• Rapidly acting pressure control mechanism (acting within sec or min)

• The chemoreceptor reflex.

• The central nervous system ischemic mechanism.

• The baroreceptor reflex.

• Intermediate-acting mechanisms (act after minutes)

• The capillary fluid shift mechanism.

• Stress-relaxation of the vasculature.

• The renin-angiotensin vasoconstrictor mechanism.

• Long-term mechanisms (after days)

• Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS)

Note:

• Renin-angiotensin vasoconstrictor mechanism is an intermediate-acting mechanism, but water conservation by RAAS is a long-term mechanism in the regulation of BP.

• Most rapidly acting: Baroreceptor reflex>>Chemoreceptor reflex

questions.question: Which of the following neurotransmitters is correctly matched with an autonomic pathway?
options: Glutamate is released by Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla (CVLM) neurons projecting to the intermediolateral nucleus (IML)
GABA is released by Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (NTS) neurons projecting to the nucleus ambiguus
GABA is released by CVLM neurons projecting to the Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (RVLM)
Glutamate is released by CVLM neurons projecting to the NTS
questions.answer: C. GABA is released by CVLM neurons projecting to the Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (RVLM)
questions.explanation:
Basic Neural Pathway involved in Regulation of BP

• NTS: Nucleus Tractus Solitarius

• CVLM: Caudal Ventrolateral Medulla

• RVLM (VMC): Rostral Ventrolateral Medulla (Vasomotor center)

• CVC (CIC): Cardiovagal center (Cardioinhibitory center

• intermediolateral nucleus (IML)

questions.question: Stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors causes:
questions.explanation:
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies can produce variable effects on heart rate-

• Direct Effect

• vagal stimulation → bradycardia

• Indirect effect

• Hypoxia →peripheral chemoreceptor stimulation→ hyperventilation and increased catecholamine secretion → tachycardia and increased cardiac output

Chemoreceptor reflex

• Receptors

• Peripheral chemoreceptors in carotid and aortic bodies

• Central chemoreceptors in the medulla

• Stimulus

• decrease in- PaO2

• increase in-Pa CO2, H+ ion conc

• Afferent

• IX (sinus nerve of Hering) and X (vagus N)

• Center for reflex

• Medulla

• Efferent

• Sympathetic and parasympathetic neurons to heart vasculature and adrenal medulla

• Response

• Direct effect- bradycardia

• Indirect effect- hyperventilation, tachycardia, vasoconstriction, increased cardiac output and increased BP

questions.question: Ptyalin is secreted by which of the following glands?
questions.explanation:
Ptyalin (salivary α-amylase) is secreted by the salivary gland.

There are 3 pairs of salivary glands

1. Parotid

2. Submandibular

3. Sublingual glands

Functions of saliva:

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false?
options: Meissner’s plexus is present in submucosa
Myentric plexus is present between inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layer
Muscularis mucosa is associated with peristalsis
Villi are absent in large intestine
questions.answer: C. Muscularis mucosa is associated with peristalsis
questions.explanation:
Muscularis propria is associated with peristalsis and not muscularis mucosa.

Contraction of muscularis mucosa alters absorptive and secretive surface area.

Meissner’s plexus (submucosal plexus) is present in the submucosa.

The myenteric plexus (Auerbach plexus) is present between the inner circular and outer longitudinal muscle layer.

Villi are absent in the large intestine but present in the small intestine.

Layers of intestinal wall from outside to inside are as follows:

• Serosa

• The longitudinal smooth muscle layer

• The circular smooth muscle layer

• Submucosa

• Mucosa

questions.question: Salivary amylase is inactivated by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Salivary amylase is inactivated by the low pH of the stomach. It is rapidly denatured at pH 4 (gastric pH is 1 to 3.5).

Salivary amylase is activated by chloride.

Salivary α amylase (Ptyalin):

• Digests starch: cleaves internal α-1,4-glycosidic bonds in starch

• Optimum pH: 7

• Denatured at pH 4

Since a large portion of a meal often remains unmixed for a considerable length of time in the stomach, the salivary enzyme may account for the digestion of as much as 75% of the starch present before it is denatured by gastric acid.

Note: Even in the absence of salivary amylase, there is no defect in carbohydrate digestion because pancreatic amylase is sufficient to digest all of the ingested starch.

questions.question: Which of the following gland secretes lingual lipase?
questions.explanation:
Lingual lipase is secreted by von Ebner’s gland.

von Ebner's gland is a serous salivary gland situated around circumvallate and foliate papillae in front of the terminal sulcus.

Lingual lipase hydrolyse dietary lipid. The optimal pH is 3-6. Unlike pancreatic lipase, it is not inhibited by bile salts, medium-chain FA, and lecithin. Hence, it remains active through the stomach and into the intestine.

questions.question: Which of the following fluids have the highest daily secretion of potassium?
questions.explanation:
The highest daily secretion of K+ is into the saliva.

In the process of formation of saliva, Na+ and Cl- are reabsorbed from the saliva, and K+ and HCO3- are secreted into the saliva.

Note: The highest concentration of K+ is in the rectal fluid.

questions.question: The secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland causing a patient to salivate, pass through which of the following ganglions?
questions.explanation:
The secretomotor fibers to the parotid gland pass through the Otic ganglion.

Salivary secretion is almost entirely controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system. Volume is mainly mediated by parasympathetic stimulation while the composition of saliva (increased proteinaceous content) is slightly modified by sympathetic input.

The parasympathetic preganglionic fibers are delivered by the glossopharyngeal and facial nerves to otic and submandibular ganglion respectively.

Regulation of salivary secretion by the parasympathetic nervous system:

questions.question: Rennin is present in_____
questions.explanation:
Rennin is present in the gastric juice. It is also called chymosin.

It is a protein-digesting enzyme (endopeptidase) found in the stomach of newborn cows. It transforms (curdles) caseinogen into insoluble casein.

In humans and in some animals that lack rennin, milk is coagulated by the action of pepsin.

Note: Renin is produced by juxtaglomerular cells of the kidney, which hydrolyzes angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.

questions.question: A patient presents with anemia and achlorhydria. After evaluation, pernicious anemia is diagnosed. Damage to which of the following cells is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Pernicious anemia develops due to autoimmune damage to the parietal cells in gastric glands.

The parietal cells secrete both HCl and intrinsic factor. Therefore, when the parietal cells are destroyed, both achlorhydria, as well as pernicious anemia, develop.

Pernicious anemia occurs due to the deficiency of the intrinsic factor of Castle, which is important for the absorption of vitamin B12.

questions.question: Which of the following is secreted by the Goblet cells?
questions.explanation:
Goblet cells secrete mucus. These cells are located on the surface of the crypts of Lieberkuhn and the villi of the small intestine.

Cells present in the crypts of Lieberkuhn:

• Goblet cells (similar to surface cells of the stomach) - secrete mucus that acts as a lubricant and protects the intestinal surface

• Epithelial cells - secrete succus entericus (intestinal secretion)

• Paneth cells - secrete lysozymes and defensins (antibacterial substances)

questions.question: In the stomach, H+ ions are secreted in exchange for which of the following ions?
questions.explanation:
H+ ions are secreted into the lumen of the stomach in exchange for K+ by the H+–K+ pump (H+, K+-ATPase).

Mechanism of HCl formation:

• In the parietal cells, CO2 and H2O are converted to H+ and HCO3–, catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase.

• H+ is secreted into the lumen of the stomach by the H+–K+ pump in exchange for K+.

• HCO3– moves out of the cell into the bloodstream in exchange for Cl– (Cl––HCO3–exchange). This Cl– moves into the lumen of the stomach.

• H+ and Cl– combine to form HCl.

As HCO3– is added to the venous blood, the pH of the blood increases. This is called alkaline tide. Eventually, this HCO3– will be secreted in the pancreatic secretions to neutralize H+ in the small intestine.

Proton pump inhibitors inhibit H+–K+ pump.

questions.question: A patient diagnosed with gastroesophageal reflux disease is found to have excess gastric secretion. All of the following are likely to increase the secretion, except:
questions.explanation:
Gastric secretion is not increased by HCl. HCl decreases gastric secretion via a negative feedback mechanism.

Low pH due to HCl in the stomach inhibits gastrin secretion, which in turn, inhibits H+ secretion. Hence, the presence of HCl inhibits gastric secretion.

Stimuli that increase acid and gastrin secretion:

• Distension of stomach

• Peptides

• Calcium

• Alcohol and caffeine

• Increased vagal discharge

Stimuli that decrease acid and gastrin secretion:

• Gastric acid

• Secretin family - secretin, glucagon, VIP, GIP

• Somatostatin

• CCK, Calcitonin

• PGE2

questions.question: A patient with recurrent abdominal pain is found to have multiple duodenal ulcers. After a detailed evaluation, he is diagnosed with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Stimulation of which of the following can inhibit gastric secretion in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Gastric secretion is inhibited by somatostatin.

It inhibits gastric secretion via both direct and indirect pathways:

• Direct pathway - somatostatin acts directly on the acid-producing parietal cells by binding to receptors on parietal cells that are coupled to adenylyl cyclase via a Gi protein. This inhibits adenylyl cyclase, and cAMP levels are reduced. In this way, somatostatin antagonizes the stimulatory effect of histamine on H+ secretion.

• Indirect pathway - somatostatin inhibits the release of histamine and gastrin and thus decreasing H+ secretion indirectly.

questions.question: Maximum gastric secretion occurs in which of the following phases?
options: Secretion is equal in all phases
questions.explanation: Maximum gastric secretion occurs in the gastric phase.

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for increasing the HCl secretion in the gastric phase?
questions.explanation:
HCl secretion in the gastric phase is increased by gastrin.

Gastrin stimulates H+ secretion by interaction with cholecystokinin B (CCKB) receptor on the parietal cell which secretes HCl.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the secretion from the exocrine pancreas?
questions.answer: D. Secretion is stimulated by cholecystokinin
questions.explanation:
Pancreatic secretion is stimulated by cholecystokinin (CCK) and Ach. It is always isotonic.

It has virtually the same Na+ and K+ concentrations as in plasma. It is rich in several digestive enzymes like amylase, trypsin, chymotrypsin, lipase, elastase, etc.

questions.question: Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice is secreted under the influence of which of the following stimulants?
questions.explanation:
Bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice is secreted under the influence of secretin.

Secretin is secreted by the S cells of the duodenum. Its primary function is to promote the secretion of bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice by the ductal cells of the pancreas and duodenum. This secretion is poor in enzymes.

Other functions:

• Augments the effects of CCK

• Inhibits gastrin release

• Decreases gastric acid secretion

• Contraction of the pyloric sphincter

• Exerts trophic effect on the pancreas

questions.question: Which among the following is the most alkaline secretion?
questions.explanation:
The most alkaline secretion is Brunner’s gland secretion with a pH of 8.0 – 8.9.

Brunner’s gland is located in the first few centimeters of the duodenal wall. It secretes large amounts of alkaline mucus in response to tactile stimuli on the duodenal mucosa, vagal stimulation, and GI hormones, especially secretin. It is inhibited by sympathetic stimulation.

The function of the mucus secreted by Brunner’s glands is to protect the duodenal wall from digestion by the highly acidic gastric juice emptying from the stomach.

Note: The second most alkaline secretion in the GI tract is the pancreatic juice.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most potent choleretic?
questions.explanation:
Bile salts (chemical choleretic) are the most potent choleretics.

Any substance that increases bile secretion is called a choleretic. Bile secretion may be increased by chemical (bile salts), hormonal (Secretin), and neural (vagal stimulation) mechanisms.

Note: Cholagogues cause contraction of the gallbladder. Eg. CCK

questions.question: Primary bile acids are synthesized from_____
questions.explanation:
Primary bile acids are synthesized from cholesterol by hepatocytes.

Bile contains bile acids, bile salts, bile pigments, phospholipids, water, and electrolytes. It is secreted by the liver and concentrated in the gall bladder.

Two primary bile acids (cholic acid and chenodeoxycholic acid) are synthesized from cholesterol by hepatocytes. When these primary bile acids are secreted into the lumen of the intestine, a portion of each is converted to secondary bile acids (deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid) by bacteria.

The liver conjugates primary and secondary bile acids with glycine or taurine to their respective bile salts. Ex: Glycocholic acid, Taurodeoxycholic acid.

Rate of bile secretion is 30 - 60 mL/hour (500 - 1000 mL/day).

Note: Bile has no digestive enzymes.

questions.question: Enterohepatic circulation is necessary for the secretion of______
questions.explanation:
Enterohepatic circulation is necessary for the secretion of bile salts.

The enterohepatic circulation of bile salts is the recycling of bile salts between the small intestine (terminal ileum) and the liver by means of the portal vein. It occurs 6-8 times a day.

The recirculation of bile salts to the liver reduces the demand to synthesize new bile salts.

questions.question: Which of the following does not belong to the secretin family?
questions.explanation:
CCK (Cholecystokinin) belongs to the gastrin family, not the secretin family.

Classification of GI hormones based on structure and function:

• Gastrin family - Gastrin, Cholecystokinin

• Secretin family - Secretin, Glucagon, VIP, GIP

• Others - Motilin, Ghrelin, Somatostatin, etc

questions.question: A patient underwent resection of the gastric antrum. A few weeks later, endoscopy revealed atrophy of the gastric mucosa. Serum levels of gastrin were found to be decreased. Which of the following is true regarding this GI hormone?
questions.explanation:
Gastrin is a peptide hormone.

It is secreted by the G cells of the gastric mucosa present in the antrum of the stomach, primarily during the gastric phase of gastric acid secretion.

It causes gastric secretion at 1000-1500 mL/day. Its primary stimulus is gastric distension.

Primary functions of Gastrin:

• Gastric acid (HCl) secretion

• Pepsin secretion

• Trophic action on the gastric mucosa

Other functions:

• Stimulates gastric motility

• Prevents gastroesophageal reflux by contraction of LES

Conditions associated with increased gastrin secretions (Ex: Zollinger-Ellison syndrome), will cause an increase in H+ secretion and hypertrophy of the gastric mucosa.

Conditions associated with reduced gastrin secretion (Ex: Resection of the gastric antrum), will cause a decrease in H+ secretion and atrophy of the gastric mucosa.

questions.question: What is the effect of cholecystokinin on GIT?
questions.explanation:
Cholecystokinin (CCK) inhibits gastric emptying.

It is secreted by the I cells of the duodenal and jejunal mucosa in response to monoglycerides, fatty acids, and amino acids.

Primary functions:

• Stimulation of pancreatic enzyme secretion

• Contraction of the gallbladder

• Relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi

Other functions:

• Augmentation of the action of secretin in producing alkaline (bicarbonate rich) pancreatic juice

• Inhibition of gastric emptying

• Trophic (growth) effect on the exocrine pancreas

• Increases the synthesis of enterokinase

• It enhances the motility of the small intestine and colon

• Along with secretin, it augments the contraction of the pyloric sphincter and thus preventing the reflux of duodenal contents into the stomach

• It promotes satiety

questions.question: What stimulates secretin secretion?
questions.explanation:
Secretin secretion is stimulated by acid.

Stimuli that increase secretin secretion:

• Low duodenal pH (2-4.5) due to acid in the chyme

• Products of protein digestion in the upper small intestine

Secretin secretion is regulated by negative feedback:

questions.question: How much is the daily secretion of gastric juice?
questions.explanation:
Daily secretion of gastric juice is between 1500-2000 mL.

Note: This is a controversial question- Daily secretion of gastric juice is

• 1500 mL according to Guyton and Hall Textbook of Medical Physiology,13th edition, Page no: 819

• 2500 mL according to Ganong's Review Of Medical Physiology - 25th Edition, Page no:464

Choose 2500 mL if given in the options. If not, choose within the range of 1500-2500 mL.

questions.question: Which of the following statement is correct regarding secretin?
questions.explanation:
Secretin increases HCO3- secretion by ductal cells of the pancreas and duodenum.

It is secreted by the S cells in the upper small intestine.

Functions of secretion are:

• Primary function

• ↑ HCO3- secretion by ductal cells of pancreas and duodenum

• Other functions

• Augments the effects of CCK

• Inhibits gastrin release

• ↓ gastric acid secretion

• Contraction of pyloric sphincter

• Exerts trophic effect on the pancreas

questions.question: Which of the following is secreted by the I cells of duodenum?
questions.explanation: I cells of the duodenum secrete CCK.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presented with abdominal pain and diarrhea. On investigations, multiple ulcers were seen in the proximal and distal duodenum and in the jejunum. The gastric pH was found to be 1.2 with a serum gastrin concentration of 2000 pg/ml. Which of the following is the primary site for the production of GI hormone raised in this patient?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. In this condition, serum gastrin concentration is raised to around >1000 pg/ml. Gastrin is primarily secreted by G cells present in the antrum of the stomach.

questions.question: Salivary amylase is activated by which of the following ions?
questions.explanation:
Salivary amylase is activated by Cl-.

Human salivary and pancreatic amylases are activated by chloride (Cl–). They have optimum activities near-neutral pH (7.4). They hydrolyze internal 1:4α linkages but spare 1:6α linkages and terminal 1:4α linkages in starch.

questions.question: Where does the digestion of disaccharides occur?
questions.explanation:
Digestion of disaccharides occurs in the small intestine.

The enzymes maltase, sucrase, isomaltase, lactase, and trehalase are located in the enterocytes covering the intestinal microvilli brush border. The disaccharides are digested into their constituent monosaccharides as they come in contact with these enterocytes.

questions.question: Which of the following is a true statement?
options: Fructose is absorbed in the intestine by secondary active transport
SGLT2 is involved in absorption of monosaccharide in intestine
GLUT2 is involved in transport of glucose from enterocyte into interstitium
GLUT4 is responsible for basal glucose uptake in many organs
questions.answer: C. GLUT2 is involved in transport of glucose from enterocyte into interstitium
questions.explanation:
GLUT2 is involved in the transport of glucose from the enterocyte into the interstitium (or out of the enterocytes).

The image below shows the function of GLUT 2 on enterocytes.

Option A: Fructose absorption is through facilitated diffusion from the intestinal lumen into the enterocyte by GLUT5 and out of the enterocytes into the interstitium by GLUT2.

Option B: SGLT1 is involved in the absorption of glucose into the enterocyte. SGLT2 is responsible for glucose transport out of the renal tubules.

Option D: GLUT1 is responsible for basal glucose uptake in many organs.

questions.question: Which of the following is the main enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of 1,6α linkage of starch?
questions.explanation:
The main enzyme involved in the hydrolysis of 1,6α linkage of starch is isomaltase.

Both salivary and the pan­creatic α-amylases hydrolyze internal 1:4α linkages but spare 1:6α linkages and terminal 1:4α linkages of starch.

questions.question: What is chymotrypsinogen?
questions.explanation:
Chymotrypsinogen is a zymogen.

Zymogens (proenzymes) are inactive precursors of the enzymes. Most of the peptidases (proteases) are present in the form of proenzymes. Trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, procarboxypeptidase A, procarboxypeptidase B are zymogens.

questions.question: Which of the following processes converts trypsinogen to trypsin?
options: Removal of a few amino acids
questions.answer: C. Removal of a few amino acids
questions.explanation:
Trypsinogen is converted to trypsin by the removal of a few amino acids.

All proenzymes are converted to their active form by selective proteolysis (removal of a few amino acids).

Enterokinase cleaves trypsinogen to yield active trypsin. It is located on the brush border of duodenal enterocytes.

questions.question: Which of the following protects the normal pancreas from autodigestion?
questions.explanation:
The synthesis and secretion of proteases as catalytically inactive proenzymes protect the normal pancreas from autodigestion.

All the protease proenzymes present in the pancreatic juice get converted to their active form only in the small intestinal lumen (site of action).

If proenzymes get activated in the pancreas (site of origin), they can digest the entire pancreas within a few hours, giving rise to the condition called acute pancreatitis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not an endopeptidase?
questions.explanation:
Carboxypeptidase is an exopeptidase, not endopeptidase.

Peptidases (proteases) are of two types:

• Endopeptidases - they act at interior peptide bonds in the peptide molecules. Ex- pepsin, trypsin, chymotrypsin, elastase.

• Exopeptidases - they hydrolyze the amino acids at the carboxyl ends of the polypeptides, one at a time. Ex- carboxypeptidase, aminopeptidase.

questions.question: Peptide transporter 1 is involved in the absorption of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Peptide transporter 1 (PepT1) is involved in the absorption of the dipeptide.

The dipeptides and tripeptides are transported along with H+ into enterocytes by a system known as peptide trans­porter 1 (PepT1).

These peptides undergo intracellular hydrolysis to release amino acids. These amino acids are absorbed into the circulation from the basolateral membrane via basolateral amino acid transporter. H+ moves out of the cell via Na+-H+ exchanger on the luminal side.

questions.question: Which of the following is passively absorbed in the gut?
questions.explanation:
Lipids are passively absorbed in the gut.

The products of lipid digestion (monoglycerides and free fatty acids) are incorporated into micelles that are formed by bile salts and diffuse across the intestinal epithelium. Short and medium-chain fatty acids can directly diffuse across the intestinal epithelium.

Note: Recent evidence suggests that specific carrier proteins (membrane transporters) may be involved in the transport of long-chain fatty acids.

questions.question: Short-chain fatty acids produced by bacteria are maximally absorbed in which part of the intestine?
questions.explanation:
Short-chain fatty acids produced by bacteria are absorbed maximally in the colon by secondary active transport.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

Maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a function of short-chain fatty acids in the colon?
options: Trophic effect on the colonic epithelial cells
questions.explanation:
Short-chain fatty acids (2–5-carbon) in the colon promote the absorption of Na+, not secretion.

Short-chain fatty acids (SCFA) in the colon are formed by the action of colonic bacteria on complex carbohydrates, resistant starches, and other components of the dietary fiber i.e the material that escapes digestion in the upper gastrointestinal tract and enters the colon.

Functions:

• Exert a trophic effect on the colonic epithelial cells

• Combat inflam­mation

• Helps in maintaining acid-base equilibrium

questions.question: Which of the following patients is most likely to have a major electrolyte imbalance?
options: A patient with duodenal resection due to a primary tumor
A patient who underwent jejunal resection due to an obstruction
A patient with ileal resection due to recurrent Crohn's disease
A patient with sigmoid resection due to a recurrent fistula
questions.answer: B. A patient who underwent jejunal resection due to an obstruction
questions.explanation:
The resection of jejunum leads to major electrolyte imbalance because most of the fluid and electrolyte reabsorption occurs in this segment.

The maximum water absorption takes place in the jejunum.

The amount of water absorbed in the intestines follows this order: Jejunum > Ileum > Colon.

Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum.

Folate is absorbed in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

questions.question: What is the amount of fluid absorbed in the intestine in a day?
questions.explanation:
The amount of fluid absorbed in the intestine in a day is around 8L.

About 2L of ingested water and 7L of various secretions enter the gastrointestinal tract. Out of this, the majority (8800 mL) is absorbed in the small intestine and colon. The small remaining volume that is not absorbed (100–200 mL) is excreted in feces.

questions.question: Which of the following is not absorbed in the colon?
questions.explanation:
K+ is not absorbed in the colon. It is secreted in the rectal fluid.

Electrolytes (Na+, Cl-), short-chain fatty acids (acetate, propionate, butyrate), and water are absorbed in the colon.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about vitamin absorption?
options: Fat-soluble vitamin digestion needs cholesterol esterase
Vitamin B12 is absorbed in ileum
Folate is absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters
Most vitamins are absorbed in upper small intestine
questions.answer: C. Folate is absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters
questions.explanation:
Folate and vitamin B12 absorption is Na+-independent.

The remaining water-soluble vitamins—thiamin, riboflavin, niacin, pyridoxine, pantothe­nate, biotin, and ascorbic acid are absorbed by carriers that are Na+ cotransporters.

Option A: Fat-soluble vitamins are ingested in the form of esters. Digestion needs hydrolysis by cholesterol esterase and absorbed after incorporating into micelles.

Options B and D: Most vitamins are absorbed in the upper small intestine, but vitamin B12 is absorbed in the ileum. Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor, a protein secreted by the parietal cells of the stomach. This complex is absorbed across the ileal mucosa.

questions.question: A patient with anemia is prescribed iron tablets. The absorption of the supplement is likely to take place in which part of the intestine?
questions.explanation:
Almost all the iron absorption occurs in the duodenum.

Most of the iron in the diet is in the ferric (Fe3+) form, whereas it is the ferrous (Fe2+) form that is absorbed.

Note: Carbohydrates, proteins, lipids are absorbed throughout the length of the small intestine. Bile acids are present throughout the small intestine, but active absorption occurs only in the ileum, and active absorbtion of folate occurs in the upper small intestine (duodenum and jejunum).

questions.question: Which of the following stimulates ferritin synthesis?
questions.explanation:
Elemental iron stimulates ferritin synthesis.

It synthesizes ferritin by causing the release of a cytoplasmic protein that binds to a specific region in the ferritin mRNA. This disruption activates ferritin mRNA and results in its translation.

Hepcidin binds to ferroportin and triggers its internalization and degradation. This results in decreased iron absorption and decreased circulating iron levels which reduces ferritin synthesis.

Note: Ferritin sequesters Fe2+, a potentially toxic molecule.

questions.question: Which of the following is inhibited by hepcidin?
questions.explanation:
Hepcidin inhibits iron absorption.

It is named for its originally described property as a hepatocellular protein with bactericidal activities.

Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.

questions.question: While prescribing iron to a patient with iron deficiency anemia, which of the following would you recommend to increase its absorption?
questions.explanation:
Ascorbic acid is given with iron to increase its absorption.

Ascorbic acid (vitamin C) forms soluble complexes with iron and reduces iron from the ferric to the ferrous state, thereby enhancing iron absorption.

Option A: Milk decreases iron absorption.

Option C: Gastric secretions increase iron absorption by dissolving the iron and allowing it to form soluble complexes with ascorbic and other substances. This helps in its reduction to the Fe2+ form. Antacid decreases the absorption of iron.

Option D: Tannins (present in tea), phytates, phosphates, and oxalates form insoluble complexes with iron and lower its absorption.

questions.question: All of the following regulates intestinal absorption of iron except:
options: State of iron stores in the body
State of erythropoiesis in bone marrow
questions.explanation:
Intestinal absorption of iron is not regulated by the daily loss of iron.

The intestinal absorption of iron is regulated by three factors:

1. Recent dietary intake of iron

2. State of the iron stores in the body

3. State of erythropoiesis in the bone marrow

questions.question: What is the end product after the action of colonic bacteria on dietary fiber?
questions.explanation:
The action of colonic bacteria on dietary fiber would give butyrate.

Colonic bacteria act on complex carbohydrates, resistant starches, and dietary fiber to form short-chain fatty acids such as acetate, propionate, and butyrate.

SCFAs are 2–5-carbon weak acids that have an average normal concentration of about 80 mmol/L in the lumen.

questions.question: Where are the cell bodies of the orexinergic neurons are present in a patient?
questions.explanation:
Cell bodies of orexigenic neurons are present in the lateral hypothalamic area. Orexin stimulates food intake.

Role of hypothalamus in gastrointestinal and feeding regulation:

• Hunger center - lateral hypothalamic area

• Satiety center - ventromedial nuclei

• Feeding reflexes such as licking the lips and swallowing - mammillary bodies.

Note: The arcuate nucleus contains at least two different types of neurons that when stimulated lead to either increased or decreased appetite.

questions.question: In a patient who is fasting, the stomach releases a hormone that increases food intake. Identify the hormone secreted.
questions.explanation:
The hormone secreted by the stomach that increases food intake is ghrelin.

Ghrelin, the hunger hormone is produced by the endocrine cells in the oxyntic glands of the stomach. It increases food intake. Its levels increase during fasting, peaks just before the beginning of food intake, or when the person is expecting a meal. The levels fall within 1 hour of the start of feeding.

Option A: Orexin is synthesized from lateral hypothalamic neurons. It increases food intake.

Option B: Leptin is produced by adipocytes. It decreases food intake.

Option C: CCK is released from the small intestine. It decreases food intake.

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding ghrelin?
questions.explanation:
Ghrelin increases gastric acid secretion.

Ghrelin is mainly produced by the endocrine cells in the oxyntic gland area of the stomach. It is also secreted by the pancreas and adrenal glands.

Functions:

• Increases appetite/food intake (orexigenic)

• Inhibits leptin release

• Stimulates growth hormone secretion by directly acting on anterior pituitary (ghrelin-growth hormone-releasing peptide)

• Increases gastric acid secretion and gastrointestinal motility to prepare the body for food intake

• Regulates the distribution and rate of use of energy

questions.question: What will be the trend of leptin levels in a patient with a BMI of 34 kg/m2.
questions.explanation:
A patient with a BMI of 34 kg/m2 is categorized as obese. Leptin levels are high in obesity.

Leptin is an appetite-suppressing hormone synthesized from adipocytes. The larger the fat stores, the more leptin is released into the blood.

Leptin resistance in obese persons may be due to its failure to cross the blood-brain barrier and reach the hypothalamus to serve its appetite-suppressing function.

Note: A recent study has indicated that triglycerides which are elevated in obesity, inhibit the transport of leptin across the blood-brain barrier.

questions.question: All of the following have a significant role in lipid digestion except:
questions.explanation:
Lingual lipases are of little quantitative significance for lipid digestion other than in the setting of pancreatic insufficiency.

Lingual lipase is secreted by Ebner glands on the dorsal surface of the tongue in some species, and the stomach also secretes lipase.

Digestion of Lipids

• Pancreatic lipase is the most important enzyme involved in lipid digestion. The main products of its action are FFA and 2-monoglycerides (2-monoacylglycerols)

• Colipase is an accessory factor secreted in the pancreatic juice that helps to stabilize pancreatic lipase in an active conformation

• Bile acids emulsify the insoluble lipids and make them reach the surface of the mucosal cells. Bile acids also activate another pancreatic lipase called cholesterol esterase

• Cholesterol esterase hydrolyzes cholesterol esters, esters of fat-soluble vitamins, phospholipids, and triglycerides

questions.question: Slow waves are maximum in which part of the intestine?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, the frequency of 'slow waves' is maximum in the ileum (8/min).

Normal intestinal motility is determined by two patterns of electrical activity - slow waves and spike potentials.

Slow waves, also known as basic electrical rhythm are partial depolarizations of smooth muscle cells, spreading along the GIT. They originate from the interstitial cells of Cajal. The smooth muscles are in a hyperpolarized state, having a resting membrane potential of -50 to -60mV.

These waves are not action potentials themselves and they do not cause any contractions. Slow waves raise the membrane potential by 5-15mV, bringing it closer to the threshold enabling spike potential (true action potential) to occur. Therefore, they set the basic rhythm of GIT.

questions.question: As a part of cranial nerves examination, swallowing reflex is performed on a patient. Which of the following is not involved in afferent limb of this reflex?
questions.explanation:
The facial nerve is a part of an efferent limb (and not afferent) of the swallowing reflex.

Swallowing/ deglutition reflex

Afferents

Trigeminal nerve

Glossopharyngeal nerve

Vagus nerve

Centre

Nucleus of the tractus solitarius

Nucleus ambig­uus

Efferents

Trigeminal nerve

Facial nerve

Hypoglossal nerve

questions.question: Chyme is propelled forward in small intestine by_______
questions.explanation:
Chyme is propelled forward in the intestine by the peristaltic movement.

Chyme is a thick semifluid mass of partially digested food and digestive secretions that is expelled by the stomach into the duodenum.

Peristalsis is a propulsive movement, which consists of a segment of contraction behind and relaxation in front.

Segmentation consists of a segment of bowel contracting at both ends, and then a second contraction occurs in the center of the segment to force the chyme both backward and forward.

It is the small intestine’s primary method of motility during digestion of a meal.

Migrating motor complexes (MMC) are the peristaltic motor patterns that occur during fasting. They migrate from the stomach to the distal ileum.

Haustrations are the characteristic saclike segments seen in the large intestine.

questions.question: Which of the following is the major initiating response for peristalsis?
questions.explanation:
The major initiating response for peristalsis is local stretching of the gut.

Peristalsis is a reflex response that is initiated when the gut wall is stretched by the contents of the lumen. It occurs in all parts of the gastrointestinal tract from the esophagus to the rectum.

The stretch initiates a circular contraction behind the stimulus and an area of relaxation in front of it. The wave of contraction then moves in an oral-to-caudal direction. This propels the contents of the lumen forward at rates that vary from 2 to 25 cm/s.

questions.question: Which of the following is seen in a patient on parasympathetic stimulation?
questions.explanation:
Parasympathetic stimulation results in increased peristalsis.

Generally, the stimulation of parasympathetic nerves (PNS) causes an increase in the activity of the entire enteric nervous system. This, in turn, enhances the activity of most gastrointestinal functions.

PNS stimulation causes:

• Contraction of smooth muscle in the wall

• Relaxation of sphincters

• ↑ Salivary secretion

• ↑ Gastric secretion

• ↑ Pancreatic secretion

SNS stimulation causes:

• Relaxation of smooth muscle in the wall

• Contraction of sphincters

questions.question: Which of the following neurotransmitters acts on the muscle, behind a bolus of food, in the process of peristalsis?
questions.explanation:
Substance P and acetylcholine are released from neurons behind the bolus of food, causing smooth muscle contraction, which propels the food downwards.

NO and VIP are released by neurons in the anterograde direction from the bolus which produces relaxation in front of the stimulus.

questions.question: Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by which of the following mechanisms?
questions.explanation:
Gastric emptying is mainly regulated by enteric reflexes.

Regulation of gastric emptying is mainly by the inhibitory feedback signals from the duodenum that includes enterogastric reflex and hormonal feedback by cholecystokinin.

Enterogastric reflex: When food enters the duodenum, multiple nervous reflexes are initiated from the duodenal wall. They strongly inhibit the pyloric pump propulsive contractions and increase the tone of the pyloric sphincter.

These reflexes are mediated by three routes:

• Directly from the duodenum to the stomach through the enteric nervous system in the gut wall (major role)

• Through inhibitory sympathetic nerve fibers to the stomach (minor role)

• Vagus nerves to the brain stem where they inhibit the normal excitatory signals transmitted to the stomach (minor role)

Hormonal feedback: Cholecystokinin is released from the mucosa of the jejunum in response to fatty substances in the chyme. This hormone acts as an inhibitor to block increased stomach motility caused by gastrin.

questions.question: Which among the following increases gastric emptying?
questions.explanation:
The distension of the stomach increases gastric emptying.

Distension activates the mechanoreceptors that trigger long and short reflexes in the stomach. This increases the force of antral contraction and gastric emptying.

questions.question: Which of the following does not delay gastric emptying?
questions.explanation:
Gastrin increases gastric emptying. It does not delay it.

Gastrin has mild to moderate stimulatory effects on motor functions in the body of the stomach. Thus, gastrin likely promotes stomach emptying.

questions.question: Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by all of the following except:
questions.answer: A. Alkaline content of small intestine
questions.explanation:
Enterogastric inhibitory reflexes are stimulated by acidic contents, not alkaline.

The duodenal factors that can initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes (enterogastric reflexes) are:

• Distention of the duodenum

• Presence of any irritation of the duodenal mucosa

• Acidity of the duodenal chyme

• Osmolality of the chyme - either hypotonic or hypertonic fluid initiate enterogastric inhibitory reflexes. Thus, the flow of non-isotonic fluids into the small intestine is regulated. This prevents rapid changes in electrolyte concentrations in the extracellular fluid during the absorption of the intestinal contents.

• Presence of certain breakdown products in the chyme, especially proteins and to a lesser extent, of fats

questions.question: A concerned mother brings her infant to the OPD for advice regarding nutrition. She says, soon after every meal, her kid defecates. What is the cause of colonic contraction in this situation?
questions.explanation:
The cause of colonic contraction in the given situation is due to gastrocolic reflex.

Distension of the stomach by food initiates contractions of the rectum and frequently, a desire to defecate. This response is called the gastrocolic reflex. Because of this response, defecation after meals is common in children. This response may be amplified by the action of gastrin on the colon.

questions.question: The following image shows which type of GI motility?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the migrating motor complex.

The image shows 3 phases:

• Phase I - quiescent period

• Phase II - period of irregular electrical & mechanical activity

• Phase III - ends with bursts of regular activity

This occurs during the inter-digestive period at intervals of about 100 min and passes in the aboral direction at the rate of 5 cm/min. Its main function is to clear intestinal contents and prepare for the next meal.

Option A: Peristalsis is a propulsive movement, which consists of a segment of contraction behind and relaxation in front.

Option B: Segmentation and mixing help in mixing intestinal contents with digestive juices and provides time for digestion and absorption.

It consists of a segment of bowel contracting at both ends, and then a second contraction occurs in the center of the segment to force the chyme both backward and forward.

Option D: Basal Electrical Rhythm is fluctuation in the resting membrane potential of smooth muscle cells of the intestine as shown below.

questions.question: Migrating motor complexes occurs at the rate of _______ and at an interval of _________
questions.explanation:
Migrating motor complex (MMC) migrates from the stomach to the distal ileum at a rate of about 5 cm/min and also occurs at intervals of approximately 100 minutes.

MMC is a type of gastrointestinal motility that occurs during fasting between periods of digestion. It is initiated by motilin. It helps to clear the stomach and small intestine of luminal contents in preparation for the next meal. Gastric secretion, bile flow, and pancreatic secretion increase during each MMC.

After ingestion of a meal, secretion of motilin is suppressed and the MMC is abolished.

Each cycle of MMC has 3 phases

• Phase I - quiescent period

• Phase II - period of irregular electrical & mechanical activity

• Phase III - ends with bursts of regular activity

Note: Disorders of MMC have been associated with gastroparesis, intestinal pseudo-obstruction, and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about gastroduodenal motor activity?
options: Migrating motor complex/MMC in the fasting state lasts for 50 minutes
Duodenal slow waves are limited to the duodenum
From the duodenum, the MMC moves distally at 5-10 cm/min
The amplitude of contraction decreases to a minimum in phase III of MMC
questions.answer: C. From the duodenum, the MMC moves distally at 5-10 cm/min
questions.explanation:
From the duodenum, the migrating motor complex (MMC) moves distally at 5–10 cm/min, reaching the terminal ileum after 1.5 hours.

In the fasting state, there is a period of quiescence in the small bowel, lasting for approximately 40 minutes (phase I). This is followed by a series of waves, also lasting for about 40 minutes, propagating from the fundus of the stomach in a caudal direction at a rate of about 3 per minute (phase II).

Duodenal slow waves are generated in the duodenum at a rate of about 10 per minute, which carry down the small bowel.

The amplitude of these contractions increases to a maximum in phase III, which lasts for about 10 minutes. This 90-minute cycle of activity is then repeated.

questions.question: Which of the following does not increase small intestinal motility?
questions.explanation:
Secretin inhibits small intestinal motility.

Factors that increase the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:

• Hormonal - gastrin, CCK, insulin, motilin, and serotonin.

• Neural - duodenal distension by chyme, gastroenteric reflexes, gastroileal reflexes, parasympathetic (Ach) stimulation.

Factors that decrease the peristaltic activity of the small intestine:

• Hormonal - secretin and glucagon.

• Neural - sympathetic stimulation.

Gastroileal reflex - On reaching the ileocecal valve, the chyme is sometimes blocked for several hours until the person eats another meal. At that time, a gastroileal reflex intensifies peristalsis in the ileum and forces the remaining chyme through the ileocecal valve into the cecum of the large intestine.

questions.question: Which part of the GIT has the longest transit time?
questions.explanation:
The longest transit time is seen in the colon.

Average transit time:

Segment

Transit time

Esophagus

2-3 seconds

Stomach

2-5 hours

Small intestine

3-6 hours

questions.question: The maximum motility of the colon is seen in which of the following part?
questions.explanation:
The maximum motility of the colon is seen in the sigmoid colon.

The rate of BER at sigmoid colon is 6/min.

questions.question: A patient is undergoing sigmoidoscopy as a part of his routine colon cancer screening. While doing the procedure, the rectum is inflated with gas. Which part of the intestine would you likely see increased peristalsis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
While doing sigmoidoscopy if the rectum is inflated with gas, increased peristalsis is seen in the distal colon.

The distention of the rectal wall initiates afferent signals. These signals spread through the myenteric plexus to initiate peristaltic waves in the descending colon, sigmoid (distal colon), and rectum.

questions.question: Which of the following controls the secretions of GIT?
questions.explanation: Secretions of GIT are controlled by the Meissner plexus.

questions.question: You will feel the first urge to defecate when rectal pressure is increased to:
questions.explanation:
The first urge to defecate occurs when rectal pressure is increased to 18 mm Hg.

When this pressure reaches 55 mm Hg, the external and the internal sphinc­ter relax, and there is reflex expulsion of the contents of the rectum.

Defecation reflex: Distension of the rectum and colon stimulates stretch receptors in the rectal wall. Then, the defecation reflexes travel from the colon and rectum to the spinal cord and back again to produce the powerful colonic, rectal, and abdominal contractions required for defecation.

chapters.chapter: Glomerular Filtration Rate, Renal Blood Flow, And Renal Clearance

questions.question: Principal cells and intercalated cells are present in which part of the nephron?
options: Distal collecting tubule and collecting duct
Proximal collecting tubule and loop of Henle
Loop of Henle and distal collecting tubule
questions.answer: A. Distal collecting tubule and collecting duct
questions.explanation:
Principal cells and intercalated cells are present in the distal collecting tubule and collecting duct.

P cell
I cell

Functions

• Na+reabsorption

• Water reabsorption

• K secretion

• Type A- H+ secretion, HCO3 reabsorption in acidosis.

• Type B- HCO3 secretion, acid reabsorption in alkalosis.

Note: Principal cells are the primary sites of action of potassium-sparing diuretics.

questions.question: How does DCT differ from PCT?
options: Carbonic anhydrase in its luminal membrane
No Na+ - K+ ATPase in its basolateral membrane
questions.explanation:
DCT has 'tight' tight junctions, while PCT has 'leaky' tight junctions.

The 'tight' tight junctions can maintain the high electrochemical gradients produced by active transcellular transport. This configuration is used to produce either highly concentrated or diluted secretions, as in the distal nephron. Hence, it can produce urine with osmolarity severalfold higher or lower than plasma.

In contrast, epithelia with 'leaky' tight junctions move large amounts of isosmotic fluids. A good example is a transport in PCT.

PCT

No brush border

Cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase (type 2 & type 4) present

Cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase (type 2 only)

Has ‘leaky’ tight junctions

Has ‘tight’ tight junctions

Paracellular transport is possible via leaky tight junctions

No paracellular transport

Na+- K- ATPase is present throughout most parts of the nephron.

questions.question: In comparison to cortical nephron, juxtamedullary nephron______
questions.answer: B. Has long loop of Henle
questions.explanation: In comparison to cortical nephrons, juxtamedullary nephrons are characterized by a long loop of Henle that descends deep into the inner medulla. It is essential for the concentration of urine.

questions.question: About what percentage of the cardiac output do the kidneys receive?
questions.explanation:
Kidneys receive approximately 20 to 25% of the cardiac output, which is approximately 1000 mL per minute.

questions.question: What is the normal resting GFR?
questions.explanation:
The GFR in a healthy adult of average size is approximately 125 mL/min.

Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) is the volume of fluid filtered from the renal glomerular capillaries into the Bowman's capsule per unit time.

The GFR is determined by

1. Sum of the hydrostatic and colloid osmotic forces across the glomerular membrane, which gives the net filtration pressure

2. Glomerular Kf (glomerular ultrafiltration coefficient)

Mathematically, it can be expressed as follows:

GFR= Kf [ forces favoring filtration- forces opposing filteration]

GFR= Kf [PG + πB -PB- πG]

Forces Favoring Filtration

PG: Glomerular hydrostatic pressure

πB: Bowman’s capsule oncotic pressure

Forces Opposing Filtration

PB: Bowman’s capsule hydrostatic pressure

πG: Glomerular capillary oncotic pressure

questions.question: What is the renal blood flow in a resting adult?
questions.explanation:
In a resting adult, the kidneys receive 1.2–1.3 L of blood per minute or just under 25% of the cardiac output. Among the given options, 1-1.5 L/min is the closest range.

Renal blood flow is determined by the pressure gradient across the renal vasculature (the difference between the renal artery and renal vein hydrostatic pressures), divided by the total renal vascular resistance. It is expressed as follows:

Note: Renal blood flow = Renal plasma flow/ 1- Hematocrit

questions.question: What is the normal renal filtration fraction?
questions.explanation:
Normal renal filtration fraction (i.e. the fraction of renal plasma flow that is filtered) averages about 0.2.

It means that 20% of the plasma flowing through the kidney is filtered through the glomerular capillaries. The remaining 80% leaves the glomerular capillaries by the efferent arterioles and becomes the peritubular capillary circulation.

It is calculated by the given equation:

When there is a fall in systemic blood pressure, the GFR falls less than the RPF because of efferent arteriolar constriction, and consequently, the filtration fraction rises.

questions.question: Which of the following does not form filtration barrier?
questions.explanation:
Mesangium does not form a filtration barrier. It is made up of mesangial cells, supporting glomerular capillaries.

The filtration barrier consists of:

• Endothelium of the capillary

• Basement membrane:

• Lamina densa - electron-dense layer. It contains type IV collagen

• Lamina rara interna - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge

• Lamina rara externa - contains glycosaminoglycan heparan sulfate which has a negative charge

• Layer of epithelial cells (podocytes) surrounding the outer surface of the capillary basement membrane

A. The endothelial cells of the glomerulus; 1. Pore (fenestra)

B. Glomerular basement membrane: 1. Lamina rara interna 2. Lamina densa 3. Lamina rara externa

C. Podocytes: 1. Enzymatic and structural protein 2. Filtration slit 3. Diaphragm.

questions.question: Two particles share the same diameter. The one which will pass through the glomerular membrane has ______
options: Filtration across GBM does not depend on charge
questions.explanation:
For any given molecular radius, positively charged molecules are filtered much more readily than are negatively charged molecules.

This is because the sialoproteins in the glomerular capillary wall are negatively charged, and this negative charge repels the negatively charged substances in the blood.

Studies have showed that for tracer molecules presumed to be of similar size, charges which are filtered are positive charge > neutral charge > negative charge.

questions.question: What size of neutral substances are permitted by the filtration barriers?
questions.explanation:
Filtration barriers permit neutral substances that have the size of 4-8 nm.

Neutral substances with diameters:

• <4 nm - freely filtered

• >8 nm - not filtered

• Between 4-8 nm - the permeability is inversely proportional to the diameter

Clinical correlation:

• Genetically abnormal basement membranes: Alport’s syndrome (α3 and α4 chains on the long arm of chromosome 2 involved in autosomal dominant and recessive pattern; α5 chain on X chromosome involved in X-linked inheritance)

• Autoimmune response to basement membrane collagen IV (α3 NC1 domain): Goodpasture’s syndrome

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus?
questions.explanation:
Glomerular mesangial cells are not a part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

Juxtaglomerular apparatus contains:

• Macula densa: Specialized cells at the end of the thick ascending limb of Henle forms the macula densa. They detect sodium concentration of the fluid in the tubule (Chemoreceptor). In response to elevated sodium, the macula densa cells trigger contraction of the afferent arteriole, reducing flow of blood to the glomerulus and the glomerular filtration rate.

• Lacis cells: Extraglomerular mesangial cells situated between afferent and efferent arteriole.

• Granular cells/JG cells: Modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole, that secrete renin. Fall in pressure in afferent arteriole stimulates renin release (mechanoreceptor), which, in turn, increases blood pressure.

Note: The distal convoluted tubule starts at the macula densa.

questions.question: In patients with renal diseases, albumin is the first to appear in the urine. What is the reason behind this?
questions.explanation:
In renal diseases, albumin is the first to appear because of its effective molecular diameter.

In minimal change nephropathy, the negative charges on the basement membrane are lost even before there are noticeable changes in kidney histology. As a result of this loss of negative charges on the basement membranes, some of the lower molecular weight proteins, especially albumin (effective molecular diameter of 7 nm), are filtered and appear in the urine, a condition known as proteinuria or albuminuria.

questions.question: How much is the inulin clearance?
questions.explanation:
Inulin clearance is equal to 125 ml/ min. Since it is used for the measurement of GFR, inulin clearance will be equal to GFR, i.e 125 ml/min

Renal clearance is the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance by the kidneys per unit time.

A higher renal clearance suggests the substance may be cleared almost completely in one pass through the kidneys while a low value describes a substance that may not be eliminated by the kidneys at all.

Clearance refers to the volume of plasma that would be necessary to supply the amount of substance excreted in the urine per unit of time. Stated mathematically,

Cx. Px = Ux. V

where Cx is the clearance rate of a substance x

Px is the plasma concentration of x

Ux is the urine concentration of that x

V is the urine flow rate

Rearranging this equation, clearance can be expressed as

questions.question: In a patient, urine flow rate is 10 mL/min; plasma inulin is 2 mg/mL; and urine inulin is 25 mg/mL. Which of the following is true assuming GFR to be normal?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, inulin clearance = GFR.

Inulin clearance is calculated by the formula:

Substituting the values given,

• Uinulin= 25 mg/mL

• Vinulin= 10 mL/min

• Pinulin=2 mg/mL

Thus, Inulin clearance=GFR (normal GFR= 125 ml/min)

Inulin is a polymer of fructose, clearance of inulin can be used for measurement of GFR, because of the following reasons:

• Freely filtered

• Neither reabsorbed nor secreted in the tubules

• Nontoxic

• Not metabolized by the body

questions.question: A patient's urine flow rate is 2 ml/min. What is the clearance of a substance x whose plasma concentration is 10mg/mL and in urine is 100mg/mL?
questions.explanation:
The clearance in the given scenario is 20 ml/ min.

C = Clearance (mL/min)

V= Urine flow rate per minute (mL/min)=2mL/min
