questions.question: What is the effect of sympathetic stimulation on GFR?
questions.answer: C. ↓ GFR with afferent arteriolar constriction
questions.explanation:
GFR decreases with sympathetic stimulation as there is afferent arteriolar constriction.

Strong activation of the renal sympathetic nerves constrict the afferent and efferent renal arterioles through the α1 receptors. As the afferent areterioles have far more α1 receptors than the efferent, it results in decreased renal blood flow and GFR.

questions.question: If a patient is on a high protein diet, what will be the effect on the GFR?
questions.explanation:
High protein intake increases GFR.

Note: Increase in the plasma protein concentration is not the same as high protein intake. An increase in the plasma protein concentration decreases GFR due to a raised oncotic pressure. A high protein intake raises the amino acid concentration in the blood, not the plasma protein concentration.

questions.question: Which of the following would cause an increase in both GFR and RPF?
questions.answer: D. Dilation of the afferent arteriole
questions.explanation:
Dilation of the afferent arteriole will increase both GFR and RPF.

• Increase renal plasma flow (RPF) - because renal vascular resistance is decreased

• Increase glomerular filtration rate (GFR) - because glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure is increased.

• Filtration fraction (FF) remains normal

Dilation of the efferent arteriole will increase RPF but decrease GFR.

questions.question: Which of the following causes relaxation of the mesangial cells?
questions.explanation:
cAMP causes relaxation of the mesangial cells. The other agents mentioned in the options cause contraction of the mesangial cells.

Agents causing relaxation of mesangial cells (mnemonic - DAnCE)

• Dopamine

• ANP

• cAMP

• PGE2

Angiotensin II is an important regulator of mesangial contraction, and there are angiotensin II receptors in the glomeruli.

questions.question: What is the effect of prostaglandins on renal blood flow?
options: Increase blood flow to cortex and medulla
Increase blood flow to cortex and decrease blood flow to medulla
Decrease blood flow to cortex and increase blood flow to medulla
Decrease blood flow to cortex as well as medulla
questions.answer: B. Increase blood flow to cortex and decrease blood flow to medulla
questions.explanation:
Prostaglandins increase blood flow in the renal cortex and decrease blood flow in the renal medulla.

PGE2 is partially responsible for the vasodilatation of the afferent arteriole, which increases blood flow to the glomerulus. This phenomenon describes why NSAIDs (which inhibit prostaglandin synthesis) result in afferent arteriole vasoconstriction. It can cause a reduced GFR in patients who rely heavily on prostaglandin synthesis to maintain renal blood flow.

questions.question: Which part of the proximal tubule is most susceptible to ischemic injury?
questions.explanation:
Regions of the kidney most prone to ischemic injury are the S3 segment of the proximal tubule and the medullary thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle (mTAL). These tubular areas exist physiologically in relatively lower oxygen conditions.

The S3 segment, in particular, has a much lower capability of producing energy through glycolysis under anaerobic conditions than the mTAL.

Based on the ultrastructure proximal tubule is divided into three segments:

• S1 segment: 1st half of PCT

• S2 segment: 2nd half of PCT and 1st half of proximal straight tubule

• S3 segment: 2nd half of proximal straight tubule

questions.question: What is the effective renal plasma flow?
questions.explanation:
In humans, the effective renal plasma flow (eRPF) averages about 625 mL/min.

Measurement of renal plasma flow (RPF) is done by measuring the clearance of para-aminohippuric acid (PAH). PAH is filtered and secreted by the renal tubules, hence it it can be used for RPF measurement.

where:

• RPF = renal plasma flow (mL/min or mL/24 hour)

• CPAH = clearance of PAH (mL/min or mL/24 hourr)

• UPAH = urine concentration of PAH (mg/mL)

• V = urine flow rate (mL/min or mL/24 hour)

• PPAH = plasma concentration of PAH (mg/mL)

Note: Renal blood flow= Renal plasma flow/ 1- Hematocrit

questions.question: Which of the following formulae is correct?
questions.explanation:
True renal plasma flow (RPF) is obtained by dividing effective renal plasma flow (ERPF) by extraction ratio.

When we inject para-aminohippuric acid, 90% of it is filtered through the glomerulus at the rate of 625mL per minute - which is the effective renal plasma flow (ERPF). Using that, to we calculate the true RPF, we divide it by the extraction ratio to account for the 10% that is not filtered by dividing the ERPF by 0.9, hence getting the final value of ~ 700mL per minute

When peripheral venous plasma concentration of PAH is used for calculation of RPF, RPF obtained is called effective renal plasma flow (ERPF). This is because PAH concentration is essentially identical to that in the arterial plasma reaching the kidney.

questions.question: In a patient with renal disease, you want to measure the filtration fraction. Which of the following substances will you use?
questions.explanation:
Inulin and PAHA are used to determine the filtration fraction. The filtration fraction is the ratio of GFR and RPF

Inulin, a polymer of fructose can be used to measure GFR. Para-aminohippuric acid (PAHA) is used to measure RPF.

questions.question: Tubuloglomerular feedback is mediated by the sensing of_____
options: Increased Na + concentration in thick ascending loop of Henle
Increased Cl - concentration in thick ascending loop of Henle
Increased Na + concentration in macula densa
Increased Cl- concentration in macula densa
questions.answer: C. Increased Na + concentration in macula densa
questions.explanation:
Tubuloglomerular feedback is mediated by the sensing of increased Na+ concentration in macula densa.

Macula densa are the specialized cells present at the distal end of the thick ascending loop of Henle where it reaches the glomerulus. Distal convoluted tubule starts from macula densa. Macula forms part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus.

While both Na+ and Cl- are delivered to the macula densa cells, it is the increased concentration of Na+ in the cells that increases the Na+-K ATPase activity leading to the feedback.

questions.question: Renal autoregulation is absent in which of the following cases?
questions.answer: C. Paralysis of vascular smooth muscle
questions.explanation:
Renal autoregulation is absent in case of paralysis of vascular smooth muscle.

Paralysis of vascular smooth muscles abolishes its action i.e., autoregulation of renal blood flow and GFR. Vascular smooth muscles act through myogenic mechanism of renal autoregulation. Paralysis of vascular smooth muscles can be brought about by administration of drugs.

Renal autoregulation is present in denervated and in iso­lated, perfused kidneys.

Feedback mechanisms intrinsic to the kidneys keep the renal blood flow and GFR relatively constant, despite marked changes in arterial blood pressure. This relative constancy of GFR and renal blood flow is referred to as autoregulation.

questions.question: The concentration of a substance is 2 mg % in afferent arteriole and 0 mg% in the efferent arteriole of a patient. This substance is
questions.explanation:
A concentration of 0 mg% is efferent arteriole indicates the substance is freely filtered.

Afferent arterioles → glomerulus (filtration) → efferent arterioles → peritubular capillaries (reabsorption+secretion).

Note: The question compares the concentration in afferent and efferent arterioles. Reabsorption and secretion happen between the tubular lumen of the nephron and the peritubular capillaries and not the efferent arteriole.

chapters.chapter: Renal Tubular Functions, Urine Concentration And Dilution

questions.question: What is implied if a drug has more renal clearance than GFR?
options: Drug is reabsorbed by the renal tubules
Drug is secreted in the renal tubules
Drug is excreted in renal tubules
Drug is neither excreted nor reabsorbed in renal tubules
questions.answer: B. Drug is secreted in the renal tubules
questions.explanation:
If drug has more renal clearance than GFR, then drug is secreted in renal tubules.

Excretion rate= (filtration rate- reabsorption rate)+ secretion rate.

The clearance of the substance:

• Equals the GFR if there is no net tubular secretion or reabsorption.

• Exceeds the GFR if there is net tubular secretion.

• Less than the GFR if there is net tubular reabsorption.

questions.question: Choose the correct formula regarding renal physiology.
questions.explanation:
The correct formula is Excretion rate = UV.

1. Filtration fraction = ( GFR / RPF ) * 100 = 20% (or ) 0.2 (approx)

2. Filtration rate = GFR * Plasma concentration

3. Clearance = U*V/P

Where,

GFR = Glomerular filtration rate

RPF = Renal plasma flow

U = Concentration of the substance in urine

V = Urine flow rate

P = Concentration of the substance in plasma

questions.question: Choose the correct option.
options: Inulin is completely secreted and never reabsorbed.
Glucose is completely reabsorbed in DCT.
PAH at any plasma concentration is completely filtered and secreted.
questions.explanation:
Creatinine is partially secreted and never reabsorbed. Clearance of creatinine (CCr) can also be used to determine GFR. Since creatinine is secreted by the tubules, the clearance of creatinine will be slightly higher than inulin. Hence, it overestimates GFR.

Inulin is completely filtered and never reabsorbed. Hence, it can be used for GFR estimation.

Glucose is completely reabsorbed below the renal threshold (i.e ~180mg/dl) in PCT.

PAH(para amino hippuric acid) at low plasma concentrations is completely filtered and secreted. Hence, it can be used for estimation of renal blood flow.

questions.question: Renal plasma flow is being calculated using PAH in a patient. The technician inadvertently uses PAH thrice the recommended dose. What will be the estimated effective renal plasma flow?
questions.explanation:
Effective renal plasma flow in this patient will be falsely low.

It is equal to the clearance of para-aminohippurate (PAH) as shown by the following equation.

Where,

• ERPF = Effective Renal Plasma Flow

• UPAH = [PAH] in urine

• V= Urine flow rate

• PPAH = [PAH] in plasma

• CPAH = Clearance of PAH

At high concentrations of PAH, as given in this question, tubular secretion attains saturation after which the clearance of PAH falls. Hence, a low ERPF will be seen.

questions.question: Which of the following transporter is present in the ascending loop of Henle?
questions.explanation:
Thick ascending limb of loop of Henle has Na+ - 2Cl- - K+ co transporter that cotransports one Na+, one K+, and 2Cl– from the tubular lumen into the tubu­lar cells. This is an example of secondary active trans­port.

Na+ is transported out of the cell into the interstitium by Na, K ATPase in the basolateral membrane of the cell.

Cl– exits in basolateral ClC–Kb Cl– channels. Barttin, a protein in the cell membrane, is essential for normal ClC–Kb function.

K+ moves from the cell to the interstitium and the tubular lumen by ROMK(renal outer medullary potassium channel) and other K+ channels.

questions.question: The principal site of absorption of Na + is_____
options: Thick ascending limb of Loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
The principal site of absorption of Na + is PCT. About 60-65% of filtered sodium is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule (PCT), coupled with the movement of H+, glucose, amino acids, organic acids, phosphate, and other electrolytes and substances.

% of filtered Na reabsorbed
Part of nephron

ENaC channels (regulated by aldosterone to permit homeostatic adjustments)

All segments of nephron are involved in sodium reabsorption except thin descending loop of Henle.

questions.question: Potassium is maximally absorbed in____
questions.explanation:
Potassium is maximally absorbed in PCT.

Potassium is freely filtered by the glomerulus. The bulk of filtered K+ is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule. In the proximal tubule, K+ absorption is primarily passive and proportional to Na+ and water through paracellular transport.

K+ reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of Henle occurs through both transcellular (Na+- K+- 2Cl- cotransport) and paracellular pathways.

K+ secretion begins in the early distal convoluted tubule and progressively increases along the distal nephron into the cortical collecting duct . Most urinary K+ can be accounted for by K+ secretion mediated by principal cells. Under conditions of K+ depletion, reabsorption of K+ occurs in the collecting duct.

It is the only electrolyte to be reabsorbed as well as secreted.

questions.question: Bicarbonate is reabsorbed across the luminal membrane with the help of ______
questions.explanation:
Bicarbonate is reabsorbed at the luminal membrane in the form of CO2 and H2O with the help of Na+ - H+ exchanger.

In the tubular cell of the PCT, CO2 and H2O recombine with the help of carbonic anhydrase II, and then dissociate into H+ and HCO3-. From here, the H+ moves back into the tubular lumen via the Na+ - H+ exchanger while the HCO3- is reabsorbed at the basolateral membrane via the Na+ - HCO3- co-transporter.

questions.question: True about renal tubular transport_____
options: H+ is absorbed in proximal tubule
Amino acid is reabsorbed in proximal tubule
questions.answer: D. Amino acid is reabsorbed in proximal tubule
questions.explanation:
Glucose and amino acids are completely reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

Option A: Maximum reabsorption occurs in proximal tubule

Option B: Urea is reabsorbed and secreted. It is reabsorbed in PCT and in collecting duct. It is secreted in thin ascending loop of henle.

Option C: H+ is secreted in PCT as well as in collecting ducts.

questions.question: Which of the following occurs along with glucose transport into the cell?
questions.explanation:
Sodium symport occurs along with glucose transport into the cell.

Sodium and glucose are co-transported across the luminal membrane of proximal tubular cells. This occurs via sodium glucose co-transporters (SGLT2 and SGLT1). The energy derived from the movement of Na+ is used to move glucose against its concentration gradient into the tubular cell. This is referred to as secondary active transport.

The Na+ is then pumped out of the cell into the interstitium, and the glucose exits by facilitated diffusion via glucose transporter (GLUT)-2 along the basolateral membrane into the interstitial fluid.

Clinical correlation:

Fanconi-Bickel syndrome: Defective GLUT2

Isolated renal glycosuria: Defective SGLT2

questions.question: Normal renal threshold (g/L) and transport maxima (mg/min) for glucose respectively are _______, _________
questions.explanation:
The actual renal threshold is about 200 mg/dL (i.e., 2 g/L ) (1g/L=100mg/dl) and the transport maximum for glucose is 375 mg/min.

For substances that are actively reabsorbed or secreted, there is a limit to the rate at which the solute can be transported, which is referred to as the transport maximum. This limit is due to saturation of the specific transport systems involved.

Normally, measurable glucose does not appear in the urine because essentially all the filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule.

The transport maximum for glucose is about 375 mg/min, whereas the filtered load of glucose is only about 125 mg/min. With large increases in GFR and/or plasma glucose concentration that increase the filtered load of glucose above 375 mg/min, the excess glucose filtered is not reabsorbed and passes into the urine.

When the plasma glucose concentration is 100 mg/100 ml and the filtered load is at its normal level (125 mg/min) there is no loss of glucose in the urine. However, when the plasma concentration of glucose rises above about 200 mg/100 ml, increasing the filtered load to about 250 mg/min, a small amount of glucose begins to appear in the urine. This point is termed as the threshold for glucose.

Splay is due to separation between filtered load and exceretion. It occurs due to different transport maximums of different nephrons.

questions.question: The image of PAH excretion is depicted below. Match the labellings.
options: a. Filtered, b. Excreted, c. Tm, d. Secreted
a. Filtered, b. Secreted, c. Tm, d. Excreted
a. Secreted, b. Filtered, c. Tm, d. Excreted
a. Excreted, b. Filtered, c. Tm, d. Secreted
questions.answer: B. a. Filtered, b. Secreted, c. Tm, d. Excreted
questions.explanation:
The labellings depticed are a. Filtered, b. Secreted, c. Tm, d. Excreted

Filtered Load: The filtered load of PAH increases linearly as the unbound concentration of PAH increases (filtered load = GFR. [P]PAH).

Secretion: At low concentrations of PAH, many carriers are available and secretion increases linearly as the plasma concentration increases. When the PAH concentration increases to a level where the carriers are saturated, Tm is reached. After this point, no matter how much the PAH concentration increases, there can be no further increase in the secretion rate.

Excretion. For a secreted substance such as PAH, excretion is the sum of filtration and secretion. At low PAH concentrations (below Tm), excretion increases steeply with increases in plasma PAH concentration because both filtration and secretion are increasing. At PAH concentrations above Tm, excretion increases less steeply (and parallels the curve for filtration) because only the filtration component increases as concentration increases; secretion is already saturated.

questions.question: In a patient with uncontrolled diabetes, what is the value of plasma clearance of glucose?
questions.explanation:
In uncontrolled diabetes, the plasma clearance of glucose is greater than zero.

Normally, all the glucose that is filtered is reabsorbed and no glucose is excreted in the urine. Hence, the clearance is zero. In uncontrolled diabetes, since the plasma glucose concentration is greater than the renal threshold for reabsorption, excess glucose is excreted in the urine and the clearance is greater than zero.

Clearance of different substances can be shown in a graph as follows:

The above graph depicts renal handling of glucose, inulin, and para-aminohippurate (PAH) and can be explained as follows:

Glucose clearance: Normally, all the glucose that is filtered is reabsorbed and no glucose is excreted in the urine. Hence, the clearance is zero. In uncontrolled diabetes, since the plasma glucose concentration is greater than the renal threshold for reabsorption, excess glucose is excreted in the urine and the clearance is greater than zero.

Inulin clearance: Inulin is freely filtered and is neither reabsorbed nor secreted. Hence, it is constant and equal to the glomerular filtration rate.

PAH clearance: PAH is both filtered and secreted. When plasma PAH is low, clearance is high. However, as plasma PAH rises above the threshold level for PAH secretion, clearance falls progressively.

questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding the concentration of solutes at the end of proximal convoluted tubule
options: Concentration of glucose in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma
Concentration of urea in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma
Concentration of bicarbonate in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma
Concentration of sodium in tubular fluid is less than that of plasma
questions.answer: B. Concentration of urea in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma
questions.explanation:
The concentration of urea in tubular fluid is more than that of plasma.

[TF/P]>1, when solute is reabsorbed less quickly than water or when solute is secreted. Ex- PAH, Creatinine, Inulin, Urea.

[TF/P]=1, when solute and water are reabsorbed at the same rate Ex - Na.

[TF/P]<1, when solute is reabsorbed more quickly than water. Ex- glucose, amino acid, bicarbonate.

questions.question: The mechanism by which majority of water is reabsorbed in PCT is
questions.explanation:
Water reabsorption in PCT mainly occurs by osmosis.

The proximal tubule reabsorbs 67% of the filtered water. The driving force for water reabsorption is a transtubular osmotic gradient established by reabsorption of solutes.

questions.question: A dehydrated patient is excreting hypertonic urine. Absorption of water in which part of the nephron causes this?
questions.explanation:
Hypertonic urine is excreted due to absorption of water in collecting duct.

The final concentration of urine is determined by the amount of water reabsorption that occurs in the collecting ducts. The changes in osmolarity of the urine (hypo/hypertonic) depends on the amount of ADH (vasopressin) acting on the collecting ducts.

The basic requirements for forming a concentrated urine (hypertonic urine) are

• A high level of ADH, which increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, thereby allowing these tubular segments to avidly reabsorb water.

• A high osmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid, which provides the osmotic gradient necessary for water reabsorption to occur in the presence of high levels of ADH.

questions.question: A patient with diabetes insipidus is prescribed vasopressin. This drug has its maximum effect on which part of the renal tubule?
questions.explanation:
Vasopressin has the maximum effect on the collecting ducts.

Vasopressin acts by inserting aquaporin 2 present in cytoplasmic vesicles of principal cells on to the apical membrane. The effect is mediated via the vasopressin V2 receptor, cyclic adenosine 5-monophosphate (cAMP), and protein kinase A. When vasopressin is absent, the collecting duct epithelium is relatively impermeable to water.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about free water clearance?
questions.explanation:
Free water clearance is regulated by ADH.

Free water clearance is defined as the amount of solute-free water generated by the kidneys, either when dilute urine or when concentrated urine is formed.

Free-water clearance is positive, when excess water is being excreted (dilute urine).

Free-water clearance is negative, when excess solutes are being removed and water is being conserved (concentrated urine).

questions.question: The following picture shows the composition of solute in the urine and plasma sample of 3 patients. Identify the true statement.
options: A shows negative free water clearance, B is isotonic, C is positive free water clearance
A shows positive free water clearance B is isotonic C is positive free water clearance
A shows positive free water clearance B is isotonic C is negative free water clearance
A shows negative free water clearance B is isotonic C is negative free water clearance
questions.answer: C. A shows positive free water clearance B is isotonic C is negative free water clearance
questions.explanation:
Patient A shows positive free water clearance B is isotonic C shows negative free water clearance.

Free water clearance is defined as the amount of solute-free water generated by the kidneys, either when dilute urine or when concentrated urine is formed.

Patient A has positive free-water clearance, since excess water is being excreted (dilute urine).

Patient C has negative free-water clearance, since excess solutes are being removed and water is being conserved (concentrated urine).

questions.question: All are true except that ____.
options: Descending limb of loop of henle is permeable to water
Thick ascending limb is permeable to water
Distal tubule is permeable to water
questions.answer: C. Thick ascending limb is permeable to water
questions.explanation: The ascending limb is always impermeable to H2O.

questions.question: The average urine osmolality in mosm/kg is _____.
questions.explanation: The average urine osmolality is 100-800 mosm/kg.

questions.question: What are the requirements for a patient to excrete concentrated urine?
options: High ADH levels and hypoosmolar renal medulla
Low ADH levels and hypoosmolar renal medulla
High ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal medulla
Low ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal medulla
questions.answer: C. High ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal medulla
questions.explanation:
The requirements for excreting concentrated urine are high ADH levels and hyperosmolar renal medulla.

A high level of ADH, which increases the permeability of the distal tubules and collecting ducts to water, thereby allowing these tubular segments to avidly reabsorb water, and a high osmolarity of the renal medullary interstitial fluid, which provides the osmotic gradient necessary for water reabsorption to occur in the presence of high levels of ADH.

questions.question: Maximum osmotic gradient is found in____
questions.explanation: Maximum osmotic gradient is found in the inner medulla. The gradient of osmolarity from the cortex (300 mosm/L) to the inner medulla (1200 mosm/L) is produced by the loops of Henle as countercurrent multipliers and maintained by operation of the vasa recta as countercurrent exchangers.

questions.question: Hyperosmolarity of renal medulla is due to____
questions.explanation:
Hyperosmolarity of the medullary interstitium is mainly due to NaCl and urea.

The major factors that contribute to the buildup of solute concentration into the renal medulla are

• Active transport of Na+ and co-transport of K+, Cl-, and other ions out of the thick portion of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle into the medullary interstitium.

• Active transport of ions from the collecting ducts into the medullary interstitium.

• Facilitated diffusion of urea from the inner medullary collecting ducts into the medullary interstitium.

• Diffusion of only small amounts of water from the medullary tubules into the medullary interstitium

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of the countercurrent mechanism?
options: Descending limb of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT) does not play a role in countercurrent mechanism.

The countercurrent mechanism consists of 2 components:

1. Countercurrent multiplier:
 a. Absorption of water via Aquaporin 1 in thin descending limb
 b. Active transport of Na+- K+- 2Cl- in thick ascending limb
 c. Flow of fluid from PCT to DCT

2. Countercurrent exchanger: Vasa recta are involved in this process. They help in maintaining the osmotic gradient in the renal medulla. This is a passive process.

questions.question: Maximum osmolality that can be reached at the tip of medulla is proportional to
options: Distribution of Na-K-2Cl channel in the thick ascending loop of Henle
Permeability of descending loop to water
questions.answer: C. Length of loop of Henle
questions.explanation:
The maximum osmolality that can be reached at the tip of the medulla is proportional to the length of the loop of Henle, because the Loop of Henle acts as Countercurrent multiplier to maitain the gradient in medulla. Greater is the length of loop of Henle, greater will be the osmolality that can be reached at the tip of the medulla.

In case of juxtamedullary nephrons with longer loops and thin ascending limbs, the osmotic gradient is spread over a greater distance and the osmolality at the tip of the loop is greater.

questions.question: Counter current blood flow is seen in all except_____
questions.explanation:
The eye does not have a countercurrent blood flow system.

Heat and substances, including gases, steroids and peptide hormones, can pass from venous blood, interstitial fluid and lymph to the arterial blood; the process is called local counter-current transfer.

Examples of countercurrent blood flow

• Heat exchange between the arteries and venae comitantes of the limbs.

• Vasa recta in the kidneys

• Testes

• Small intestine

chapters.chapter: Acid Base Balance, Renal Hormones And Micturition Reflex

questions.question: Principal site of acidification of urine______
questions.explanation:
Principal site of acidification of urine is collecting duct. Acidification occurs in both distal tubule and collecting duct, but collecting duct is more important.

The urinary pH of 4.5 (limiting pH) is normally reached in the collecting ducts.

In the late distal tubules and collecting ducts, the tubular epithelium secretes H+ by primary active transport. Primary active secretion of H+ occurs in type A intercalated cells of the late distal tubule and in the collecting tubules. H+ concentration can be increased as much as 900-fold in the collecting tubules.

questions.question: Most important extracellular buffer_____
questions.explanation:
The most important extracellular buffer is bicarbonate. The source of bicarbonate is plasma by filteration. It is a non inducible buffer.

Proteins: Are the most abundant intracellular buffer.

Phosphate: minor buffer in kidney. The source is plasma by filteration. It is a noninducible buffer.

Ammonia is a minor buffer, locally produced by tubular cells. Its production increases in metabolic acidosis. It is the only inducible buffer.

questions.question: Normal anion gap is mostly due to_____
questions.explanation:
Normal anion gap is mostly due to unmeasured proteins.

Normally in the plasma, the concentrations of anions and cations are equal to maintain electrical neutrality. Thus no real "anion gap" exists in the plasma and this is purely a diagnostic concept.

Diagnostically, when the electrolytes are measured in the blood, routinely only certain cations and anions are measured. These are Na+, Cl- and HCO3-. The anion gap is the difference between the unmeasured anions and unmeasured cations. This is estimated as :

Plasma anion gap= [Na+] - [Cl-] - [HCO3-]

The unmeasured cations include calcium, magnesium and potassium.

The unmeasured anions include albumin, phosphate, sulphate and organic anions.

This is primarily used in measurement of different causes of metabolic acidosis.

questions.question: Normal anion gap is _________mEq / L.
questions.explanation:
The normal anion gap ranges between 8 and 16 mEq/L.

The concentrations of anions and cations in plasma must be equal to maintain electrical neutrality. Therefore, there is no real “anion gap” in the plasma.

However, only certain cations and anions are routinely measured in the clinical laboratory. The cation normally measured is Na+, and the anions are usually Cl− and HCO3−.

The “anion gap” (which is only a diagnostic concept) is the difference between unmeasured anions and unmeasured cations and is estimated as

Plasma anion gap = [Na+ ] − [HCO3− ] − [Cl− ]=144−24−108 =12 mEq/L

The anion gap will increase if unmeasured anions rise or if unmeasured cations fall.

The most important unmeasured cations include calcium, magnesium and potassium and the major unmeasured anions are albumin, phosphate, sulfate and other organic anions.

Usually the unmeasured anions exceed the unmeasured cations and the anion gap ranges between 8 and 16 mEq/L.

questions.question: Endocrine functions associated with kidney include all of the following except______
questions.explanation:
ANP is secreted by the heart.

Endocrine/Paracrine Functions of the Kidney:

Substance
Site of secretion

Renin
Granular cells or juxtaglomerular cells (JG cells) of the juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)

Erythropoietin
Interstitial cells in the peritubular capillary bed

Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)
Renal medullary interstitial cells (RMICs), macula densa, and by cells of collecting duct

PGI2 and other prostaglandins
Arterioles and glomeruli

1,25-Dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol or vitamin D3)
Cells of proximal tubules of the kidneys.

questions.question: The major prostanoid synthesized in kidney is ________
questions.explanation:
PGE2 is the major prostanoid synthesized in the kidney.

It is secreted by:

• RMICs (Renal Medullary Interstitial Cells)

• Macula densa

• Cells in the collecting ducts.

Prostacyclin (PGI2) and other prostaglandins are secreted by the arterioles and glomeruli.

Renal medullary interstitial cells (RMICs) are specialized fibroblast-like cells which are major site of cyclooxygenase 2 (COX-2) and prostaglandin synthase (PGES) expression.

questions.question: All of the following results in increased renin secretion except _____.
options: Increased amount of Na+ in DCT
Decreased amount of Na+ in PCT
questions.answer: B. Increased amount of Na+ in DCT
questions.explanation:
The increased amount of Na+ and Cl- reabsorption across macula densa (DCT) is inhibitory to renin secretion. All other factors increase renin secretion.

Renin leads to a series of events through the Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone pathway that finally, in simple terms, leads to salt and water retention and increases blood pressure. Therefore, it is easy to remember that all factors that cause decreased effective volume, pressure, or sodium delivery will increase the renin levels and vice versa.

Note: Renin is secreted by the juxtaglomerular cells (granular cells) which are epitheloid cells located in the media of afferent arterioles of the glomerulus.

questions.question: Angiotensin II causes all of the following except_____
questions.explanation:
Angiotensin II is one of the most potent vasoconstrictors in the body.

It constricts efferent arteriole, thereby increasing filteration fraction and glomerular filteration rate, when there is decreased renal bloodflow

questions.question: Vasopressin secretion is increased by_____
questions.explanation:
Vasopressin (ADH) secretion increases in response to decreased ECF volume to bring about water retention to restore the ECF volume.

ADH exerts its antidiuretic effect by acting on the V2 receptors and involves the insertion of aquaporin 2 (AQP2) into the apical (luminal) membranes of the principal cells of the collecting ducts.

questions.question: A patient who got into an accident is brought to the casualty and is bleeding from his right leg. His blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg. Which of the following plays the most important role for sodium and water retention in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The renin-angiotensin system plays the most important role for sodium and water retention in this patient as the patient has hypovolemia due to blood loss. (refer to figure)

The plasma concentration of renin is the rate-limiting step in the renin-angiotensin system; it is the major determinant of plasma angiotensin II concentration.

Angiotensin II stimulates the aldosterone and ADH secretion; it also constricts the blood vessels and causes thirst, which helps in maintaining blood pressure.

questions.question: Atriopeptin (ANP) acts at _____
questions.explanation:
ANP acts on the collecting duct.

ANP is secreted by the atria in response to an increase in ECF volume. It decreases Na+ reabsorption in the late distal tubule and collecting ducts. It causes natriuresis.

ANP causes dilation of afferent arterioles and constriction of efferent arterioles resulting in an increased RBF(Because the dilatory effect of ANP on afferent arterioles is more than the constrictor effect on efferent arterioles, there is an overall decrease in renal vascular resistance and resulting
increase in RBF) and increased GFR.

questions.question: ANP secretion is raised by all except____
questions.explanation:
It is ↑ in ECF volume and not hypovolemia that causes increased secretion of ANP.

Stimuli that increase the secretion of ANP

• ↑atrial stretch or ventricular stretch

• ↑isotonic saline administration

• ↑ECF volume

Stimuli that decrease ANP secretion

• Rising from supine to standing position (as this decreases the central venous pressure).

questions.question: Several hormones regulate the tubular reabsorption of water and electrolytes at different sites in the nephron physiologically in a patient. Which of the following combination is correct?
questions.explanation:
The combination which is correct is Aldosterone in collecting ducts.

Aldosterone acts on principal cells and intercalated cells, which are present in collecting ducts. It regulates ECF volume and Na+ content. Major stimulus for aldosterone secretion is Hyperkalemia. The functions of aldosterone are Na+ and H2O reabsorption, K+ and H+excretion.

Option A: Angiotensin II acts on efferent arteriole. It causes vasoconstriction increasing BP. It causes constriction of efferent arteriole, increases filteration fraction, preserving GFR when RBF ↓.

Option B: ADH acts on principal cells in collecting ducts. It primarily regulates serum osmolarity. Stimulates reabsorption of water in collecting ducts via Aquaporin-2.

Option D: ANP is released from atria and BNP is released from ventricles in response to ↑ volume, it inhibits RAAS, relaxes mesangial cells and promotes natriuresis.

questions.question: The areas associated with micturition reflex is/are ______________
questions.explanation:
The micturition center is located in the pons. The paracentral lobule is also associated with micturition.

The micturition reflex is an autonomic spinal cord reflex, but it can be inhibited or facilitated by centers in the brain.

These centers include-

• A strong facilitative and inhibitory centers in the brain stem, located mainly in the pons.

• Centers located in the cerebral cortex that are mainly inhibitory but can become excitatory.

questions.question: Hypoxia-induced factors stimulate ___________ cells of the kidney to initiate erythropoiesis.
questions.explanation:
Hypoxia induced factors stimulate interstitial cells to initiate erythropoiesis

Erythropoietin is produced by interstitial cells in the peritubular capillary bed of the kidney.

Erythropoietin inturn initiates erythropoiesis

questions.question: Choose the correct option mentioning the correct site of product conversion
questions.explanation:
Angiotensin 1 → angiotensin 2 @ lungs

Cholecalciferol → 25 hydroxy vitamin D3 @ liver

25 hydroxy vitamin D3 → 1,25 dihydroxy vitamin D3 @ Kidney

 Angiotensin I is converted to Angiotensin II by Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (ACE) which is expressed in the lungs.

questions.question: Ureteric peristalsis is mainly due to_____
options: Pacemaker activity of smooth muscles of renal pelvis
questions.answer: D. Pacemaker activity of smooth muscles of renal pelvis
questions.explanation:
Urine flowing from the collecting ducts into the renal calyces stretches the calyces and increases their inherent pacemaker activity, which in turn initiates peristaltic contractions occur­ring 1 to 5 times per minute that spread to the renal pelvis and then downward along the length of the ureter, thereby forcing urine from the renal pelvis toward the bladder.

• The walls of the ureters contain smooth muscle and are innervated by both sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, as well as by an intramural plexus of neurons and nerve fibers that extends along the entire length of the ureters.

• As with other visceral smooth muscle, peristaltic contractions in the ureter are

• Enhanced by parasympathetic stimulation

• Inhibited by sympathetic stimulation

questions.question: In micturition reflex, the first change to occur is_____
questions.explanation:
• One of the initial events is the relaxation of the muscles of the pelvic floor, and this may cause a sufficient downward tug on the detrusor muscle to initiate its contrac­tion.

• Micturition Reflex

• Micturition is fundamentally a spinal reflex facili­tated and inhibited by higher brain centers and is subject to voluntary facilitation and inhibition.

• These centers include

• strong facilitative and inhibitory centers in the brain stem, located mainly in the pons

• several centers located in the cerebral cortex that is mainly inhibitory but can become excitatory.

• The micturition reflex is the basic cause of micturition, but the higher centers normally exert final control of micturition.

• Micturition Reflex is the result of a stretch reflex initiated by sensory stretch receptors in the bladder wall, especially by the receptors in the posterior urethra when this area begins to fill with urine at the higher bladder pressures.

• Sensory signals from the bladder stretch receptors are conducted to the sacral segments of the cord through the pelvic nerves and then reflexively back again to the bladder through the parasympathetic nerve fibers by way of these same nerves. (refer figure)

• As the bladder continues to fill, the micturition reflexes become more frequent and cause greater contractions of the detrusor muscle.

• Once a micturition reflex begins, it is “self-regenerative.”

• It is a single complete cycle of

• The progressive and rapid increase of pressure,

• A period of sustained pressure, and

• Return of the pressure to the basal tone of the bladder.

• As the bladder becomes more and more filled, micturition reflexes occur more and more often and more and more powerfully.

• Once the micturition reflex becomes powerful enough, it causes another reflex, which passes through the pudendal nerves to the external sphincter to inhibit it. If this inhibition is more potent in the brain than the voluntary constrictor signals to the external sphincter, urination will occur. If not, urination will not occur until the bladder fills still further and the micturition reflex becomes more powerful.

questions.question: How much urine in the bladder will cause the first urge to void in a patient?
questions.explanation:
The first urge to void is felt at a bladder volume of about 150 mL, and a marked sense of fullness at about 400 mL.

Cystometrogram (refer figure)

A plot of intravesical pressure against the volume of fluid in the bladder is called a cystometrogram.

The curve shows

• An initial slight rise in pressure when the first increments in the volume are produced(Ia);

• A long, nearly flat segment as further increments are produced(Ib);

• A sudden, sharp rise in pressure as the micturition reflex is triggered(II).

• The flatness of segment Ib is a manifestation of the law of Laplace.

• This law states that the pressure in a spherical viscus is equal to twice the wall tension divided by the radius.

• P= 2T/R

• In the case of the blad­der, the tension increases as the organ fill but so does the radius. Therefore, the pressure increase is slight until the organ is relatively full.

questions.question: In a patient, pO2 is 85mmHg, pCO2 is 50mmHg, pH is 7.2, and HCO3- is 36mmol/L. Identify the condition.
options: Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis
Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic acidosis
questions.answer: A. Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
questions.explanation:
This patient has respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis.

pH is decreased (<7.35) so it is acidosis.

The CO2 levels are increased (>45mmHg), which is in line with the change in pH (in respiratory acidosis CO2 is expected to raise), thus the primary problem is respiratory.

The HCO3- levels are increased (>30mmol/L), which is opposite to change in pH (i.e there is acidosis and HCO3- levels are high), thus, there is compensatory metabolic alkalosis.

Thus, this is a case of respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis.

questions.question: A patient with salicylic acid poisoning has the following arterial blood gas analysis report: pH = 7.1, pCO2 =18mmHg, HCO3-=12mmol/L. Identify the acid-base disorder here.
options: Respiratory acidosis with compensatory metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis
questions.answer: A. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory alkalosis
questions.explanation:
The acid-base disorder here is a mixed disorder of metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

It should not be confused with metabolic acidosis with uncompensated respiratory alkalosis. This can be understood by the following calculation:

Step 1: The pH in this patient is 7.1 (pH <7.35) which indicates acidosis

Step 2: HCO3- is 12 mmol/L (Normal HCO3- - 22–30 mmol/L). In metabolic acidosis, HCO3- levels decrease.

Hence, this is a case of metabolic acidosis.

Step 3: As per Winter's formula, the expected respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis can be calculated using,

 pCO2 =( 1.5 x [HCO3-] ) +8 ± 2

In this case, Expected pCO2 = ( 1.5 x [12] ) +8 ± 2

 = 26 ± 2

 = 24 - 28 mmHg

The pCO2 in this patient is 18 mmHg, which implies there is an overcompensation of pCO2. This overcompensation can happen only if there is an additional component of respiratory alkalosis contributing to reduced pCO2.

Hence, this patient has a mixed disorder - metabolic acidosis and respiratory alkalosis.

questions.question: Which of the following patients will have metabolic alkalosis?
options: A patient with chronic renal failure who is recommended dialysis
A patient who was diagnosed with hyperaldosteronism
A patient who took a whole bottle of aspirin to get rid of the headache
questions.answer: C. A patient who was diagnosed with hyperaldosteronism
questions.explanation:
Metabolic alkalosis is seen in patients with hyperaldosteronism.

In hyperaldosteronism: increased aldosterone levels cause increased H+ secretion by the distal tubule and increased reabsorption of HCO3- → Metabolic alkalosis.

questions.question: In a patient with metabolic acidosis, which of the following changes are seen?
questions.explanation: K+ secretion into the renal tubules is decreased when the H+ secretion is increased (Intracellular Buffering of H+). Thus in metabolic acidosis, there is decreased K+ excretion.

questions.question: A normal anion gap metabolic acidosis occurs in patients with_____
questions.explanation:
Diarrhoea is a cause of normal anion gap metabolic acidosis produced as a result of increased HCO3- loss in feces.

This is because a decrease in HCO3- is replaced by an increase in the concentration of Cl-. This is a measurable anion and hence the anion gap is normal.

Extra - edge : Siggard-Anderson curve normogram is used to plot the acid-base composition of the blood

questions.question: Which of the following is secreted from acidophilic cells of pituitary?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone is secreted from acidophilic cells of anterior pituitary.

Acidophilic cells secrete growth hormone and prolactin.

Basophilic cells secrete TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is suffering from hypertension, buffalo hump and hyperpigmentation of the skin, including oral mucosa. He is diagnosed with Cushing syndrome due to pituitary cause. Which of the following is responsible for the hyperpigmentation seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
ACTH is more responsible than MSH for the hyperpigmentation seen in a patient with Cushing syndrome due to pituitary cause (ACTH hypersecretion).

ACTH is a derivative of POMC (Pro-opiomelanocortin). POMC is the precursor of ACTH, melanocyte­ stimulating hormone (MSH), β ­lipotropin and β ­endorphin. Since the melanocyte-stimulating hormone is the byproduct of ACTH synthesis from POMC, any disease process which leads to ACTH overproduction will also lead to an increased level of MSH. ACTH has mild MSH activity, hence elevated levels of ACTH acts on melanotropin-1 receptors causing generalized hyperpigmentation.

A similar manifestation will also be seen in Addison's disease where the ACTH level is high.

questions.question: A patient with a known brain tumour learns that his pituitary stalk has been affected. Secretion of which of the following hormones is increased after the sectioning of the pituitary stalk?
questions.explanation:
The secretion of prolactin is increased after the sectioning of the pituitary stalk.

Prolactin is unique among the pituitary hormones because the predominant central control mechanism is inhibitory, i.e., dopamine inhibits prolactin secretion. Hence, sectioning of the pituitary stalk (Ex: In head trauma or compressive skull lesions) prevents this inhibition and leads to increased secretion of prolactin.

Note:

If the pituitary stalk is cut above the pituitary gland but the entire hypothalamus is left intact, the posterior pituitary hormones (ADH & Oxytocin) show a transient decrease because they are initially synthesized in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus and are then transported down to the nerve endings to the posterior pituitary gland, requiring several days to reach the gland.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a cause of elevated prolactin level?
questions.explanation: L- Dopa is not a cause of increased prolactin level, it decreases prolactin secretion by increasing the formation of dopamine (prolactin inhibitory hormone).

questions.question: Which of the following is the effect of continuous GnRH administration?
questions.explanation:
Continuous GnRH administration suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary axis.

Pulsatile GnRH stimulates the pulsatile release of LH and FSH.

Note: Long-acting GnRH agonists are used to suppress gonadotropin levels in children with precocious puberty and in men with prostate cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following actions of GH is mediated by IGF–1?
questions.explanation:
Antilipolysis is mediated by IGF-1.

The actions of growth hormone-mediated via IGF-1 (somatomedin-C) are the indirect effects of growth hormone and include:

• Antilipolytic activity

• Insulin-like activity

• Protein synthesis

• Epiphyseal growth

The direct effects of GH include:

• Sodium retention

• Decreased insulin sensitivity

• Lipolysis

• Protein synthesis

• Epiphyseal growth

questions.question: GH has its effect on bone growth through______
questions.answer: D. Both directly and via IGF-1
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone (GH) has both direct and indirect effects on bone growth.

GH stimulates prechondrocytes to differentiate into chondrocytes. GH strongly stimulates osteoblasts and chondrocytes causing increased deposition of proteins → bone growth. GH also increases insulin-like growth factor (IGF) levels, which stimulate bone growth.

Note: The pygmies of Africa have a congenital inability to synthesize significant amounts of somatomedin C (IGF-I). Therefore, even though their plasma concentration of growth hormone is either normal or high, they have diminished amounts of IGF-I in the plasma, which accounts for the short stature. Some other dwarfs (e.g., the Levi-Lorain dwarf) also have this problem.

questions.question: Which of the following hormones demonstrates the fluctuations depicted below?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone demonstrates the depicted fluctuations. Growth hormone is secreted in a pulsatile fashion, with increase during strenuous exercise and during the early period of sleep, (Non-REM Sleep) as shown in the graph. It is reduced during the later stages of sleep. (REM sleep)

Other options:

Option A: ACTH levels are high in the early morning and low in the late evening.

Option C: TSH is secreted in pulses, but the fluctuations are less in comparison to other pituitary hormones because of the low amplitude of the pulses and the relatively long half-life of TSH.

Option D: Prolactin is secreted in a pulsatile fashion, with the highest secretory peak between 4:00 and 6:00 a.m. (REM Sleep)

questions.question: Growth hormone level is decreased in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Growth hormone(GH) level is decreased during deep sleep. Specifically, it is reduced during REM sleep as the levels of GHRH reduces and levels of cortisol are higher compared to slow wave sleep.

Hypoglycemia, fasting, and exercise cause an increase in GH secretion. GH levels are increased during non-REM sleep.

GH levels also decline with age and obesity.

questions.question: A 35 yr old man presents with hypertension, coarse facial features, frontal bossing, large hands and feet, mandibular enlargement and a large fleshy nose. His age-matched serum IGF-I levels are elevated. What is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acromegaly and is due to excess growth hormone (GH).

Acromegaly occurs when excessive GH is secreted after puberty (after fusion of long bone epiphysis). Features include

• Prognathism (protrusion of jaw), hypertrophy of frontal bones

• Acral enlargement in hands and feet (due to thickening of soft tissues)

• Visceromegaly: Enlargement of most organs especially the tongue, thyroid, salivary gland, liver, spleen, kidney, and prostate

Serious complications include cardiomyopathy with arrhythmias, diabetes mellitus, obstructive sleep apnoea, and increased risk of colonic polyps and cancer. Age-matched IGF-I levels are elevated.

questions.question: What does the neurohypophysis release?
questions.explanation:
The posterior pituitary or neurohypophysis releases oxytocin and anti-diuretic hormone (ADH or vasopressin)

Note: ADH and oxytocin are synthesised by the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei of the hypothalamus. Thereafter, they are stored and released from the posterior pituitary.

questions.question: Which pair of vasopressin receptors is incorrect?
questions.explanation:
The pair V4-CNS is incorrect.

Vasopressin mediates its effect via 3 kinds of receptors- V1a, V1b and V2. There is no V4.

questions.question: Sodium-iodide symport is absent in which of the following sites?
questions.explanation:
Sodium-iodide symport is absent in the pituitary.

Na+/I– symporter is present in

• Basolateral membranes of thyrocytes facing the capillar­ies.

• Salivary glands

• Gastric mucosa

• Placenta

• Ciliary body of the eye

• Choroid plexus

• Mammary glands

questions.question: A 35-year-old lady is diagnosed with Hashimoto thyroiditis and a positive antibody titer against thyroid peroxidase enzyme. Which of the following is not a function of the affected enzyme?
questions.explanation:
Iodide trapping (iodide uptake) is not catalyzed by thyroid peroxidase. Oxidation, organification, and coupling are catalyzed by it.

Steps in synthesis and secretion of thyroid hormone:

• Iodide uptake: The basolateral sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) actively takes up I-(iodide) from the circulation into the follicular cells. It is then transported into the colloid through a pendrin (chloride-iodide) transporter

• Thyroglobulin synthesis: Thyroglobulin (Tg), is a large glycoprotein rich in tyrosine residues. It is synthesized by follicular cells.

• Iodination of thyroglobulin: This is regulated by the thyroid peroxidase (TPO) enzyme. TPO has three functions:

• Oxidation: TPO oxidizes I- to I2 (iodine) in the presence of H2O2

• Organification: TPO links tyrosine residues of thyroglobulin with iodine (I2) to form monoiodotyrosine (MIT), diiodotyrosine (DIT)

• Coupling reactions: TPO combines iodinated tyrosine residues to make MIT + DIT = T3 (triiodothyronine), DIT + DIT = T4 (tetraiodothyronine)

• Storage: Thyroid hormones are bound to thyroglobulin and stored in the follicular lumen as colloids. The colloid has hormone reserves for 2-3 months

• Release: Iodinated thyroglobulin is taken up by the thyroid follicles via endocytosis and fuses with lysosomes. It is cleaved by lysosomal proteolytic enzymes into MIT, DIT, T3, and T4. T4 (80%) and T3 (20%) are released into the blood

• Peripheral T3 conversion: T4 undergoes deiodination in extrathyroidal tissue to form T3, which is the active form of the hormone

questions.question: A patient with hyperthyroidism is planned for thyroidectomy. In order to achieve a euthyroid status preoperatively, he is started on Lugol's iodine solution. Which of the following best describes its mechanism of action?
options: Inhibition of organification and synthesis of thyroid hormones
questions.answer: D. Inhibition of organification and synthesis of thyroid hormones
questions.explanation:
Introduction of exogenous iodine in the form of lugol's iodine solution leads to transient inhibition of organification and synthesis of thyroid hormones. This is known as the wolff-chaikoff effect.

In individuals with a normal thyroid, the gland escapes from this inhibitory effect and iodide organification resumes; but the suppressive action of high iodide may persist in patients with hyperthyroidism due to underlying autoimmune thyroid disease.

Note: Jod-Basedow effect is iodine-induced hyperthyroidism, usually occurring after the use of an I-based contrast agent. It is often seen in the presence of pre-existing thyroid conditions like multinodular goitre.

questions.question: How long is thyroxine stored in thyroid follicles?
questions.explanation:
Thyroxine is stored in the thyroid follicles for 2-3 months, bound to thyroglobulin.

Serves as a reserve of T3 and T4, thus delaying the occurrence of hypothyroidism, if thyroid secretion ceases.

questions.question: The major thyroxine-binding protein is _____.
questions.explanation:
Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the major thyroxine-binding protein.

Other thyroxine-binding proteins are:

• Albumin

• Transthyretin (TTR)/ thyroxine-binding pre-albumin (TBPA)

• Lipoproteins

questions.question: Which of the following is false regarding thyroid hormone?
options: T3 is more avidly bound to nuclear receptor than T4
T3 is more active than T4
T4 has shorter half- life than T3
questions.answer: D. T4 has shorter half- life than T3
questions.explanation:
T4 doesn't have a shorter half-life than T3, rather T3 has a shorter half-life and more rapid action than T4.

The table compares T4 and T3:

T3
T4

More potent (4x)
Less potent

Less active

Slow onset of action

Longer half-life (7 days)
